Gross margins have held between 37% and 44% and operating margins near 30% across twenty periods, and returns on equity have stayed between 29% and 45%. That kind of steadiness points to real pricing power and a durable moat. At about 12 times earnings, and with free cash flow near $9.28 a share against a price of roughly $103, you're getting close to a 9% cash yield on a business earning 38% on equity, and that's a wonderful business at a fair-to-attractive price. I'm not blind to the warts. Revenue has turned slightly negative, free cash flow per share has slipped from $12.09 to $9.28, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.67, apparently to fund buybacks, which is why book value per share has stalled. So I'd hold this with solid but not unbounded conviction, and keep an eye on whether the cash generation stabilizes.

This is a remarkably profitable enterprise. Gross margins run around 62%, net margins around 22%, the balance sheet carries almost no debt (D/E 0.03) and a current ratio above 5, and free cash flow per share (25.54) fully covers reported earnings (24.81). That is the signature of a real economic moat, and revenue is still growing about 15% a year. The ROE of around 14% understates the underlying economics because of the large pile of unleveraged capital. Once you adjust for what looks like a share split, book value per share has been compounding at a low double-digit rate. I would watch two things. Operating margins have slipped from about 32% to 26%, and at roughly 28 times earnings (a free cash flow yield near 3.5%) I am paying a full, though not foolish, price for a wonderful business. That makes me a willing but measured buyer rather than an enthusiastic one.

This is plainly a fine franchise that is losing altitude. Gross margin has slid from 78% to 62% and operating margin from 39% to 24%, which tells me the moat is being eroded, not widened. Revenue has now shrunk for four straight periods. Free cash flow per share, the thing I care most about, has gone essentially nowhere, about $2.87 then versus $3.12 now. Meanwhile debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.2 to 0.75 and book value per share has fallen, so management is leaning harder on the balance sheet to hold the numbers up. At roughly 27 times earnings and about 18 times free cash flow for a shrinking business with deteriorating economics, the price asks me to pay for a recovery I can't see in the figures.

This business once earned 27% on equity at under ten times earnings, but the trend has run the wrong way for three years. Return on equity has fallen to 8%, EPS has dropped from 9.82 to 3.11, and free cash flow per share has shrunk from about 5 to 0.70. Book value per share has not grown in roughly twelve periods, while debt-to-equity has tripled to 0.24 and the current ratio sits below 1, so management is not compounding owner capital. I can't name the moat here, and paying 28 times shrinking earnings for a manufacturer whose revenue fell 34% in the latest reported year asks you to bet on a recovery the numbers don't yet show.

This is a steady, understandable financial business. Revenue grows about 7-8% a year, net margins hold near 10-11%, earnings per share have climbed from about $7.28 to $9.94 over recent periods, and free cash flow runs consistently at $6-7 a share. The jump in share count and the -81% book-value CAGR look like a change in share basis, not a collapse in the business. Still, a return on equity of about 9% is respectable rather than wonderful, and recent book value growth of roughly 2-3% a year is no compounding machine. At about 14.5 times earnings and roughly 1.4 times book, the price is fair but offers no real margin of safety for a business earning single-digit returns on equity, so I'd be content to own it but not eager to back up the truck.

This is plainly a formidable retail franchise. Revenue is still growing about 26% a year on a very large base, and gross margin has climbed steadily from 23% to 34%. Free cash flow per share has risen from under a dollar to about $15, and leverage has fallen from 0.92 to 0.50 debt-to-equity, which tells me the economics are far better than the reported earnings suggest. But the price is about 189 times earnings and roughly 50 times free cash flow, with thin 3% operating margins and a 12% ROE that has only just appeared. That price assumes years of flawless execution, so I admire the business but cannot say I'm buying it at a sensible price.

This is plainly a high-quality franchise. Gross margins have held near 69% for twenty periods, net margins run around 22%, ROE sits in the low 20s, debt is modest at 0.32 of equity, and the current ratio is a comfortable 2.8, so the moat and the balance sheet look real. What gives me pause is that revenue has shrunk for three straight periods, EPS has stalled at about $5.50, and book value per share has compounded only about 3%, while the market has pushed the P/E from roughly 17.6 to 20.9. At about 21 times earnings, and with free cash flow near $5.23 a share (a yield of roughly 4.5%), I'd be paying a full price for a wonderful business that currently isn't growing, so I'd rather wait for either a lower price or evidence that the top line has turned.

This is a remarkable business on the numbers. Gross margins have widened from 73% to 85%, operating margins have reached 40%, revenue is still growing about 50% a year, and there is no debt with a current ratio above 12. Book value per share has compounded from about $6.76 to $17.54, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily. The headline ROE near 12% understates the economics, because a mountain of cash and acquisition equity is swelling the denominator. But I'm paying about 60 times earnings and roughly 48 times free cash flow for an advertising-driven technology franchise whose durability ten years out I can't predict with the confidence I'd want. A wonderful business, yes, but the price already assumes years of near-flawless growth, so I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than swing.

This is a heavily indebted business, with debt about twice equity, earning a mediocre return on equity of around 10% in its good years. It has recently strung together four periods of losses, while gross margin slid from the high 50s to 49% and book value per share fell from about $13.45 to $9.91. Free cash flow per share has eroded from roughly $2 to $0.75, and the market still prices it at 41 times depressed earnings and around a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield. That combination of a shrinking moat, heavy leverage and a full price is not what I want to own for ten years.

This looks like a capital-heavy communications franchise with sticky customers. But the numbers don't show a compounding machine: book value per share has grown about 1% a year across the whole record, ROE averages near 10%, and earnings keep getting knocked down by what look like large write-downs, with EPS swinging from roughly 3.40 to 0.66 and back. The recent 17% revenue jump, alongside a sudden rise in book value per share, suggests growth bought through a share-financed acquisition rather than earned. Debt at about 1x equity and a current ratio below 1 leave little margin for error. At roughly 16.5 times earnings and an FCF yield near 7%, the price isn't demanding, so I'd call it a fair business at a fair price and neither buy nor sell.

This is plainly a wonderful business. It has 62% gross margins, operating margins in the mid-20s and revenue still growing 17% a year, with almost no debt and a current ratio above 5. The reported 14% ROE understates the franchise, because it is weighed down by an enormous cash pile, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $17 to $29 over the last seven periods. But operating margins have slid from 32% to 26% over the period shown, so the business is spending heavily to keep growing. At 30 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3.6% leaves me paying for a great deal of future growth up front, and the split-distorted per-share history keeps me from judging owner compounding cleanly. So it is a wonderful company at a full price, and I would rather watch and wait for a better pitch than swing here.

This is a fine business by any owner's yardstick. Gross margins have held near 70% for twenty periods, returns on equity run in the low 20s, debt is modest at 0.36 times equity, and the current ratio is above 3. Earnings are consistent and free cash flow roughly matches reported profit, which tells me the moat is real. A wonderful company at a fair price is worth owning, but paying more each year for flat-to-declining earnings is not a bargain, so I'd hold my fire until either growth resumes or the price comes back to me.

Free cash flow per share has risen from under a dollar to about $15, and leverage has fallen from 0.92 to 0.50 debt-to-equity, which tells me the economics are far better than the reported earnings suggest. But the price is about 189 times earnings and roughly 50 times free cash flow, with thin 3% operating margins and a 12% ROE that has only just appeared. That price assumes years of flawless execution, so I admire the business but cannot say I'm buying it at a sensible price.

This is a fine business by any owner's yardstick. Gross margins have held near 70% for twenty periods, returns on equity run in the low 20s, debt is modest at 0.36 times equity, and the current ratio is above 3. Earnings are consistent and free cash flow roughly matches reported profit, which tells me the moat is real. What gives me pause is that revenue has shrunk in each of the last four periods and EPS has gone sideways around $5.40 for two years, yet the market has lifted the multiple from about 17.6 to 23 times earnings, leaving roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield. A wonderful company at a fair price is worth owning, but paying more each year for flat-to-declining earnings is not a bargain, so I'd hold my fire until either growth resumes or the price comes back to me.

This is a remarkable business on the numbers. Gross margins have widened from 73% to 85%, operating margins have reached 40%, revenue is still growing about 50% a year, and there is no debt with a current ratio above 12. Book value per share has compounded from about $6.76 to $17.54, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily. The headline ROE near 12% understates the economics, because a mountain of cash and acquisition equity is swelling the denominator. But I'm paying about 60 times earnings and roughly 48 times free cash flow for an advertising-driven technology franchise whose durability ten years out I can't predict with the confidence I'd want. A wonderful business, yes, but the price already assumes years of near-flawless growth, so I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than swing.

This business once earned a steady 10-12% on equity with gross margins near 60%. Over the last several years gross margins have slid to about 50%, and the company posted four straight periods of losses. Book value per share has shrunk from roughly $13.45 to $9.48, and free cash flow has gone from a reliable $1.40-1.90 a share to negative $0.28 in the latest period. That is not the record of a widening moat or of management compounding owners' capital. Leverage near 2x equity leaves little room for error, and paying 27 times earnings that have only just recovered prices in a turnaround the cash flows don't yet confirm, so I'd pass and wait for proof.

This looks like a big, capital-hungry network business. It earns about a 10% average return on equity, and book value per share has compounded at roughly 1% a year across twenty periods, which is not the record of a compounding machine. Debt runs about equal to equity with a current ratio under 1, and the recent 22% revenue jump plus the step-up in book value look bought through a large deal rather than grown organically. That gives me pause about capital allocation. On the other side, free cash flow of about $2.84 a share against a price near $43 is roughly a 6.6% yield, so the price doesn't demand perfection, but a fair price on a mediocre, leveraged business isn't enough for me to get excited.

This is a remarkably consistent franchise. Gross margins have held between 37% and 44% and operating margins near 30% across twenty periods, and returns on equity have stayed between 29% and 45%. That kind of steadiness points to real pricing power and a durable moat. At about 12 times earnings, and with free cash flow near $9.28 a share against a price of roughly $103, you're getting close to a 9% cash yield on a business earning 38% on equity, and that's a wonderful business at a fair-to-attractive price. I'm not blind to the warts. Revenue has turned slightly negative, free cash flow per share has slipped from $12.09 to $9.28, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.67, apparently to fund buybacks, which is why book value per share has stalled. So I'd hold this with solid but not unbounded conviction, and keep an eye on whether the cash generation stabilizes.

This is plainly a wonderful business. It has 62% gross margins, operating margins in the mid-20s and revenue still growing 17% a year, with almost no debt and a current ratio above 5. The reported 14% ROE understates the franchise, because it is weighed down by an enormous cash pile, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $17 to $29 over the last seven periods. But operating margins have slid from 32% to 26% over the period shown, so the business is spending heavily to keep growing. At 30 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3.6% leaves me paying for a great deal of future growth up front, and the split-distorted per-share history keeps me from judging owner compounding cleanly. So it is a wonderful company at a full price, and I would rather watch and wait for a better pitch than swing here.

At roughly 27 times earnings and about 18 times free cash flow for a shrinking business with deteriorating economics, the price asks me to pay for a recovery I can't see in the figures.

This is a business earning a 34% return on equity with 21% net margins and a gross margin that has held steady around 39-40% for years. Free cash flow of about $9.94 a share runs ahead of reported earnings of $8.39, which tells me the profits are real cash. At roughly 15 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of about 7-8%, the price is sensible for a franchise of this quality. The concerns are real but not fatal: revenue has shrunk for two periods, margins have slipped from their peak, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.66, most likely to fund buybacks, so I'd watch that leverage closely even while I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

This is a remarkably consistent business: net margins have held near 22% for years, revenue is still growing about 20%, debt is negligible at 0.03 debt-to-equity, and a 6.3 current ratio suggests a fortress of cash. Free cash flow of $37 a share against $28 of earnings shows real owner earnings, and at roughly 29 times earnings that works out to about a 4.6% free-cash yield on a business still compounding near 20%, which is a fair price for a wonderful company. My reservations are that operating margins have slipped from 32% to 26% and gross margin has eased from 65% to 61%. The modest 14% ROE also looks weighed down by all that idle capital, so I'd want to see management put the cash to work or return it. Even so, I'd be comfortable owning this for ten years.

This is a remarkably consistent business: net margins have held near 22% for years, revenue is still growing about 20%, debt is negligible at 0.03 debt-to-equity, and a 6.3 current ratio suggests a fortress of cash. This is a steady, large financial business, and the numbers are consistent. Net margins hold around 10%, revenue grows 5-10% a year, and book value per share has compounded at roughly 9% a year over the comparable recent periods. The -0.79 book value CAGR is plainly an artifact of a change in share basis, not real destruction of value. But an ROE stuck at 8-9% is ordinary for a business I'd want to own forever, and at about 18x earnings (roughly 1.4x book, from EPS 9.14, BVPS 118.71 and a P/E of 18.2) the market now pays more than it did a year or two ago, when it paid 14x for similar or better earnings. The FCF yield near 7.5% is respectable, and with no leverage data I can't fully judge financial strength, so I'd call this a fair price for a sound but unspectacular business and wait for a better pitch.

This is plainly a fine business. Gross margins have held near 70% for twenty periods, ROE runs in the low 20s, debt is modest at 0.46 of equity, a current ratio of 2.5 leaves plenty of liquidity, and free cash flow tracks reported earnings nearly dollar for dollar, which is the mark of real pricing power and honest accounting. My hesitation is that the growth engine has idled. Earnings per share are roughly where they were ten periods ago (5.70 then, 5.95 now), revenue grows only about 3%, and book value per share has barely compounded, yet the market has lifted the multiple from about 17.7 to 20.7 times earnings. At a free-cash-flow yield near 5%, I'd be paying a full price for a wonderful franchise that is currently standing still, so I'd hold my fire and wait for either renewed growth or a better price.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Gross margins have widened from 73% to 86%, operating margins sit at 45%, revenue is still compounding above 50% a year, and trailing EPS has climbed from about a penny to $3.93, with free cash flow keeping pace ($4.44 a share against $3.93 of EPS). The balance sheet is a fortress: no debt and a current ratio above 12. ROE of 19% is climbing even while the company sits on a mountain of cash, which tells me the operating business earns far higher returns than the headline suggests. Thirty-eight times earnings is no bargain, and a business built on advertising and attention sits closer to the edge of my circle of competence than I'd like. But with earnings growing this fast, the multiple has compressed from triple digits to something a patient owner can live with, so I'm constructive while respecting what I may not fully understand.

This business has gone backward. Gross margins have slid from about 62% to 50%, and book value per share has shrunk from $13.45 to $8.58, after a stretch of four loss-making periods that erased years of retained earnings. Free cash flow per share has swung from a steady $1.40–1.80 to negative $0.87, and debt still runs at 1.7 times equity, so the company is not generating the cash it would need to fix itself. Paying 30 times shrunken earnings, with revenue down 13% in the latest period, is paying for a recovery the numbers haven't shown yet, and I'd rather wait on the sidelines than bet on a turnaround.

This is an understandable, capital-heavy communications business with a real toll-bridge quality, but the numbers don't show a compounding machine. ROE averages about 10%, book value per share has crept up only about 3% a year, and gross margin has slipped. The recent jump in revenue growth came alongside a jump in book value and debt, which looks bought rather than earned. Debt runs about 1x equity, the current ratio sits below 1, and earnings have swung from $0.75 to $3.42 a share, so the business is not the steady, lightly levered franchise I prefer. That makes it a fair company at a fair-to-decent price rather than a wonderful one, so I'd watch rather than back up the truck.

ROE of 19% is climbing even while the company sits on a mountain of cash, which tells me the operating business earns far higher returns than the headline suggests. Thirty-eight times earnings is no bargain, and a business built on advertising and attention sits closer to the edge of my circle of competence than I'd like. But with earnings growing this fast, the multiple has compressed from triple digits to something a patient owner can live with, so I'm constructive while respecting what I may not fully understand.

This business has gone backward. Gross margins have slid from about 62% to 50%, and book value per share has shrunk from $13.45 to $8.58, after a stretch of four loss-making periods that erased years of retained earnings. Free cash flow per share has swung from a steady $1.40–1.80 to negative $0.87, and debt still runs at 1.7 times equity, so the company is not generating the cash it would need to fix itself. Paying 30 times shrunken earnings, with revenue down 13% in the latest period, is paying for a recovery the numbers haven't shown yet, and I'd rather wait on the sidelines than bet on a turnaround.

This is an understandable, capital-heavy communications business with a real toll-bridge quality, but the numbers don't show a compounding machine. ROE averages about 10%, book value per share has crept up only about 3% a year, and gross margin has slipped. The recent jump in revenue growth came alongside a jump in book value and debt, which looks bought rather than earned. Debt runs about 1x equity, the current ratio sits below 1, and earnings have swung from $0.75 to $3.42 a share, so the business is not the steady, lightly levered franchise I prefer. In its favor, free cash flow of roughly $2.88 a share is durable, and at about 15 times earnings the price is sensible, likely a FCF yield near 8%. That makes it a fair company at a fair-to-decent price rather than a wonderful one, so I'd watch rather than back up the truck.

This is a remarkably profitable enterprise. It has earned 29-45% on equity with net margins above 20% across the whole record, and free cash flow of $10.12 a share runs comfortably ahead of reported earnings of $8.58. That points to a real moat, even though gross margins have slipped from 44% to 38% and revenue has shrunk for four straight periods while EPS has stalled around $8.50. Debt/equity climbing from 0.14 to 0.73 while book value per share barely moved tells me management is borrowing to return capital. That is tolerable at these cash flows, but I'd watch it. At 17 times earnings, roughly a 7% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair rather than cheap after a big re-rating from under 10x. I'd own it for the durability of the franchise, but without the conviction I'd have if the top line were growing again.

This business earns a steady 61-62% gross margin and 26% operating margin quarter after quarter. Revenue growth has picked up from 13% to 22%, and there is essentially no debt, with a current ratio above 7. The reported 14% ROE understates the franchise because so much of the equity is idle cash. Free cash flow of about $40 a share against roughly $30 of EPS says the earnings are real. At 31 times earnings, or roughly a 4.3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full but not foolish price for a wonderful business compounding in the high teens, though the lack of dividends and a cash pile growing faster than it is deployed keep my conviction short of exceptional.

This is plainly a franchise business. It earns 20%-plus returns on equity with net margins near 20%, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $2.70 to $3.64 even as reported earnings stumbled. That cash generation tells me the moat hasn't been breached. But I can't ignore the other signals: gross margins have slid from 76% to 61%, revenue has gone nowhere for several years, and debt-to-equity has risen from under 0.2 to 1.2 while book value per share shrank. At 30 times earnings, or roughly 19 times free cash flow, I'm paying a full price for a business whose growth and economics are visibly changing, so I'd watch rather than buy today.

This business once earned 27-28% on equity with almost no debt. Over the past five years ROE has slid to 6%, EPS has fallen from about $9.50 to $2.40, and revenue has declined in every annual reading shown. Book value per share has sat near $41 for years, debt/equity has more than tripled to 0.24, and the current ratio remains below 1, so I see no compounding and a moat that appears to be eroding. The slight uptick in earnings and free cash flow at t-0 is welcome, but paying 34 times depressed earnings for a shrinking business is a bet on a turnaround, and I'd rather wait for proof than pay for hope.

This is a steady, large financial business, and the numbers are consistent. Net margins hold around 10%, revenue grows 5-10% a year, and book value per share has compounded at roughly 9% a year over the comparable recent periods. The -0.79 book value CAGR is plainly an artifact of a change in share basis, not real destruction of value. But an ROE stuck at 8-9% is ordinary for a business I'd want to own forever, and at about 18x earnings (roughly 1.4x book, from EPS 9.14, BVPS 118.71 and a P/E of 18.2) the market now pays more than it did a year or two ago, when it paid 14x for similar or better earnings. The FCF yield near 7.5% is respectable, and with no leverage data I can't fully judge financial strength, so I'd call this a fair price for a sound but unspectacular business and wait for a better pitch.

My hesitation is that the growth engine has idled. At a free-cash-flow yield near 5%, I'd be paying a full price for a wonderful franchise that is currently standing still, so I'd hold my fire and wait for either renewed growth or a better price.

EPS has sat around $5.90 for several periods and revenue is growing only 2%, yet debt/equity has climbed from 0.20 to 0.48 and the current ratio fell sharply from 2.52 to 1.34 in the latest period. At 22.6 times earnings, roughly a 4.8% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full price for a wonderful but slow-growing business with a weakening balance sheet, so I'd hold off rather than swing here.

Five years ago this business earned 27% on equity with almost no debt. Today it earns 7%, EPS has fallen from about $9.70 to $2.77, and revenue has declined in several periods, which is not what a durable moat looks like. Book value per share has crept from $36.57 to $42.29, a poor rate of compounding for owners, while debt/equity has tripled to 0.23 and the current ratio sits below 1. Free cash flow is recovering and earnings may have bottomed, but paying 29 times depressed earnings means betting on a return to past glory I can't verify from these numbers, so I'll pass.

This looks like a large, steady financial institution: net margins have climbed from about 17-19% to 27%, leverage has come down from roughly 1.5x to 1.2x debt/equity, and book value per share has compounded at about 7% a year with only one real earnings stumble. But a 10% return on equity is respectable, not wonderful. It tells me the business earns roughly its cost of capital rather than showing a wide moat with real pricing power. At 13.75 times earnings and about 1.26 times book, the market has already re-rated the shares from the 9-11x multiples of a few years back. So I'm paying a fair price for a fair business, and I'd want either a lower price or clearer evidence of rising returns before committing for the long haul.

This looks like a large, understandable lending franchise. But the trend worries me: EPS has sat flat near $4 for roughly three years, revenue growth has fallen to zero, ROE has drifted down from 13% to 11%, and debt-to-equity has climbed from about 1.1 to 1.63. At 13 times flat earnings and roughly 1.3 times book, I'd be paying a fair price for a business that is currently treading water. This is a remarkable economic engine. It has earned 30-45% on equity for five years straight, holds operating margins near 27-30%, and throws off free cash flow per share (9.84) that exceeds reported earnings (8.83). At roughly 17.8 times earnings, that is about a 6% free-cash-flow yield, a fair price for a business of this quality, though no longer the bargain it was at 10 times a year and a half ago. My reservations are real: revenue has barely grown for two years, gross margin has slipped from 44% to 39%, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.82, apparently to fund buybacks, since book value per share has gone nearly nowhere. Still, a wonderful business at a fair price is one I'd be content to own for a decade, provided management doesn't keep leaning on borrowed money to flatter per-share results.

This business grows revenue at roughly 20% a year while holding operating margins in the mid-20s and gross margins near 60%, which points to a real moat and pricing power. At about 35 times trailing earnings the price is not cheap, and the latest dip in operating margin from 26% to 23% bears watching. Still, free cash flow of about $36 a share on a roughly $970 share price is near a 4% yield growing close to 20%, which is a fair price for a wonderful business I'd be content to own for a decade.

This business sells mostly intangible products at 62% gross margins and earns 29% on equity. Free cash flow of $4.01 a share runs well ahead of reported earnings of $2.71, so at roughly 27 times earnings I'm really paying about 18 times owner earnings, a yield near 5.5%. That's a fair price for a franchise whose operating margin has climbed back from 17% to 25% and whose revenue has turned from shrinking to growing 5%. What keeps me from pounding the table: gross margin has slid from 75% to 62%, debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.2 to 1.2, and book value per share has barely budged because management is handing capital back rather than compounding it. Still, a current ratio near 2.5 and steadily rising free cash flow per share make this a wonderful business at a fair price that I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. But reported earnings are thin, with net margins of 1-2% and EPS falling from 5.31 to 3.93 in the latest period, so at a P/E near 260 and roughly 44 times free cash flow I'd be paying today for profits that management may keep reinvesting rather than harvesting. It's a wonderful business I admire, but at this price I can't say with confidence what it will earn in ten years, and a margin of safety is hard to find, so I'll watch rather than buy.

What gives me pause is that per-share earnings have gone essentially nowhere, hovering around $5.50-6.00 for about three years, while the P/E has expanded from roughly 18 to 24, debt/equity has more than doubled from 0.20 to 0.48, and the current ratio has dropped abruptly from about 2.5 to 1.3. At roughly a 4.8% free-cash-flow yield with low single-digit growth, I'd be paying a full price for a great franchise that the market has already recognized, so I'd happily own it but would rather wait for a better pitch.

This manufacturer once earned 27% on equity with almost no debt, but returns have slid to about 7%. Earnings per share fell from $9.70 to a trough of $1.88, and book value per share has barely moved in five years, so whatever moat existed has been badly tested. The recent upturn in both earnings and free cash flow ($3.57/share, back near earlier levels) is encouraging, and leverage is still modest. But at roughly 27 times depressed earnings and about 2 times book for a 7% return, I'm paying for a recovery that hasn't been proven. I'd want to see returns sustainably back in the high teens before calling this a wonderful business at a fair price.

This is a large, understandable lender. It has compounded book value at about 7% a year, cut leverage from roughly 1.5x to 1.2x debt/equity, and lifted net margins from the high teens to about 27%. Those are the marks of a steadier, better-run franchise. But a 10% return on equity is respectable rather than wonderful, and it doesn't show the durable pricing power I look for in a moat. At about 14.5x earnings and roughly 1.36x book, after the market cap climbed from 206B to 350B, the bargain has largely been harvested, so this is a fair company at a fair price rather than one I'd back up the truck for.

This looks like a big, understandable deposit-gathering franchise. It has earned 11-13% on equity for years and compounded book value per share at about 7%, which tells me the core business is sound and management has not been reckless. But the trend is going the wrong way: ROE has slipped from 13% to 10%, earnings per share have gone nowhere for roughly three years and dipped to $3.87, revenue has stalled, and net margin is edging down. At 14.6 times earnings and about 1.35 times book, I'd be paying a full price for a business that has stopped growing, so I'd rather wait until either the returns recover or the price comes down.

This is a wonderful economic engine. Returns on equity have held at 30-45% for twenty periods, net margins sit steady around 21-23%, and free cash flow per share (9.74) runs ahead of reported earnings, which is the kind of consistency only a real moat produces. What gives me pause is that per-share earnings are essentially flat versus eight periods ago (9.21 vs 9.22), and the multiple has expanded from about 10x to 18.7x, while debt/equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.86 to fund what looks like heavy buybacks, so I'm paying up for a business whose growth has recently stalled. Still, a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 5.6% on a franchise of this quality is a fair price rather than a demanding one, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, though not with the conviction I had at 10x.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Revenue has compounded around 20% a year for years, gross margins sit near 60%, net margins are about 20%, and there is essentially no debt alongside a current ratio near 6. The modest 13-14% ROE mostly reflects a mountain of retained cash rather than weak economics. But operating margins have slipped from 26% to 24%, and per-share earnings have grown only about 13% a year, well behind revenue. At 34 times earnings and roughly a 3.4% free-cash-flow yield, the price already pays generously for the moat, so I'd happily own it at a better price but won't stretch for it here.

This is a cash machine. Free cash flow per share of $4.14 comfortably exceeds reported EPS of $2.83, returns on equity have held in the mid-20s across most of the record, and after a stretch of shrinking revenue the top line is growing again at 7% while net margins have recovered to 24%. I don't love that gross margin has slid from 75% to 63%, or that debt/equity climbed from 0.2 to nearly 1.0, but a 3.1 current ratio says the balance sheet is liquid, and flat book value per share alongside rising EPS suggests capital is going back to owners rather than being squandered. At roughly 28 times earnings the headline price isn't cheap, but a free-cash-flow yield of about 5% for a business of this quality and durability is a fair price for a wonderful company, so I'd be a patient buyer, though not an aggressive one.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. Revenue has grown 20-27% a year for twenty straight periods, gross margin has climbed steadily from 25% to 36%, and free cash flow per share has gone from pennies to about $21. That tells me customers keep coming back and the business has real scale advantages. But reported owner earnings are thin: net margin is about 1%, ROE is 8%, and the stock trades at 280 times earnings and roughly 44 times the last reported free cash flow. On top of that, debt-to-equity just jumped from 0.38 to 1.05 in a single period, likely from a large acquisition I can't yet judge. I admire the business, but at this price I'm paying for a decade of perfection in advance, so I'll watch from the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This business shows the marks of a real moat: gross margins widened from 73% to 87%, operating margins climbed from about 10% to 48%, and revenue is still growing near 50% a year while earnings per share rose roughly fivefold in two years. The balance sheet is a fortress, with no meaningful debt, a current ratio above 13, and free cash flow per share of $5.32 that exceeds reported earnings, which tells me the profits are real cash. Book value per share has compounded steadily without leverage, and ROE has risen from single digits to 21% even as equity piled up, so management is reinvesting at attractive returns. At 35 times earnings the price is not cheap, and I'd want to watch for any slowing in growth. Still, the multiple has come down from over 100 while earnings have exploded, and for a business of this quality and growth that looks like a fair price for a wonderful company.

This is a large financial and insurance business that has never earned much on its equity. ROE has sat around 8-10% for years and has now slipped to 6%, while net margins compressed from 12% to 8% even as revenue grew 10-11%. That tells me growth is not reaching the owners, and trailing EPS has fallen from $10.34 to $7.57. Book value per share keeps compounding at a respectable 4-5% a year, and free cash flow per share has risen nicely to $13.38. But paying about 25 times shrinking earnings and roughly 1.5 times book for a 6% return on equity is paying for a recovery that isn't in the numbers yet, so I'd wait for either better economics or a better price.

On owner earnings the price is closer to 22x, about a 4.5% yield, on a business that is growing revenue again at 8%. I don't love the gross margin sliding from 75% to 63% or leverage rising to 1.14x equity, though a current ratio near 3 shows ample liquidity. This is a wonderful business at a fair, not cheap, price, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. Revenue has grown 20-27% a year for twenty straight periods, gross margin has climbed steadily from 25% to 36%, and free cash flow per share has gone from pennies to about $21. That tells me customers keep coming back and the business has real scale advantages. But reported owner earnings are thin: net margin is about 1%, ROE is 8%, and the stock trades at 280 times earnings and roughly 44 times the last reported free cash flow. On top of that, debt-to-equity just jumped from 0.38 to 1.05 in a single period, likely from a large acquisition I can't yet judge. I admire the business, but at this price I'm paying for a decade of perfection in advance, so I'll watch from the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This business shows the marks of a real moat: gross margins widened from 73% to 87%, operating margins climbed from about 10% to 48%, and revenue is still growing near 50% a year while earnings per share rose roughly fivefold in two years. The balance sheet is a fortress, with no meaningful debt, a current ratio above 13, and free cash flow per share of $5.32 that exceeds reported earnings, which tells me the profits are real cash. Book value per share has compounded steadily without leverage, and ROE has risen from single digits to 21% even as equity piled up, so management is reinvesting at attractive returns. At 35 times earnings the price is not cheap, and I'd want to watch for any slowing in growth. Still, the multiple has come down from over 100 while earnings have exploded, and for a business of this quality and growth that looks like a fair price for a wonderful company.

This is a large financial and insurance business that has never earned much on its equity. ROE has sat around 8-10% for years and has now slipped to 6%, while net margins compressed from 12% to 8% even as revenue grew 10-11%. That tells me growth is not reaching the owners, and trailing EPS has fallen from $10.34 to $7.57. Book value per share keeps compounding at a respectable 4-5% a year, and free cash flow per share has risen nicely to $13.38. But paying about 25 times shrinking earnings and roughly 1.5 times book for a 6% return on equity is paying for a recovery that isn't in the numbers yet, so I'd wait for either better economics or a better price.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have held near 69-70% for twenty periods, returns on equity sit steadily in the low twenties, and free cash flow per share has climbed to $6.75, all marks of a durable moat and real pricing power. What gives me pause is that per-share earnings have gone essentially nowhere, hovering around $5.50-6.00 for about three years, while the P/E has expanded from roughly 18 to 24, debt/equity has more than doubled from 0.20 to 0.48, and the current ratio has dropped abruptly from about 2.5 to 1.3. At roughly a 4.8% free-cash-flow yield with low single-digit growth, I'd be paying a full price for a great franchise that the market has already recognized, so I'd happily own it but would rather wait for a better pitch.

This manufacturer once earned 27% on equity with almost no debt, but returns have slid to about 7%. Earnings per share fell from $9.70 to a trough of $1.88, and book value per share has barely moved in five years, so whatever moat existed has been badly tested. The recent upturn in both earnings and free cash flow ($3.57/share, back near earlier levels) is encouraging, and leverage is still modest. But at roughly 27 times depressed earnings and about 2 times book for a 7% return, I'm paying for a recovery that hasn't been proven. I'd want to see returns sustainably back in the high teens before calling this a wonderful business at a fair price.

This is a large, understandable lender. It has compounded book value at about 7% a year, cut leverage from roughly 1.5x to 1.2x debt/equity, and lifted net margins from the high teens to about 27%. Those are the marks of a steadier, better-run franchise. But a 10% return on equity is respectable rather than wonderful, and it doesn't show the durable pricing power I look for in a moat. At about 14.5x earnings and roughly 1.36x book, after the market cap climbed from 206B to 350B, the bargain has largely been harvested, so this is a fair company at a fair price rather than one I'd back up the truck for.

This looks like a big, understandable deposit-gathering franchise. It has earned 11-13% on equity for years and compounded book value per share at about 7%, which tells me the core business is sound and management has not been reckless. But the trend is going the wrong way: ROE has slipped from 13% to 10%, earnings per share have gone nowhere for roughly three years and dipped to $3.87, revenue has stalled, and net margin is edging down. At 14.6 times earnings and about 1.35 times book, I'd be paying a full price for a business that has stopped growing, so I'd rather wait until either the returns recover or the price comes down.

This is a wonderful economic engine. Returns on equity have held at 30-45% for twenty periods, net margins sit steady around 21-23%, and free cash flow per share (9.74) runs ahead of reported earnings, which is the kind of consistency only a real moat produces. What gives me pause is that per-share earnings are essentially flat versus eight periods ago (9.21 vs 9.22), and the multiple has expanded from about 10x to 18.7x, while debt/equity has climbed from 0.14 to 0.86 to fund what looks like heavy buybacks, so I'm paying up for a business whose growth has recently stalled. Still, a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 5.6% on a franchise of this quality is a fair price rather than a demanding one, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, though not with the conviction I had at 10x.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Revenue has compounded around 20% a year for years, gross margins sit near 60%, net margins are about 20%, and there is essentially no debt alongside a current ratio near 6. But operating margins have slipped from 26% to 24%, and per-share earnings have grown only about 13% a year, well behind revenue. At 34 times earnings and roughly a 3.4% free-cash-flow yield, the price already pays generously for the moat, so I'd happily own it at a better price but won't stretch for it here.

That kind of consistency, even through a stretch of shrinking revenue, tells me customers keep paying up and the moat is real. At roughly 16.5 times earnings, with free cash flow of about $10.22 a share against a price near $160 (a free-cash-flow yield above 6%), I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business. My reservations are that per-share earnings have only crept up from about $9.22 to $9.74 over nine periods, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.13 to 0.87, apparently to fund buybacks, so I'd watch that leverage. This is a remarkable economic engine. Revenue is still growing better than 20% a year, operating margins have held around 24-26% for twenty periods, debt is negligible at 0.03 debt-to-equity, and a current ratio above 5 means it is swimming in cash. The latest drop in net margin to 11%, with operating margin unchanged, looks like a one-time charge below the operating line rather than any erosion of the franchise. On normalized earnings of roughly $30 a share, the true multiple is in the mid-30s, not 59, and the free cash flow yield is about 3%. That is a full price, but not a foolish one for a business compounding at this rate. My hesitations are the modest 14% ROE, which is depressed by a mountain of idle cash, and a slight slide in gross margin, so I'd own it with conviction tempered by the price paid.

This is plainly a formidable retail franchise. Revenue is still compounding at better than 25% a year at enormous scale, gross margin has widened steadily from 25% to 37%, and book value per share has more than tripled. That combination tells me customers keep coming back and the business is gaining pricing power in its mix. But reported owner earnings are thin: a 2% net margin, ROE that has only just reached 11%, a recent jump in leverage to 0.90 debt-to-equity, and free cash flow per share no longer shown in the data. At 232 times earnings I would be paying for a decade of flawless execution up front, so I admire the business and stand aside on the price.

These are extraordinary economics. Gross margins have widened from 73% to 87% and operating margins from 10% to 50%, with no debt and a current ratio near 13. Revenue is still growing about 47% a year, and book value per share has roughly quadrupled while free cash flow per share climbed from $0.31 to $5.91, which tells me the moat is widening, not eroding. A 21% ROE carried on a balance sheet stuffed with cash understates the true return on the operating assets. At 36 times earnings and about a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying up, but for a business compounding like this it's a fair price rather than a demand for perfection. My main reservation is that I can't see from these numbers how durable the product's grip on its users is over ten years.

The apparent collapse in book value per share is an artifact of a change in share basis around t-13, not real destruction. On a consistent basis, book value per share rose from 97.45 to 141.16 over twelve periods, roughly 13% a year, and it did not decline in any period. Free cash flow per share has roughly doubled, from 6.83 to 13.81, which puts the stock near a 6.6% free-cash-flow yield at about 1.5 times book. That is a fair price for a steady insurance-and-finance compounder, even though reported ROE averages only about 9% and the latest 18.21 EPS looks swollen by non-recurring gains, so the 11.6x P/E flatters it. Without balance-sheet leverage data I can't fully judge financial strength, but consistent earnings, rising book value and a sensible price make this a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade, with moderate conviction.

This business has earned 20-23% on equity for twenty straight periods with gross margins pinned near 69-70%, which is the signature of a real moat and pricing power. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $4.15 to $6.48. The latest period's collapse in reported EPS to $0.47 looks like a large one-time charge, since cash generation didn't flinch. Still, it cut book value per share from $27.54 to $22.42, and together with debt/equity rising from roughly 0.2-0.3 to 0.60 and the current ratio sliding from about 2.5 to 1.4, it tells me the balance sheet is carrying more weight than it used to. At roughly $130 a share, the price is about 22-23 times normalized earnings and about 20 times free cash flow, a fair price for a wonderful franchise growing slowly. I'd be a willing owner, but not a table-pounder until I know that charge isn't the first of several.

This is a cyclical manufacturer, not a franchise. ROE slid from 27% to 5% before recovering to 11%, net margins swing between 4% and 8%, and book value per share has compounded at only about 4% a year. That tells me the business earns roughly its cost of capital over a cycle rather than enjoying durable pricing power. The balance sheet is sensible at 0.22 debt/equity, though a current ratio persistently below 1 is worth watching. Free cash flow has recovered nicely to $3.45 a share, and at roughly 1.7x book and 16x recovering earnings the price is fair but not a bargain, so I'd watch rather than buy.

This looks like a large, steady financial institution. Its margins are consistent around 25%, but its return on equity is stuck near 10%, which is respectable but not the mark of a business with a wide moat. Book value has compounded at about 7% a year, yet it has stalled lately (74.47 to 74.50), and trailing EPS just slipped from 6.93 to 6.31. Meanwhile the market has rerated the shares from about 9x to 18.6x earnings, roughly 1.6x book. At that price I'd be paying a full multiple for an average-return business, so I'll stay on the sidelines rather than bet against it.

My main reservation is that a business growing this fast in a young industry is harder to forecast ten years out than a candy company, so I hold back from full conviction.

The recent dips in net margin look like one-time charges, since operating margin has barely moved, but other trends give me pause: gross margin has eroded about three points and free cash flow per share has fallen from roughly $40 to $30 even as sales grew. At about 43 times reported and the mid-30s on normalized earnings, with a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a full price for a great company whose spending is rising, so I'd admire it from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a high-quality franchise. Gross margins have held above 60% for five years, operating margins have climbed back from 17% to 26%, and free cash flow per share has risen steadily from about $2.68 to $4.30 even through a stretch of shrinking revenue, which is the mark of a durable moat. The headline P/E of 64 looks alarming, but net margin halved while operating margin held steady, which suggests a one-time charge rather than a weaker business. On owner earnings the price works out to roughly 22 times free cash flow, about a 4.6% yield with revenue growing 8% again. Leverage has crept up to about 1:1 debt to equity and book value per share has barely grown, likely because capital is going to buybacks, so I'll call this a wonderful business at a fair price rather than a bargain.

This retailer shows real signs of a widening moat. Gross margin climbed steadily from 26% to 38%, revenue growth has sped up to 36%, book value per share compounded about 29% a year, and free cash flow per share rose from under $1 to about $21 before the data stops. But reported net margins of 1-2% and a 13% ROE don't yet prove the durable earning power I like to pay for, and the free cash flow figures are missing for the last four periods. At roughly 200 times earnings the price assumes years of flawless execution, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines rather than swing at a pitch I can't value with confidence.

This business keeps 86 cents of every revenue dollar as gross profit and half as operating profit, carries essentially no debt and holds nearly ten times its current liabilities in current assets. That kind of economics usually signals a powerful franchise with real pricing power, and the numbers get better each year: ROE has climbed from 5% to 23%, and per-share book value, earnings and free cash flow have all compounded strongly. At about 29 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share above reported EPS, the price is not cheap in the old-fashioned sense. But for a debt-free business still growing revenue over 40% with widening margins, it looks like a wonderful company at a fair price. My main reservation is that a business growing this fast in a young industry is harder to forecast ten years out than a candy company, so I hold back from full conviction.

The apparent collapse in book value per share is an artifact of a change in share basis around t-13, not real destruction. On a consistent basis, book value per share rose from 97.45 to 141.16 over twelve periods, roughly 13% a year, and it did not decline in any period. Free cash flow per share has roughly doubled, from 6.83 to 13.81, which puts the stock near a 6.6% free-cash-flow yield at about 1.5 times book. That is a fair price for a steady insurance-and-finance compounder, even though reported ROE averages only about 9% and the latest 18.21 EPS looks swollen by non-recurring gains, so the 11.6x P/E flatters it. Without balance-sheet leverage data I can't fully judge financial strength, but consistent earnings, rising book value and a sensible price make this a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade, with moderate conviction.

This business has earned 20-23% on equity for twenty straight periods with gross margins pinned near 69-70%, which is the signature of a real moat and pricing power. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $4.15 to $6.48. The latest period's collapse in reported EPS to $0.47 looks like a large one-time charge, since cash generation didn't flinch. Still, it cut book value per share from $27.54 to $22.42, and together with debt/equity rising from roughly 0.2-0.3 to 0.60 and the current ratio sliding from about 2.5 to 1.4, it tells me the balance sheet is carrying more weight than it used to. At roughly $130 a share, the price is about 22-23 times normalized earnings and about 20 times free cash flow, a fair price for a wonderful franchise growing slowly. I'd be a willing owner, but not a table-pounder until I know that charge isn't the first of several.

This is a cyclical manufacturer, not a franchise. ROE slid from 27% to 5% before recovering to 11%, net margins swing between 4% and 8%, and book value per share has compounded at only about 4% a year. That tells me the business earns roughly its cost of capital over a cycle rather than enjoying durable pricing power. The balance sheet is sensible at 0.22 debt/equity, though a current ratio persistently below 1 is worth watching. Free cash flow has recovered nicely to $3.45 a share, and at roughly 1.7x book and 16x recovering earnings the price is fair but not a bargain, so I'd watch rather than buy.

This looks like a large, steady financial institution. Its margins are consistent around 25%, but its return on equity is stuck near 10%, which is respectable but not the mark of a business with a wide moat. Book value has compounded at about 7% a year, yet it has stalled lately (74.47 to 74.50), and trailing EPS just slipped from 6.93 to 6.31. Meanwhile the market has rerated the shares from about 9x to 18.6x earnings, roughly 1.6x book. At that price I'd be paying a full multiple for an average-return business, so I'll stay on the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This looks like a big lender. It has earned double-digit returns on equity for years, with net margins steady around 25%, and book value per share has compounded from about $30.60 to $42.42. That is the mark of a real franchise, not a flash in the pan. But the engine has stalled: earnings per share are $4.10 today, the same as three years ago, revenue growth is essentially zero, ROE has slipped from 13% to 11%, and leverage has crept up from roughly 1.1x to 1.6x debt/equity. At about 14 times earnings and roughly 1.35 times book, I'd be paying a fair price for a good business whose returns are eroding. That is not a wonderful business at a fair price, so I'll wait for either a cheaper price or evidence that earnings are growing again.

This is a remarkably steady money machine. Across twenty periods gross margins have held near 38-40% and net margins near 21-23%, and returns on equity have run 30-45%. That kind of consistency, even through a stretch of shrinking revenue, tells me customers keep paying up and the moat is real. At roughly 16.5 times earnings, with free cash flow of about $10.22 a share against a price near $160 (a free-cash-flow yield above 6%), I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business. My reservations are that per-share earnings have only crept up from about $9.22 to $9.74 over nine periods, and debt-to-equity has climbed from 0.13 to 0.87, apparently to fund buybacks, so I'd watch that leverage. Even so, I'd be comfortable owning this for ten years.

This is a large, steady insurance-and-finance enterprise. Over the comparable recent stretch, from t-13 to t-0, book value per share has compounded from about $97 to $141, roughly 12% a year. Returns on equity are only modest at 9-13%, which is no spectacular moat on paper. At about 12 times earnings and roughly 1.4 times book, you're paying a fair price for a durable compounder, so I'd lean in, tempered by the lumpiness of recent earnings, flat revenue growth at t-0 and the lack of leverage data.

This business has earned roughly 20-23% on equity with gross margins near 70% for about twenty periods, which is the mark of a real moat and pricing power. The collapse in reported EPS to $0.46 and the P/E of 274 look like a large one-off charge rather than broken economics. Free cash flow per share actually rose to $6.72, the highest in the series, and revenue growth has picked up to 9%. At an implied price of about $126, I'm paying roughly 19x free cash flow and about 21x normalized earnings, a fair price for a wonderful company. I temper my conviction because book value per share has gone nowhere, debt/equity has roughly doubled from 0.2-0.3 to about 0.5, and I can't tell from these numbers alone whether that charge is truly non-recurring.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer. Earnings per share fell from nearly $8 to under $2 and have only climbed back to $4.77, while book value per share has crept from about $38 to $44 over five years, roughly 4% a year. That is not the record of a business with durable pricing power. The balance sheet is sensible at 0.22 debt-to-equity, and free cash flow has recovered to about $3.41 a share. But a current ratio below 1, ROE of 11% against a past near 20%, and revenue swings of -34% and +18% tell me I'm buying the cycle rather than a moat. At 16 times recovering earnings and roughly a 4.5% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair, not a bargain, so I'd stand aside rather than bet either way.

This looks like a large, steady financial institution. ROE has held near 10% for five years, net margins sit in the mid-20s, book value per share has compounded about 7% a year, and it came through a soft patch (ROE dipping to 7-8%) without losing ground. The trouble is that the price has run ahead of the business. The market cap has nearly doubled from about $206B while earnings per share rose only from roughly $6.00 to $7.03, so the P/E has expanded from about 9 to 15. At roughly 1.4 times book for a business earning 10% on equity, I'd be paying a fair price for a decent, not wonderful, franchise. I'd be content to own it, but I'd rather wait for the kind of pricing Mr. Market offered a few years back.

This looks like a large, steady financial institution. This is a remarkable business in the making. This is plainly a formidable franchise: revenue is still growing about 24% a year at this scale, gross margins sit near 57%, and there is essentially no debt (D/E 0.02) and a current ratio above 4. This business has compounded book value per share at about 31% a year with no debt. It earns 84% gross margins and turns better than a third of revenue into net profit, all while still growing revenue above 40%. The market has marked it down from roughly $561B to $436B, taking the multiple from 36x to about 23x earnings. The reported -79% book value CAGR is almost certainly an artifact of a change in per-share basis. On a consistent basis, book value per share has compounded steadily from about 97 to 145 over the recent periods, which is the mark of patient, sensible capital allocation in a large insurance-anchored financial business. Returns on equity near 9-13% are respectable rather than spectacular, and reported earnings swing around (P/E from 25 down to 11), likely reflecting investment gains and losses. At roughly 1.4 times book, about 11 times trailing earnings and a free cash flow yield near 4-5%, I'm paying a fair price for a durable, conservatively financed compounder I'd be comfortable holding for a decade. The missing leverage and balance-sheet data keep my conviction short of high.

This business once earned 19-20% on equity. It then fell into a deep trough, with EPS dropping from about $7.95 to $1.88 and revenue down 34% in one period, before recovering to $4.91 and an 11% ROE. That kind of swing tells me it is cyclical and has no durable moat that protects earnings. Book value per share has compounded only about 3% a year, and a current ratio around 0.8 bears watching, though debt at 0.22 of equity is modest and free cash flow has recovered to about $3.17 a share. At roughly 16 times recovering earnings and about a 4% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair but offers no margin of safety for a business whose returns have proven this unreliable, so I'd stand aside rather than swing.

For two decades of reported periods this business earned 20%-plus on equity with gross margins near 70% and steady, rising free cash flow. That is the signature of a real moat. Over the last four periods reported earnings collapsed to a 2% margin and book value per share fell from about $27.5 to $22–24, yet free cash flow per share held steady at roughly $6.70–6.80 and revenue growth actually improved to around 9%. That pattern suggests a large non-cash charge, a write-down or a restructuring, rather than a broken franchise, though the data doesn't tell me which. Judged on cash earnings, the price is about 20 times free cash flow, roughly a 5% yield, which is fair for a durable business with modest debt. The book-value write-down is a black mark on past capital allocation and is why my conviction is only moderate.

That pattern suggests a large non-cash charge, a write-down or a restructuring, rather than a broken franchise, though the data doesn't tell me which. Judged on cash earnings, the price is about 20 times free cash flow, roughly a 5% yield, which is fair for a durable business with modest debt. The book-value write-down is a black mark on past capital allocation and is why my conviction is only moderate.

This looks like a large, diversified lender that has come through a rough patch. Earnings per share have climbed steadily from $0.36 to $2.11, net margin has recovered from 6% to 26%, and leverage has come down from roughly 2x debt-to-equity to about 1x. Returns on equity of 9% are still only middling for a bank, and book value has compounded at just 4% a year, so this is not yet a wonderful franchise by my yardsticks. But at about 12.6 times earnings, and a price near book value of roughly $26.60 a share, I'm paying a fair price for a strengthening balance sheet and rising profitability, which is enough to make me a patient owner.

This is a remarkably steady franchise. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and operating margins at 26-30% across twenty periods, including a stretch when revenue shrank 8%, and that kind of stability tells me customers pay up and keep coming back. Management is shrinking the share count aggressively, which is why book value per share looks flat while EPS has doubled from 6.00 to 12.20 and FCF per share has climbed from 7.59 to 12.98. The high ROE therefore reflects both real earning power and a thinner equity base. I'd watch debt/equity, which has crept from 0.14 to 0.97, but with a 1.3 current ratio and roughly $13 a share of free cash flow it looks manageable. At 13.5 times earnings and about a 7% free-cash-flow yield, down from a 16-18x multiple a year earlier, this looks like a wonderful business at a fair-to-attractive price, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a remarkable business in the making. Gross margin has climbed steadily from 27% to 40%, revenue is still compounding above 30% a year, ROE has risen from losses to 23%, book value per share has more than tripled, and free cash flow of $26.53 a share outruns reported earnings of $17.86, which tells me the accounting is conservative rather than flattering. But at 92 times earnings and roughly 60 times free cash flow, I'm paying today for a decade of flawless execution. The reported 1% average net margin means the moat is visible mainly in gross economics and cash flow rather than in bottom-line history, which makes future owner earnings hard for me to pin down. So I'd call it a wonderful company at a price that leaves little margin of safety, and I'd rather watch than buy here.

This is plainly a formidable franchise: revenue is still growing about 24% a year at this scale, gross margins sit near 57%, and there is essentially no debt (D/E 0.02) and a current ratio above 4. That is a fortress balance sheet and the mark of a real moat. But the trend lines trouble me. Operating margin has slid from 26% to 20% and net margin from about 22% to 14%, and free cash flow per share has fallen from roughly $40 to $33 even as sales keep climbing, which tells me heavy reinvestment or rising costs are eating the growth. At about 40 times earnings and roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, with ROE only around 11% because of the idle cash pile, I'd be paying a wonderful-company price while the numbers are moving the wrong way. So I'll watch rather than buy.

This business has kept gross margins in the 61-70% range through every period shown, and operating margins have climbed from the low 20s back to 33% while revenue growth has accelerated to 16%. That tells me the moat is intact and pricing power is real. Reported earnings have been lumpy, with the dip at t-3 and t-4 and the jump to $4.31 at t-0 looking like one-time items. This business earns 40% net margins and 83% gross margins with no debt and a current ratio above 7. ROE has climbed from 7% to 26% without leverage, which points to a real economic franchise rather than financial engineering. Book value per share has compounded rapidly, revenue is still growing 37%, and the P/E has come down from over 100 to about 22, a fair price for a business of this quality and growth. I am tempering my enthusiasm for two reasons: operating margins have slipped from 50% to 45%, and free cash flow per share has fallen from 6.36 to 5.26 even as EPS rose, which tells me reinvestment needs are climbing. I'd want to understand the durability of this franchise better before making it a core holding, but on the numbers this is a wonderful business at a sensible price.

This looks like a diversified financial and insurance enterprise whose book value per share has compounded from about 97 to 153 over the last sixteen periods, roughly 12% a year. The reported -0.79 book value CAGR is plainly a unit break in the older data, not a collapse, so I've disregarded it. At roughly 1.4 times book and a P/E near 8.6, the price looks sensible for a business that keeps compounding owner capital without visible strain. My caution is that recent ROE of 16% and a 25% net margin are likely flattered by investment gains that won't repeat, while free cash flow per share has slipped from about 13.8 to 8.7. So I'd judge it on steady book value growth, not headline earnings, and on that basis I'm a willing but not exuberant owner.

This looks like a big, steady financial franchise. Book value per share has compounded at about 7% a year without a single down period, and earnings per share have nearly doubled from $4.35 to $8.09 as net margins widened from 19% to 28% and revenue growth turned from shrinking to 7%. Leverage has come down from 1.54 to 1.29, which is sensible for a lender. At about 13.5 times earnings and roughly 1.4 times book, I'm paying a fair price for an 11% ROE business that is improving. That isn't a spectacular moat by my standards, and with a bank the opacity of the balance sheet always tempers my conviction, but it's a durable business at a reasonable price.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer. Earnings per share ran near $7.50–8.00, fell to $1.88 at the trough, and have recovered to $5.44, with returns on equity swinging between 5% and 19%. That pattern looks like a business at the mercy of its cycle rather than one with pricing power, and missing margin data keeps me from confirming any moat. The balance sheet is sensible, with debt at about 0.2 times equity, and free cash flow has climbed back to about $3.94 a share. But book value has compounded at only about 2% a year, and I can't tell from these figures whether that reflects generous payouts or a lack of worthwhile reinvestment. A current ratio under 1 is another thing I'd want explained. At roughly 15 times recovering earnings the price is fair but not a bargain for a business this cyclical, so I'd sit on my hands.

This is a formidable franchise. Revenue has grown 20% or more a year for years, net margins sit around 20%, there is essentially no debt and the current ratio is near 4. That combination of fortress balance sheet and steady growth speaks to a real moat, and book value per share has compounded at about 14%. The reported ROE of 13-17% understates the economics because a mountain of idle capital sits on the balance sheet. At about 26 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3%, I'd call it a wonderful business at a fair, not bargain, price. I'd own it, but with measured rather than full conviction.

This looks like a large, diversified insurance and finance business whose reported earnings swing with the market value of its investment portfolio. The t-0 P/E of 124 and ROE of 1% look like mark-to-market accounting noise, since free cash flow per share held steady at about $9.29. The -0.80 book value CAGR is an artifact of a change in share basis; on a consistent basis, book value per share grew from about $97 to $142 over the last 16 periods, roughly 9-10% a year, with steady FCF. At about 1.4 times book and an FCF yield near 4.6%, I'm paying a fair price for a durable compounder. Returns on equity of around 9-10% are sound rather than spectacular, so my conviction is moderate rather than high.

This looks like a large, well-run financial institution whose earnings power has steadily improved. ROE has climbed from about 7% to 13%, net margins have widened from 17% to 30%, and EPS has more than doubled from $3.90 to $9.00. Book value per share has compounded about 7% a year while earnings rose, so management is growing intrinsic value and returning capital rather than piling on leverage, with debt/equity holding in a sensible 1.2-1.5 range. At roughly 11.7 times earnings and about 1.3 times book for a business now earning 13% on equity, I'm paying a fair price for a durable franchise, though as with any bank I'm trusting the balance sheet more than I can see it from these figures.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer. Earnings per share went from $7.95 down to $1.88 and back to about $4.90, and that swing tells me it has no durable pricing power. Book value per share has crept from roughly $41 to $45 over the whole period, about 2% a year, and average ROE of 11% is ordinary rather than the mark of a moat. On the plus side, leverage is modest at 0.20 debt-to-equity and free cash flow has recovered to about $3.85 a share. Even so, a current ratio below 1 and a P/E of 16 on mid-cycle earnings leave no bargain here, so I'd call it a fair business at a fair price and pass until the price or the returns improve.

This is a business with gross margins near 70% and returns on equity in the low-20s for the better part of five years, and the cash kept coming even when reported earnings collapsed to about $0.50 a share for four periods. Free cash flow per share held near $6.70-6.80 throughout, which tells me that dip was a large non-cash charge rather than a broken franchise, and FCF per share has compounded from roughly $5 to $6.79. At about 24 times restored earnings and a free cash flow yield near 5%, with revenue growing again at 7-11%, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business, which is a trade I'll gladly make. My enthusiasm is tempered by debt/equity climbing from 0.20 to 0.55, book value per share shrinking, gross margin slipping about two points, and not knowing what caused that big charge or whether it will recur.

This is a large, leveraged financial institution. What I understand is that it has spent years digging out of a hole: ROE has climbed from about 2% to 11%, net margin from 6% to 31%, and EPS from $0.36 to $2.61. Debt-to-equity has also come down from around 2x to under 1x, which tells me management has been repairing the balance sheet rather than chasing growth. At roughly 11 times earnings and only about 1.07 times book (price near $29 against $27.47 BVPS), I'm paying a fair price for a business whose earning power is plainly recovering. The caveats are that book value per share has compounded only slowly and a bank's fortunes hinge on credit discipline I can't fully see from these figures, so my conviction is solid but not exceptional.

But at 81 times earnings and roughly 47 times free cash flow, a free-cash-flow yield of about 2%, the price already assumes many more years of this performance. A wonderful company is only a wonderful investment at a sensible price, so I'd admire this one and wait for a better pitch.

This is a cash machine. Revenue is still compounding above 20% a year, net margins sit near 20%, debt is almost nonexistent at 0.02 debt/equity, and a current ratio near 4 means the balance sheet is a fortress. The ROE of 13-15% looks ordinary, but I read that as a mountain of idle cash diluting returns rather than a weak business, and free cash flow per share keeps climbing. What gives me pause is operating margin sliding from 26% to 18% while gross margin drifts down, which suggests heavy reinvestment or eroding pricing power, and at roughly 30 times earnings (about a 3% free-cash yield) I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a wonderful business I'd be glad to own for a decade.

This looks like a large, well-run financial institution whose earnings power has steadily improved. ROE has climbed from about 7% to 13%, net margins have widened from 17% to 30%, and EPS has more than doubled from $3.90 to $9.00. Book value per share has compounded about 7% a year while earnings rose, so management is growing intrinsic value and returning capital rather than piling on leverage, with debt/equity holding in a sensible 1.2-1.5 range. At roughly 11.7 times earnings and about 1.3 times book for a business now earning 13% on equity, I'm paying a fair price for a durable franchise, though as with any bank I'm trusting the balance sheet more than I can see it from these figures.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer. Earnings per share went from $7.95 down to $1.88 and back to about $4.90, and that swing tells me it has no durable pricing power. Book value per share has crept from roughly $41 to $45 over the whole period, about 2% a year, and average ROE of 11% is ordinary rather than the mark of a moat. On the plus side, leverage is modest at 0.20 debt-to-equity and free cash flow has recovered to about $3.85 a share. Even so, a current ratio below 1 and a P/E of 16 on mid-cycle earnings leave no bargain here, so I'd call it a fair business at a fair price and pass until the price or the returns improve.

This is a business with gross margins near 70% and returns on equity in the low-20s for the better part of five years, and the cash kept coming even when reported earnings collapsed to about $0.50 a share for four periods. Free cash flow per share held near $6.70-6.80 throughout, which tells me that dip was a large non-cash charge rather than a broken franchise, and FCF per share has compounded from roughly $5 to $6.79. At about 24 times restored earnings and a free cash flow yield near 5%, with revenue growing again at 7-11%, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business, which is a trade I'll gladly make. My enthusiasm is tempered by debt/equity climbing from 0.20 to 0.55, book value per share shrinking, gross margin slipping about two points, and not knowing what caused that big charge or whether it will recur.

This is a large financial institution that has come back from a near-death earnings trough. EPS has risen from $0.36 to $2.69 and ROE has recovered from 2% to 11%, with net margins climbing steadily to 31%. It isn't a wide-moat compounder: book value per share has grown only about 5% a year, and a bank's true leverage sits beyond what a 0.93 debt/equity ratio shows, so I'm relying on scale and deposit franchise rather than proven pricing power. Still, paying roughly 11 times earnings and only about 1.1 times book for a business now earning 11% on equity and still improving is a sensible price, and I'd be comfortable owning it for the long haul.

This is a remarkably steady franchise. I'd watch debt/equity, which has crept from 0.14 to 0.97, but with a 1.3 current ratio and roughly $13 a share of free cash flow it looks manageable.
