The -0.80 book-value CAGR is plainly a per-share unit change at t-18, not a loss of capital: on the consistent basis since t-17, book value per share rose from about 97 to 150, roughly 10-11% a year, with no evident leverage strain. At about 19.5 times depressed-but-recovering earnings, roughly 1.4 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 4%, the price is fair rather than cheap. The slide in FCF per share from about 13.8 to 9.1 and modest revenue growth keep this from being a high-conviction call, but a steady compounder at a sensible price is one I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This looks like a large, well-run bank. Return on equity has climbed steadily from about 7% to 13%, and net margins widened from 17% to 30%, with book value per share compounding every single period while earnings per share more than doubled. At roughly 12 times earnings and about 1.4 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business earning 13% on equity, which gives me close to a 9% earnings yield plus book-value growth. My caution is that banks are leveraged by nature, and I can't see credit quality, deposit costs or capital ratios here, so I hold this with solid but not exceptional conviction.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer, not a compounding franchise. EPS fell from about $7.95 to $1.88 when revenue dropped 34%, and book value per share has crept from roughly $41 to $45 over some twenty quarters, a 1% annual rate that tells me the owners haven't been getting richer. Returns on equity of 10-11% and a 7% net margin don't suggest much pricing power. The balance sheet is sensible, with debt at about 0.21 of equity, but the current ratio sits below 1 and earnings have slipped again from $5.44 to $4.34. At nearly 18 times earnings and about a 4% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair-to-full price for an ordinary business, so I'd stay on the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This is a durable franchise. Gross margins have held in a tight 66-70% band for twenty periods and underlying ROE runs in the low-to-mid 20s. The earnings collapse in t-2 through t-5 looks like a one-time charge, not a business problem: free cash flow per share never missed a beat and climbed steadily from about $4.80 to $6.84. What gives me pause is the balance sheet drifting the wrong way, with debt/equity up from 0.20 to 0.50, the current ratio down from above 2.5 to 1.44, and book value per share shrinking. Still, at roughly $142 a share the owner is getting close to a 5% free-cash-flow yield on a steady compounder, which is a fair price for a wonderful business rather than a bargain.

This is a large financial institution that has come back from a near-death earnings trough. EPS has risen from $0.36 to $2.69 and ROE has recovered from 2% to 11%, with net margins climbing steadily to 31%. It isn't a wide-moat compounder: book value per share has grown only about 5% a year, and a bank's true leverage sits beyond what a 0.93 debt/equity ratio shows, so I'm relying on scale and deposit franchise rather than proven pricing power. Still, paying roughly 11 times earnings and only about 1.1 times book for a business now earning 11% on equity and still improving is a sensible price, and I'd be comfortable owning it for the long haul.

This is a manufacturer with remarkably steady economics. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% for about five years, through both revenue declines and 28% growth spurts. That kind of consistency tells me customers pay up and competitors can't dent the franchise. Free cash flow per share has climbed from about $8 to $12.73. Book value per share is flat only because management is shipping capital back to owners, which is why ROE has risen to the 50s. I'd note that some of that ROE lift comes from debt/equity rising from 0.26 to 1.06. At roughly 17.6 times earnings and about a 6% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business. My caution is that revenue growth has slowed to 4%, EPS dipped slightly last period and leverage is creeping up, but I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

This business is getting better, not worse. Gross margin has climbed steadily from 28% to 41% over twenty periods, ROE has gone from roughly zero to 25%, book value per share has more than quadrupled, and free cash flow per share has grown from about $2 to $41, all while debt-to-equity fell to 0.52 and revenue still grows 25% a year on an enormous base. That pattern suggests a real and widening moat with increasing pricing power or a shift toward higher-margin activities. But at 81 times earnings and roughly 47 times free cash flow, a free-cash-flow yield of about 2%, the price already assumes many more years of this performance. A wonderful company is only a wonderful investment at a sensible price, so I'd admire this one and wait for a better pitch.

This is a cash machine. Revenue is still compounding above 20% a year, net margins sit near 20%, debt is almost nonexistent at 0.02 debt/equity, and a current ratio near 4 means the balance sheet is a fortress. The ROE of 13-15% looks ordinary, but I read that as a mountain of idle cash diluting returns rather than a weak business, and free cash flow per share keeps climbing. What gives me pause is operating margin sliding from 26% to 18% while gross margin drifts down, which suggests heavy reinvestment or eroding pricing power, and at roughly 30 times earnings (about a 3% free-cash yield) I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a wonderful business I'd be glad to own for a decade.

This business has rebuilt its economics. Operating margins have climbed from 17% to 33%, revenue growth has reaccelerated from a 9% decline to 15%, and ROE now sits at 37%. Gross margins holding at 65% through the cycle suggest real pricing power. Free cash flow per share has risen steadily from about $2.80 to $4.34, debt/equity has come down from 1.23 to 0.77, and a current ratio near 3 means the balance sheet is no worry. Book value per share has compounded slowly, but alongside rising cash flow that looks like capital being returned to owners rather than wasted. At roughly 28 times earnings and a ~3.5% free-cash-flow yield (price implied from the P/E), I'm paying a full but fair price for a wonderful business growing mid-teens, which is a trade I'd make and hold for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Gross margins hold at 83-87%, there is no debt, the current ratio is above 5, book value per share has compounded at roughly 29% a year, and free cash flow per share has quadrupled over this stretch while revenue still grows 32%. What gives me pause is the recent trend. Operating margin has slipped from 50% to 39%, net margin from 40% to 33%, and growth keeps decelerating, which suggests heavier spending or pressures I can't see from these figures alone. At about 29 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a business whose moat looks wide but whose margins are now heading the wrong way. So I'd own it with moderate rather than high conviction.

This business has rebuilt its economics. Operating margins have climbed from 17% to 33%, revenue growth has reaccelerated from a 9% decline to 15%, and ROE now sits at 37%. Gross margins holding at 65% through the cycle suggest real pricing power. Free cash flow per share has risen steadily from about $2.80 to $4.34, debt/equity has come down from 1.23 to 0.77, and a current ratio near 3 means the balance sheet is no worry. Book value per share has compounded slowly, but alongside rising cash flow that looks like capital being returned to owners rather than wasted. At roughly 28 times earnings and a ~3.5% free-cash-flow yield (price implied from the P/E), I'm paying a full but fair price for a wonderful business growing mid-teens, which is a trade I'd make and hold for a decade.

This business has plainly gotten better. Gross margins climbed steadily from 29% to 41%, ROE went from losses to 23%, book value per share compounded from about $22 to $107, and free cash flow per share of $44 now runs well ahead of reported earnings of $24. That points to a widening moat and management that reinvests heavily and well, and the balance sheet is sensible at 0.47 debt-to-equity with debt coming down. But at roughly 80 times earnings and about a 2.3% free-cash-flow yield on a thin 5% net margin, the price already assumes years of 20%-plus growth. So I admire the business but can't call the price a bargain, and I'm staying on the sidelines rather than betting against it.

This is a business I can understand. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% for roughly twenty periods, through both a revenue contraction and a recovery. That kind of steadiness points to real pricing power and customer loyalty rather than luck. Management is plainly turning a torrent of free cash flow, about $12.66 a share and running ahead of reported earnings, into share repurchases. That explains why book value per share is shrinking and debt-to-equity has climbed to 1.12, and why ROE has been pushed toward 58%, so I don't read that ROE as a true measure of the franchise. My hesitation is that revenue growth has slowed to 1% and EPS has gone flat for three periods. Still, at about 18 times earnings, which works out to a free-cash-flow yield near 6%, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful, cash-gushing enterprise, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade provided the borrowing to fund buybacks doesn't get out of hand.

This is a business growing revenue about 20% a year for years on end. It earns net margins above 20%, carries almost no debt (D/E 0.02), holds a current ratio near 4, and throws off about $40 a share in free cash flow. The reported -5% book value CAGR is misleading because the oldest period appears to be before a share split. From t-18 to today, book value per share rose from about $154 to $277, and the reported ROE of 13-18% is held down by a mountain of idle cash rather than weak economics. I do note gross margin slipping from 62% to 56% and operating margin from 26% to 21%, which tells me they are spending heavily to keep growing, and I want to watch that. Still, at about 25 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, this is a wonderful franchise at a fair price, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine: 82% gross margins, revenue still growing 29% a year, no debt, a current ratio above 4, and book value per share compounding at roughly 28% without borrowed money. But the trend worries me. Operating margin has slid from 50% to 34%, net margin from about 40% to 27%, and EPS has dropped from $7.57 to $5.90 over three periods even as sales climbed, so costs are growing faster than revenue and pricing power may be facing new headwinds. At 34 times earnings and roughly 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying for a business whose margins I can't yet see stabilizing, so I'd admire it from the sidelines and wait for either clarity on the cost base or a better price.

This looks like a large, diversified financial and insurance enterprise whose reported earnings swing on mark-to-market gains (EPS of 1.63 one year, 25.16 the year before). So I judge it on book value, not quarterly P/E. The -0.80 book-value CAGR is plainly a per-share unit change at t-18, not a loss of capital: on the consistent basis since t-17, book value per share rose from about 97 to 150, roughly 10-11% a year, with no evident leverage strain. At about 19.5 times depressed-but-recovering earnings, roughly 1.4 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 4%, the price is fair rather than cheap. The slide in FCF per share from about 13.8 to 9.1 and modest revenue growth keep this from being a high-conviction call, but a steady compounder at a sensible price is one I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a high-quality franchise. Gross margins have held in the high-60s for twenty periods, ROE runs in the low-to-mid 20s outside one charge-laden stretch, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $5 to $6.8. That climb held even in the year reported earnings collapsed to 2% margins, which tells me the hit was an accounting or legal charge and not a broken business. At roughly 22 times earnings and about a 5% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair rather than cheap. Leverage is sensible at about 0.5 debt-to-equity. My reservations are real: per-share earnings have gone essentially nowhere in five years, gross margin has slipped three points, book value per share has shrunk, and liquidity has tightened. So I'd own it as a durable cash generator at a fair price, but without the conviction I reserve for a business that is compounding.

This looks like a large, well-run bank. Return on equity has climbed steadily from about 7% to 13%, and net margins widened from 17% to 30%, with book value per share compounding every single period while earnings per share more than doubled. At roughly 12 times earnings and about 1.4 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business earning 13% on equity, which gives me close to a 9% earnings yield plus book-value growth. My caution is that banks are leveraged by nature, and I can't see credit quality, deposit costs or capital ratios here, so I hold this with solid but not exceptional conviction.

At about 30 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a full price rather than a bargain, but it is a fair price for a wonderful business I'd happily own for ten years.

Book value per share has compounded only about 5%, likely because cash is being returned to owners, so it understates the progress. At roughly 26 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3.6%, this isn't a bargain. But it is a fair price for a durable, cash-gushing enterprise I'd be content to own for a decade.

This business is getting better in ways that matter. Gross margin has climbed steadily from 29% to 41%, ROE has gone from negative to around 20%, debt-to-equity has fallen from 1.05 to 0.45, and book value per share has roughly quintupled while revenue still grows at 20%. Free cash flow of about $40 a share, well above reported earnings of $22.57, tells me the true economics are stronger than the thin 4% net margin suggests. But at 78 times earnings and roughly a 2.3% free-cash-flow yield, while revenue growth has slowed from 39% to 20% and trailing earnings slipped this period, the price already assumes a great deal of future success, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines until the price gives me more margin of safety.

This business has the marks of a real franchise. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% for twenty straight periods, through revenue growth of +28% and declines of -8%. That kind of steadiness points to genuine pricing power rather than luck. Management is plainly returning capital: book value per share has shrunk while EPS and free cash flow per share held near $12. That tells me heavy buybacks are lifting ROE toward 60%, though rising debt to 1.19x equity helps too, and I'd watch that closely. The catch is price. Earnings have been flat for about three years while the P/E has climbed from 13.5 to about 21, so I'm no longer getting a bargain. Still, a free cash flow yield of roughly 5% on a business this durable is a fair price for a wonderful company, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a business that has grown revenue about 20% a year across twenty periods, keeps net margins near 20%, carries almost no debt (D/E 0.02) and holds current assets nearly four times its current liabilities. Its 14-17% ROE is held down by what looks like a heavy pile of idle capital, and book value per share has compounded about 14% a year, so the economic engine is strong and the moat looks durable. I do note some slippage: gross margin fell from 62% to 56%, operating margin from 26% to 21%, and free cash flow per share has barely moved over the last ten periods (about 40 to 41) as spending rose. Still, paying roughly 27 times earnings, or a 3.3% free-cash-flow yield, for a fortress balance sheet growing near 20% is a fair price for a wonderful business, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Gross margins sit above 80%, there is no debt, the current ratio is near 4.7, revenue is still growing 28%, and book value per share has compounded at roughly 22% while free cash flow per share climbed from $1.36 to $6.80. What gives me pause is the trend: operating margins have slid from 50% to 34% and EPS has fallen from its $7.57 peak even as sales grew, which tells me heavy spending or costs are eating into the moat's returns, and I want to understand why before I fully trust it. At about 31 times earnings and roughly a 3.6% free cash flow yield, the price is fair rather than cheap for a business still compounding this fast, so I lean positive with moderate conviction.

Book value per share has compounded at about 11% a year, from roughly $97 to $163 across these periods, and that is the kind of steady accretion I like to see in a financial business. But the underlying earning power is ordinary. ROE sits around 7-9%, reported earnings swing sharply (EPS of $25 one period, $1.63 the next, which suggests mark-to-market noise), and free cash flow per share has slipped from about $13.8 to $8.9. At roughly 20 times earnings and about 1.3 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business earning single-digit returns on equity, and with no leverage data to judge its financial strength I can't call this a bargain or a clear pass.

This is plainly a franchise business. Gross margins have held in the high 60s for twenty periods and returns on equity sit in the low-to-mid 20s outside one year of what looks like a large one-time charge. Free cash flow per share has climbed from about $4.81 to $7.38, so at roughly $129 a share I'm paying about a 5.7% free-cash-flow yield, which is a fair price for a durable business. What gives me pause is that the business isn't compounding. EPS of $5.25 is below the $5.70 of five years ago, revenue growth has stalled at zero, gross margin has slipped about three points, book value per share has shrunk, and the current ratio has fallen from about 2.5 to 1.26 as leverage crept up. A wonderful moat at a fair price, but with stagnant earnings and a weaker balance sheet, I'd hold rather than back up the truck.

This looks like a large, well-run bank, a business I understand. Returns on equity have climbed steadily from about 9% to 13%, net margins have widened from 23% to 31%, and EPS has nearly doubled from $5.29 to $10.15 while book value per share compounded at roughly 7%. At about 12.7 times earnings and roughly 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a franchise that is earning more on each dollar of equity, not a price that demands perfection. Banks carry leverage by nature and credit cycles will come, which is why my conviction is solid rather than exceptional, but the steady book value growth through the soft revenue years suggests management allocates capital sensibly.

This is a toll-bridge kind of business. Operating margins run around 65% and net margins above 50%, returns on equity have climbed from the high teens to 35% on modest leverage (D/E under 0.5), and free cash flow per share tracks reported earnings nearly dollar for dollar, which tells me the profits are real. Earnings per share have roughly doubled in about two and a half years while revenue keeps compounding at double digits, the mark of a durable moat with pricing power. At 29 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3.4% I'm not getting a bargain, but for a wonderful business like this a fair price is worth paying, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a large, capital-hungry manufacturer. Returns on equity have slid from 19% to about 8%, net margins sit at a thin 6–8%, and book value per share has crept from roughly $41.6 to $44.9 over five years, about 2% a year. That does not look like a business with a durable moat or pricing power. Revenue is now shrinking 9%, EPS has fallen from $5.44 to $3.44 in four periods, and the current ratio sits below 1, though debt is modest. At about 21 times depressed earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 3%, I'd be paying a premium price for a mediocre, cyclical business, and I'd rather wait.

Book value per share has compounded at about 11% a year, from roughly $97 to $163 across these periods, and that is the kind of steady accretion I like to see in a financial business. This looks like a large, well-run bank, a business I understand. Returns on equity have climbed steadily from about 9% to 13%, net margins have widened from 23% to 31%, and EPS has nearly doubled from $5.29 to $10.15 while book value per share compounded at roughly 7%. At about 12.7 times earnings and roughly 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a franchise that is earning more on each dollar of equity, not a price that demands perfection. Banks carry leverage by nature and credit cycles will come, which is why my conviction is solid rather than exceptional, but the steady book value growth through the soft revenue years suggests management allocates capital sensibly.

This is a toll-bridge kind of business. Operating margins run around 65% and net margins above 50%, returns on equity have climbed from the high teens to 35% on modest leverage (D/E under 0.5), and free cash flow per share tracks reported earnings nearly dollar for dollar, which tells me the profits are real. Earnings per share have roughly doubled in about two and a half years while revenue keeps compounding at double digits, the mark of a durable moat with pricing power. At 29 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3.4% I'm not getting a bargain, but for a wonderful business like this a fair price is worth paying, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a large, capital-hungry manufacturer. Revenue is now shrinking 9%, EPS has fallen from $5.44 to $3.44 in four periods, and the current ratio sits below 1, though debt is modest. At about 21 times depressed earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 3%, I'd be paying a premium price for a mediocre, cyclical business, and I'd rather wait.

This business has widened its moat. Gross margins rose from 61% to 68% and operating margins from about 23% to 37%, while revenue growth recovered from shrinking to a steady 13%. At about 29 times earnings and roughly a 3% free cash flow yield, I'm paying a full price rather than a bargain one. This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Gross margins have held at 38-40% for twenty periods, net margins sit around 21-23%, and free cash flow per share of $14.36 exceeds reported earnings. That is the signature of real pricing power and a durable moat. Management has been shrinking the share count aggressively, which lifted EPS from about $8.4 to $12.7 even though revenue growth has stalled at roughly 0-2%. But it has financed part of that with rising leverage, taking debt/equity from 0.34 to 1.21, and book value per share has drifted down, so the soaring ROE flatters more than it informs. I'd gladly have owned this at 10-14 times earnings. At 25.5 times, a free cash flow yield of about 4.4%, and top-line growth that has gone flat, the market is now paying up for the quality, so I'd hold what I had rather than chase it.

This is a business that has grown revenue about 20% a year across twenty periods, keeps net margins near 20%, carries almost no debt (D/E 0.02) and holds current assets nearly four times its current liabilities. Still, paying roughly 27 times earnings, or a 3.3% free-cash-flow yield, for a fortress balance sheet growing near 20% is a fair price for a wonderful business, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

Management has been shrinking the share count aggressively, which lifted EPS from about $8.4 to $12.7 even though revenue growth has stalled at roughly 0-2%. But it has financed part of that with rising leverage, taking debt/equity from 0.34 to 1.21, and book value per share has drifted down, so the soaring ROE flatters more than it informs. I'd gladly have owned this at 10-14 times earnings. At 25.5 times, a free cash flow yield of about 4.4%, and top-line growth that has gone flat, the market is now paying up for the quality, so I'd hold what I had rather than chase it.

This business has compounded book value per share at about 14% a year with virtually no debt, a current ratio above 3, and revenue still growing near 18% at enormous scale. Twenty-plus percent net margins and steadily rising free cash flow per share (about $19 to $45 over the period) point to a real moat. Returns on equity in the mid-teens understate the underlying economics because they are diluted by a large cash pile. The slow slide in gross margin from 62% to 56% tells me the business is spending heavily to defend its position, so I watch it, but operating margins have held around 21%. At roughly 29 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, this is not a bargain. It is a fair price for a wonderful, fortress-balance-sheet business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. It carries 82% gross margins and no debt, holds a current ratio above 4, grows revenue 27% a year and has compounded book value per share at over 20% annually. That is the kind of economic castle I admire. But the moat's toll is rising: operating margins have slid from 50% to 34% and ROE from 26% to 18%, and EPS of $6.43 is barely above where it stood two years ago, which tells me heavy new costs are eating the growth. At roughly 33 times earnings and about a 3.5% free-cash-flow yield, I'd be paying a full price for a business whose profitability is still heading the wrong way, so I'd rather wait for either the margins to stabilize or the price to come to me.

Reported earnings here swing wildly, with P/E ranging from 6.6 to 124. That pattern tells me unrealized investment gains and losses are running through the income statement, so I set EPS aside and look at book value per share. It has compounded steadily from about $98 to $174 over the nineteen quarters shown, roughly 13% a year, and fell only once (t-5 to t-4). Free cash flow has stayed positive every period, and revenue has kept growing. By my arithmetic the price is about 1.27 times book, cheaper than the roughly 1.46 times at the start of the series. Debt and liquidity figures aren't provided, which tempers my conviction somewhat, but paying a modest premium to book for a business that compounds book at low double digits is a fair price for a wonderful business, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is plainly a franchise. Gross margins have held in the 66-70% range for years, returns on equity run in the low-to-mid 20s outside one year of what looks like a large one-time charge, and free cash flow per share has climbed from $4.88 to $7.42, which is the kind of owner earnings I like to see. The trends are less comforting. Revenue growth has stalled at 0-1%, gross margin has slipped about three points, debt-to-equity has nearly doubled from 0.28 to 0.49, the current ratio has fallen from about 2.5 to 1.26, and book value per share has actually shrunk. At roughly 26 times earnings but about a 5% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a wonderful business that has stopped growing its top line. So I'd hold it comfortably but wouldn't back up the truck at this price.

This looks like a large, well-run financial franchise. Return on equity has climbed steadily from about 9% to 14%, net margins have widened from 24% to 32%, and earnings per share have nearly doubled from $5.46 to $10.72. Book value per share has compounded at about 6% a year, and it has done so while market cap stayed roughly flat and EPS rose. That tells me capital is going back to owners through buybacks and dividends rather than being wasted, and leverage has come down from 1.43x to 1.27x debt-to-equity. At under 12 times earnings and roughly 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business earning mid-teens on equity. The usual banking caveats apply: I can't see the loan book, and today's margins may be near a cyclical high. Those unknowns keep my conviction solid rather than exceptional.

This is a toll-bridge kind of business: operating margins near 65%, net margins above 50%, and return on equity rising from about 20% to 35%, all with modest leverage of 0.47 debt to equity. Free cash flow per share has more than doubled from $2.67 to $6.41 over the period while revenue keeps compounding at roughly 11%, which tells me the moat is widening, not eroding. Book value per share grows slowly only because the owners are handed the surplus cash, and that is the right thing to do with a business that needs so little capital. At about 31 times earnings, a roughly 3% starting yield, I'm paying a full price rather than a bargain one, but a wonderful company at a fair price is a deal I'll take and hold for a decade.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer earning ordinary returns. ROE has averaged around 9% and is now 7%, and book value per share has crept from about $41 to $45 over twenty periods, roughly 2% a year, which is not the compounding a durable moat produces. Revenue is shrinking 9%, EPS has slid from $5.44 to $3.36, and free cash flow per share has fallen from $3.94 to $1.25, all with a current ratio below 1. At roughly 16 times declining earnings, about 1.2 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 2.4%, I'd be paying a fair price for a fair-to-weakening business, and that's not a trade I'd make to hold for ten years.

At about 23 times earnings, roughly a 5% free cash flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful franchise. My enthusiasm is tempered by a few things: revenue growth has stalled near 1%, gross margin has slipped about 4 points, book value per share has drifted lower, and the current ratio has fallen from near 3 to 1.3. Those tell me the moat is holding but not widening, so I'd own it for the long haul, just without the conviction I'd want for a large position.

This looks like a large, well-run financial franchise. Over the full record it earned steady 10-14% returns on equity and held net margins in the high 20s to low 30s. Book value per share compounded about 6% a year while the share count fell from roughly 3.7 billion to about 3.05 billion, so owners were rewarded both by dividends and by buybacks. The market has marked it down about 28% in one period, and trailing EPS slipped from 10.72 to 8.85, which tells me credit costs are rising. Leverage near 1.34x debt to equity is conservative for a bank, and at roughly 10x earnings and barely above book value (about 1.06x) I'm being offered a durable, compounding business at a fair-to-attractive price. I'd accept some near-term earnings pain to own it for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Operating margins hold at about 65%, net margins exceed 50%, and ROE has climbed from roughly 20% to 36%. Earnings per share have more than doubled, from 2.66 to 6.42, across these twenty periods, and free cash flow tracks reported earnings closely, which tells me the profits are real cash and not accounting. Debt at about half of equity is modest for a business throwing off this much cash, and the slow growth in book value per share reflects capital being returned to owners rather than hoarded. At 27 times earnings, roughly a 3.5% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue still growing about 10%, I'm not getting a bargain. But it is a fair price for a wonderful business I'd be happy to own for a decade, and the multiple has come down from 31.55 last period.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer that has never earned the kind of returns I look for. ROE has averaged about 9% and is now sliding to 6%, and book value per share has barely moved, from roughly $41 to $43 across twenty periods, so retained earnings are not compounding for owners. The trend is plainly worsening: revenue has fallen three periods running, net margin has slipped from 8% to 4%, free cash flow per share has collapsed from $3.94 to $0.60, debt/equity has risen to 0.33, and the current ratio sits below 1. At roughly book value and 16x shrinking earnings the price isn't outrageous, but it's a fair price for a deteriorating, moatless business, and that's a bargain I'd rather pass on.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick. Returns on equity have climbed from the mid-teens to 40%, operating margins have widened from 19% to 37%, and gross margins are drifting upward. That is pricing power and a widening moat showing up in the numbers. Management has shrunk debt/equity from about 1.2 to 0.58 and holds a current ratio near 2.9, while free cash flow per share has roughly doubled over the period and revenue is still growing 13% a year. The catch is price: at about 30 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, you are paying up front for years of continued excellence, so this is a great company at a full but not foolish price, and I'd own it for a decade with measured rather than exuberant conviction.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. Revenue has compounded above 20% a year for five years, gross margin has widened steadily from 31% to 41%, book value per share has grown roughly fivefold, and debt has come down to 0.38 times equity. Those are the fingerprints of a real and widening moat. But at 109 times earnings and roughly 60 times free cash flow, I'm paying for a great deal of future that hasn't happened yet. Meanwhile ROE has slid from 25% to 16% and EPS has dipped even as the multiple expanded, so it's a wonderful business at a price that leaves me no margin of safety, and I'm content to watch rather than buy.

This business shows a real moat. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% for twenty straight periods, through revenue declines as well as booms. That kind of steadiness points to pricing power and customer loyalty. The shrinking book value per share and rising ROE are not signs of trouble. Management is sending a gusher of free cash flow, now $15.13 a share against $12.79 of earnings, back to owners. Earnings per share have climbed from about $8.30 to $12.80 even while revenue growth stalled. My reservations are that the multiple has expanded from roughly 10-14x to 22.6x, top-line growth is only low single digits, and debt/equity has crept up to 1.4. Even so, a free cash flow yield of about 5% on a business of this quality is a fair price for a wonderful company. I would be comfortable owning it for a decade, though not at a bargain entry.

This is a fortress. Debt is practically nil at 0.02 debt-to-equity, the current ratio is 3.66, net margins run around 20%, revenue is still growing in the high teens, and book value per share has compounded at about 14% a year without borrowed money. The blemishes are real: gross margin has slid from 63% to 55% and operating margin from 26% to 21%, and ROE of about 17% is held down by what looks like a large idle balance sheet. At roughly 27 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a wonderful, growing, unlevered business, and that's a trade I'm comfortable holding for a decade.

This business has the economics I look for. It earns 82% gross margins and nearly 30% net margins with no debt and a current ratio above 4. Book value per share has compounded at about 23% a year, and free cash flow per share has more than quintupled over the period shown. What gives me pause is operating margin sliding from 50% to 36% while revenue growth slowed from the 50s to 24%, which suggests costs are rising faster than the moat is widening. Still, at 28 times earnings and roughly a 4% free cash flow yield, with revenue still growing at 24% on an unleveraged balance sheet, the price looks fair for a wonderful business, though I'd want to understand why margins are compressing before buying heavily.

This looks like a large financial and insurance conglomerate whose reported earnings swing wildly, with EPS going from 1.63 to 33.41 to 4.12. That smells of mark-to-market investment gains and losses rather than changes in the underlying business, so I look through it to book value and cash. Book value per share has compounded at roughly 9% a year across these periods, and free cash flow has held steady at about $9 per share. At roughly 1.16 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 5%, the price asks nothing heroic. The 9% average ROE is respectable rather than wonderful, revenue growth has slowed to about 2%, and the latest 12% drop in book value tempers my enthusiasm. Still, a durable, cash-generative balance sheet at a modest premium to book is the kind of fair-price purchase I'm happy to hold for a decade.

Management has shrunk debt/equity from about 1.2 to 0.58 and holds a current ratio near 2.9, while free cash flow per share has roughly doubled over the period and revenue is still growing 13% a year. The catch is price: at about 30 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, you are paying up front for years of continued excellence, so this is a great company at a full but not foolish price, and I'd own it for a decade with measured rather than exuberant conviction.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. Revenue has compounded above 20% a year for five years, gross margin has widened steadily from 31% to 41%, book value per share has grown roughly fivefold, and debt has come down to 0.38 times equity. Those are the fingerprints of a real and widening moat. But at 109 times earnings and roughly 60 times free cash flow, I'm paying for a great deal of future that hasn't happened yet. Meanwhile ROE has slid from 25% to 16% and EPS has dipped even as the multiple expanded, so it's a wonderful business at a price that leaves me no margin of safety, and I'm content to watch rather than buy.

This business shows a real moat. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% for twenty straight periods, through revenue declines as well as booms. That kind of steadiness points to pricing power and customer loyalty. The shrinking book value per share and rising ROE are not signs of trouble. Management is sending a gusher of free cash flow, now $15.13 a share against $12.79 of earnings, back to owners. Earnings per share have climbed from about $8.30 to $12.80 even while revenue growth stalled. My reservations are that the multiple has expanded from roughly 10-14x to 22.6x, top-line growth is only low single digits, and debt/equity has crept up to 1.4. Even so, a free cash flow yield of about 5% on a business of this quality is a fair price for a wonderful company. I would be comfortable owning it for a decade, though not at a bargain entry.

This is a fortress. Debt is practically nil at 0.02 debt-to-equity, the current ratio is 3.66, net margins run around 20%, revenue is still growing in the high teens, and book value per share has compounded at about 14% a year without borrowed money. The blemishes are real: gross margin has slid from 63% to 55% and operating margin from 26% to 21%, and ROE of about 17% is held down by what looks like a large idle balance sheet. At roughly 27 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain, for a wonderful, growing, unlevered business, and that's a trade I'm comfortable holding for a decade.

This business has the economics I look for. It earns 82% gross margins and nearly 30% net margins with no debt and a current ratio above 4. Book value per share has compounded at about 23% a year, and free cash flow per share has more than quintupled over the period shown. What gives me pause is operating margin sliding from 50% to 36% while revenue growth slowed from the 50s to 24%, which suggests costs are rising faster than the moat is widening. Still, at 28 times earnings and roughly a 4% free cash flow yield, with revenue still growing at 24% on an unleveraged balance sheet, the price looks fair for a wonderful business, though I'd want to understand why margins are compressing before buying heavily.

This looks like a large financial and insurance conglomerate whose reported earnings swing wildly, with EPS going from 1.63 to 33.41 to 4.12. That smells of mark-to-market investment gains and losses rather than changes in the underlying business, so I look through it to book value and cash. Book value per share has compounded at roughly 9% a year across these periods, and free cash flow has held steady at about $9 per share. At roughly 1.16 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 5%, the price asks nothing heroic. The 9% average ROE is respectable rather than wonderful, revenue growth has slowed to about 2%, and the latest 12% drop in book value tempers my enthusiasm. Still, a durable, cash-generative balance sheet at a modest premium to book is the kind of fair-price purchase I'm happy to hold for a decade.

This business has earned roughly two-thirds of every sales dollar as gross profit for twenty periods, with returns on equity in the mid-20s and net margins near 20%. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from 4.81 to 7.40, and even the four-period collapse in reported earnings didn't dent the cash, which marks it as a one-time charge rather than real damage. At about 23 times earnings, roughly a 5% free cash flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful franchise. My enthusiasm is tempered by a few things: revenue growth has stalled near 1%, gross margin has slipped about 4 points, book value per share has drifted lower, and the current ratio has fallen from near 3 to 1.3. Those tell me the moat is holding but not widening, so I'd own it for the long haul, just without the conviction I'd want for a large position.

This looks like a large, well-run financial franchise. Over the full record it earned steady 10-14% returns on equity and held net margins in the high 20s to low 30s. Book value per share compounded about 6% a year while the share count fell from roughly 3.7 billion to about 3.05 billion, so owners were rewarded both by dividends and by buybacks. The market has marked it down about 28% in one period, and trailing EPS slipped from 10.72 to 8.85, which tells me credit costs are rising. Leverage near 1.34x debt to equity is conservative for a bank, and at roughly 10x earnings and barely above book value (about 1.06x) I'm being offered a durable, compounding business at a fair-to-attractive price. I'd accept some near-term earnings pain to own it for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Operating margins hold at about 65%, net margins exceed 50%, and ROE has climbed from roughly 20% to 36%. Earnings per share have more than doubled, from 2.66 to 6.42, across these twenty periods, and free cash flow tracks reported earnings closely, which tells me the profits are real cash and not accounting. Debt at about half of equity is modest for a business throwing off this much cash, and the slow growth in book value per share reflects capital being returned to owners rather than hoarded. At 27 times earnings, roughly a 3.5% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue still growing about 10%, I'm not getting a bargain. But it is a fair price for a wonderful business I'd be happy to own for a decade, and the multiple has come down from 31.55 last period.

This is a big, cyclical manufacturer that has never earned the kind of returns I look for. ROE has averaged about 9% and is now sliding to 6%, and book value per share has barely moved, from roughly $41 to $43 across twenty periods, so retained earnings are not compounding for owners. The trend is plainly worsening: revenue has fallen three periods running, net margin has slipped from 8% to 4%, free cash flow per share has collapsed from $3.94 to $0.60, debt/equity has risen to 0.33, and the current ratio sits below 1. At roughly book value and 16x shrinking earnings the price isn't outrageous, but it's a fair price for a deteriorating, moatless business, and that's a bargain I'd rather pass on.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and net margins at 21-23% across twenty periods, a sign of real pricing power. Free cash flow per share has climbed from about $9.65 to $16.47, and the shrinking book value reflects heavy buybacks, not losses, which is why ROE has risen to 81%. But the price has run far ahead of the business: market cap jumped from about $1.25 trillion to $1.82 trillion in a single period while EPS rose only 3% and revenue grew 6%, pushing the P/E from the low teens to 32 and the free-cash-flow yield under 4%. I'd happily own this for ten years at a sensible price, but at today's multiple, with debt/equity climbing to 1.56 to fund repurchases, I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than pay for perfection.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I use. Returns on equity climbed from the mid-teens to roughly 37-40%, gross margins widened from 61% to 68%, and operating margins rose from 17% to 37%. Free cash flow per share has doubled across the record, and debt-to-equity fell from about 1.2 to 0.54, which tells me management is compounding sensibly rather than borrowing its growth. My hesitation is price. At 35 times earnings and only about a 3% free cash flow yield, the multiple has expanded sharply from the mid-20s just a few periods ago, and it already discounts many years of mid-teens growth. I would be delighted to own this for a decade, but today I'd rather wait for the market to offer it at a fairer price than pay up for perfection.

This is plainly a formidable business. Revenue has grown 20-39% a year for five years, gross margin widened from 32% to 40%, ROE climbed from 3% to 18%, and book value per share compounded roughly fivefold. Free cash flow per share has quadrupled, and leverage has come down to 0.47 debt/equity, which tells me management reinvests shrewdly rather than recklessly. But the net margin is still only about 4% and the operating margin 5%, so this is a thin-margin retailer being priced at over 120 times earnings and roughly a 1.7% free-cash-flow yield. That price already assumes years of flawless execution, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines rather than pay today's price.

This is a formidable franchise. Debt is negligible at 0.02 debt-to-equity, the current ratio sits above 3, and book value per share has compounded about 13% a year. Free cash flow per share has more than doubled, from roughly $21 to $46, and that is the kind of owner earnings I like to see. But the trend lines trouble me. Gross margin has slipped from 63% to 54% and operating margin from 26% to 20%. Revenue growth has cooled from the mid-20s to 12%, and trailing EPS fell even as sales grew. Returns on equity of about 15% are respectable rather than spectacular, weighed down by a mountain of retained capital. At nearly 33 times earnings and roughly a 3% free cash flow yield, I'd be paying for a wonderful business while its economics are visibly compressing, so I'd rather wait for either a better price or evidence that margins have stabilized.

This is plainly a wonderful business on the numbers: gross margins above 80%, no debt, a current ratio of 6, and book value per share compounding at about 23% a year. That is the fingerprint of a real moat. But the trend gives me pause. Operating margins have slid from 50% to 37%, revenue growth has decelerated from over 50% to 20%, and free cash flow per share fell from $8.08 to $6.54 in the latest period. At 31 times earnings and roughly a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full price for a business whose cost structure is visibly rising, in an industry at the edge of my circle of competence. I'd be happy to own it at a better price, but today it's a great company at a fair-to-rich price, so I'll watch rather than swing.

This is a toll-bridge kind of business: 64% operating margins, 50%-plus net margins, ROE that has climbed from about 20% to the mid-30s, and free cash flow per share that has more than doubled over the period, all carried on modest debt of 0.59x equity. That is a moat you can see in the numbers, and I'd be happy to own it for ten years. But at 31 times earnings the free cash flow yield is only about 3%, and the latest year shows revenue growth slowing to 3% while EPS slipped from 6.42 to 6.05. A wonderful company at a price that already assumes the growth resumes leaves me no margin of safety, so I'd wait for a fatter pitch.

This is plainly a franchise business. Gross margins have held in the mid-60s for twenty periods, ROE runs in the low-to-mid 20s outside one heavy one-time charge, and free cash flow of $6.50–7.40 per share has been steady as a metronome. But the engine has stopped growing: revenue is flat to slightly down, EPS today ($5.69) is about where it was five years ago, book value per share has shrunk, gross margin has slipped about four points, and liquidity has thinned from a current ratio near 3 to 1.25. At 26 times earnings and roughly a 4.4% free-cash-flow yield, I'd be paying a growth price for a business showing no growth, so I'll admire it from the sidelines until the price or the trajectory improves.

This is a wonderful toll-bridge of a business. Operating margins have held above 50% for twenty periods, free cash flow per share has grown from about $3.11 to $8.14, and the sky-high ROE comes from aggressive buybacks shrinking equity, not from anything wrong with the business. The leverage (D/E 1.93) looks heavier than it is, since it mostly reflects returning capital, and a current ratio near 2 tells me the company can pay its bills. But the latest period shows revenue growth slowing to 3% and EPS falling from $7.94 to $7.22, and the market is still paying about 43 times earnings, roughly a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield, which leaves little margin of safety if the slowdown lingers. I'd love to own it, but at this price I'd rather wait for Mr. Market to offer a fairer entry.

This is a big, steady manufacturer with a roughly 50% gross margin that has held for years, and free cash flow per share has climbed every period from about 3.4 to 5.2, which tells me the underlying franchise is real. But reported operating margin halved from about 20% to 10% four periods ago and has only partly recovered. ROE now sits near 10%, book value per share is shrinking, and debt/equity has risen to 0.78 with a current ratio below 1, none of which I like to see. At roughly 65 times reported earnings and about 23 times free cash flow, for a business growing revenue only 1-5% a year, I'm paying a full price for a good but not wonderful company, so I'll stay on the sidelines.

At 34 times earnings and roughly a 3% free cash flow yield, much of the recent gain in market value came from a richer multiple rather than earnings alone. Still, if the business keeps compounding owner earnings in the low-to-mid teens, a fair price for a business this durable should serve a ten-year owner well, so I lean bullish with tempered conviction.

This is a formidable retail franchise. Revenue is still compounding at roughly 30% a year at enormous scale, gross margin has widened from 33% to 40%, and book value per share has grown about sixfold with debt/equity falling from above 1.0 to 0.40. That is the fingerprint of a widening moat and capable capital allocation. But the price is the rub: at nearly 89 times earnings and around a 1.6% free-cash-flow yield on a 5% net margin, today's buyer is paying for another decade of flawless execution. I'd admire it from the sidelines rather than pay a price that leaves no margin of safety.

This is plainly a wonderful business. It earns net margins around 20%, carries almost no debt (D/E 0.07), holds a current ratio above 3, and has compounded book value per share about 13% a year while free cash flow per share roughly doubled over the period. Still, I'd note that gross margin has slid from 62% to 54% and operating margin from 26% to 20%, while revenue growth has cooled from the mid-20s to 11%. Paying about 31 times earnings and roughly 32 times free cash flow, a 3% owner's yield, leaves little margin of safety for a business whose economics are drifting down rather than up. I'd be glad to own it for ten years, but at this price I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a remarkable economic engine: 81% gross margins, a 32% net margin, no debt, a current ratio above 5, and book value per share compounding at over 20% a year. Those are the fingerprints of a real moat. But operating margins have slid from about 50% to 36%, gross margin is drifting lower, and free cash flow per share ($6.64) lags reported earnings ($8.78), which tells me the business is spending more heavily to keep its position. At roughly 30 times earnings and something like a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue growth slowing from the 50s to 19%, I'm paying a full price for a wonderful but changing business whose long-term competitive dynamics sit at the edge of my circle of competence. So I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than swing.

This looks like a financial business that holds a large portfolio of marketable securities. The wild swings in reported EPS, from 1.63 to 33.41, move in step with market values rather than operating reality, so I look through them to book value and cash. On those measures the record is sound. Book value per share compounded from about $104 to $177, roughly 12% a year, and it dipped only modestly in bad stretches. Free cash flow per share has stayed steady at roughly $9–14 and never went negative. At about $221 a share (15.29 EPS × 14.49 P/E), you pay roughly 1.25 times book and get a free-cash-flow yield near 5%, which is a fair price for a steady compounder. I'm not more confident for three reasons: the modest ~9% average ROE, revenue that has now slipped for two periods, and missing leverage and liquidity data, which for a financial company is exactly what I'd want to see before committing heavily.

This is a remarkable toll-road of a business. Operating margins have held near 64-66% and net margins near 50% for years, ROE sits around 30%, and free cash flow is steady with little capital needed. That points to a durable moat and real pricing power. But revenue has turned down 5% and EPS has slipped from $6.42 to $5.58, while the market has pushed the valuation up to 37x earnings and roughly a 2.4% free-cash-flow yield. Even on a normalized $6.40 or so of earnings you're paying over 30x. I'd love to own it, but at this price I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than swing now.

This is plainly a high-quality franchise. Gross margins run in the mid-60s, returns on equity sit around 25%, and free cash flow of roughly $6.50–7.40 a share has come in steadily year after year, even through a stretch where some large charge knocked reported earnings to near zero. But revenue has gone flat to slightly negative, gross margin has slipped from 70% to 66%, and book value per share hasn't compounded at all while debt has crept up. At about 23 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 4.7%, I'd be paying a fair price for a wonderful business that has stopped growing, so I'm content to wait for either a better price or evidence that growth has returned.

This is plainly a wonderful toll-bridge business. Operating margins have held above 50% for most of two decades of reporting periods, net margins run around 40%, and free cash flow per share has roughly doubled from 3.44 to 7.52. The flat book value per share alongside rising debt/equity (now 2.17) tells me management is returning essentially everything through buybacks, which inflates ROE but is sensible given the capital-light model. What gives me pause is the price. Revenue just turned negative (-4%), EPS has slipped from 7.94 to 6.66 over three periods, and yet the market still asks nearly 44 times earnings, about a 2% free-cash-flow yield, which prices in a swift return to double-digit growth. I'd happily own this franchise, but at a fairer price than one that assumes the recent stumble is temporary.

This is a steady franchise. Gross margins have held near 50% for twenty periods, operating margins sit in the low 20s, and free cash flow per share has climbed without interruption from $4.27 to $5.76. That is a moat that shows up in the numbers. The dips in reported earnings look like charges, not a broken business, since cash flow never wavered. The book value decline mostly reflects capital returned rather than capital destroyed. But at roughly 27 times earnings and about 25 times free cash flow, for a business growing revenue around 5% with a current ratio under 1, I'm paying a full price for a fine company. I'd be happy to own it, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins have held near 38% and net margins near 21% across twenty periods, which points to real pricing power and a durable franchise. Free cash flow per share has climbed from 2.83 to 4.19, and the falling book value is the shrinking share count from buybacks, not losses. That shrinking equity base, along with debt/equity rising to 1.72, flatters the 88% ROE, though the cash generation makes that leverage tolerable. My trouble is the price: the P/E has tripled from about 10 to 33 while EPS grew only from 2.36 to 3.28 and revenue grows about 6%, so today's roughly 3.8% free-cash-flow yield leaves little margin of safety. I'd happily keep owning it, but I wouldn't be eager to pay up for more here.

This is plainly a franchise business. Gross margins sit in the mid-60s, returns on equity run in the mid-20s in normal years, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $5.23 to $7.56. That is the signature of real pricing power and a durable moat, and the one-year collapse in earnings around t-9 to t-12 looks like a one-time charge rather than a broken business. But the trend lines trouble me: revenue has been flat for two years, gross margin has slipped from 70% to 66%, debt-to-equity has nearly doubled to 0.60, the current ratio has fallen from about 3 to 1.2, and book value per share has not compounded at all. At roughly 29 times earnings and about a 4.7% free-cash-flow yield, I'd be paying a fair-to-full price for a wonderful business that has stopped growing, so I'll wait for either better growth or a better price.

This is a toll-road business of the rarest kind. Operating margins run above 50% and net margins around 40%, and returns on equity sit near or above 100%. Book value per share stays flat only because nearly all free cash flow goes back to owners through buybacks, and I call that a moat, not an accident. A wonderful company is worth a fair price, but this price already assumes a swift, full recovery and years of compounding, so I'd admire it from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is the kind of business I understand: gross margins have held near 50% for years and operating margins have widened from about 20% to 24%. That points to real pricing power and a durable franchise. Free cash flow per share has compounded steadily from $3.54 to $6.20 with hardly a hiccup, even through the stretch where a large write-down cut reported earnings to about $1.50 a share. At roughly 25 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 4.7%, this is not a bargain, but it is a fair price for a wonderful business, and I'd be content to own it for ten years.

But revenue is now shrinking about 9% and EPS has slipped from 7.94 to 6.52, while the market cap has climbed to 385B, pushing the P/E near 60. Even if earnings recover, I'd be paying a price that assumes perfection, so I'll admire this one from the sidelines until the price comes closer to the value.

This is a business I can understand. Gross margins have held around 50% and edged up to 52%, operating margins recovered to 24%, and ROE sits near 30%. That kind of durable profitability points to real pricing power and a strong franchise. The best sign is free cash flow per share, which climbed steadily from about $3.54 to $6.30 over these periods and never missed a beat, even through the stretch where reported earnings were depressed by what looks like a one-time charge. The shrinking book value per share, the sub-1 current ratio and moderate leverage (0.64 debt/equity) look like a cash-rich company returning capital to owners rather than a sign of distress. At roughly 25 times earnings and about a 4.6% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price rather than a bargain for a wonderful business, so I'd own it for ten years but not with maximum conviction.

This is a remarkably steady franchise. Gross margins have held at 38-40% and operating margins near 25-29% for twenty periods, while free cash flow per share has more than doubled from $2.32 to $5.34. That kind of consistency, now paired with 21% revenue growth, speaks to real pricing power and customer loyalty. The shrinking book value and rising debt-to-equity look to me like management buying back stock heavily out of abundant cash flow rather than a weakening business, though I'd want to watch that leverage and a thin 1.14 current ratio. The price is no bargain: the P/E has gone from 12 to 30 and the free cash flow yield is roughly 4%. Still, a wonderful business at a full-but-fair price is one I'd be content to own for a decade, so I'm bullish with tempered conviction.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I use: returns on equity around 40%, gross margins inching up from 62% to 68%, and operating margins widening from 24% to 40%. Revenue is compounding at mid-teens rates and book value per share has roughly doubled, all while debt/equity fell from over 1.1 to 0.43, which tells me there is real pricing power and disciplined capital allocation. But at nearly $2 trillion and about 36 times earnings, with a free-cash-flow yield under 3%, the price already assumes years of flawless execution. I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than pay up for perfection today.

This is a remarkable compounding machine. Book value per share has grown roughly sixfold over the period, ROE has climbed from single digits to 26%, gross margins have widened from 34% to 40%, and debt/equity has fallen to 0.32 while revenue is still growing about 40% a year. Those are the fingerprints of a real moat and of management that reinvests well. But I'm paying 66 times earnings, and free cash flow of about $42 a share, below reported EPS, works out to roughly a 1.2% cash yield on the implied price. That leaves me depending on many more years of exceptional growth to earn a satisfactory return. A wonderful business at a price that leaves little margin of safety is one I admire from the sidelines rather than chase.

This is a wonderful business on the evidence. Revenue has grown in the high teens to mid-twenties for five years, and earnings per share nearly tripled from about $26 to $75. Free cash flow per share matches reported earnings dollar for dollar, and the balance sheet carries almost no debt (D/E 0.07) with a current ratio above 3. Book value has compounded at roughly 14% while ROE has climbed back to 22%, which tells me management is reinvesting and returning capital sensibly rather than stretching. The one blemish is gross margin sliding from 62% to 54%, a sign the business mix is getting more capital-intensive, and at about 31 times earnings I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain. I'd still be comfortable owning this for ten years at that price.

This is a remarkably profitable enterprise. Gross margins hold above 80%, operating margins have recovered from 34% to 40%, and it carries no debt and a current ratio of 6. Book value per share has compounded about 23% a year, which tells me management is growing the business, not just the share count. That kind of economics usually signals a real moat, likely network effects, though I'd admit the data can't show me how durable that moat is against changing user habits or regulation, and that puts it near the edge of my circle of competence. At 28 times earnings and roughly a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price rather than a bargain. With revenue still growing 29% and earnings per share nearly doubling over the past eight periods, a wonderful business at a fair price is a deal I'll take, sized with some humility.

This looks like a diversified financial and insurance enterprise whose reported earnings swing wildly, from a 1.63 to a 45.53 EPS, because unrealized investment gains and losses run through the income statement. So I judge it by book value, and book per share has compounded about 14% a year, from 106.67 to 196.18 over roughly five years, with only one meaningful dip. At about $279 a share, implied by 45.53 EPS at 6.1x, the price is roughly 1.4x book and about 21x free cash flow. That is a fair price for a steady compounder, though not a steal, and the headline P/E of 6 flatters the stock. Flat-to-declining revenue and an underlying ROE nearer 8-10% temper my enthusiasm, but a business that reliably grows intrinsic value at double digits and carries no evident balance-sheet strain is one I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a toll-bridge business of the finest kind. Operating margins have held at about 64-65% for years, net margins sit near 50%, and ROE runs close to 30% on modest leverage. Earnings power has held up even as revenue shrank 11% this past year, and free cash flow per share of $5.80 still exceeds earnings, which tells me the moat is intact. But at 43 times earnings that are temporarily depressed, the free cash flow yield is roughly 2.4%, and the price already assumes a full recovery and then some. I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than pay a price that leaves little margin of safety.

This is a franchise with staying power. Gross margins have held around 66-70% for twenty periods, ROE runs in the low-to-mid 20s, and debt is a sensible half of equity. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about 4.81 to 7.80 even as reported earnings were knocked around by one-time charges, which tells me the underlying engine is sound. The rub is growth: revenue is barely moving and book value per share has gone nowhere. A 28.75 P/E is rich on reported earnings, but a roughly 4.8% free cash flow yield on a business this durable is a fair price for a wonderful company, so I'd own it without expecting fireworks.

This is a business I'd love to own. Returns on equity have climbed to 43%, gross margins have widened from 61% to 69%, operating margins have nearly doubled to 42%, and book value per share has roughly doubled while debt/equity fell from above 1.2 to 0.41, with free cash flow tracking earnings closely. That is a wide and widening moat run by people who allocate capital sensibly. But at roughly 36 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 2.6%, the market has already priced in years of 15%-plus compounding, which leaves little margin of safety if growth merely normalizes. So I'd admire it from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a remarkable business. Revenue is growing close to 40% a year at enormous scale, gross margins have widened from 35% to 41%, ROE has climbed to 26%, and book value per share has compounded roughly sixfold over the period with leverage kept sensible. That is the kind of widening moat I admire. But at about 58 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share collapsing to $13.75 from over $42 as capital spending surges, I'd be paying a price that already assumes years of flawless execution, a free-cash yield well under 1%. A wonderful company at a fair price is my game; this is a wonderful company at a full price, so I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This is a very good business with a solid balance sheet: net margins near 29%, operating margins up from 20% to 28% over the last four periods, almost no debt (D/E 0.06), a current ratio above 3, and book value per share compounding at about 14% a year. Free cash flow per share has risen from about $34 to $88 over the period, so the earnings are real cash, and the steady 11-25% revenue growth points to a durable franchise with real pricing power. My hesitations are that gross margin has slipped from 62% to 56%, that ROE averaged only about 15% for years because of a large cash pile before this recent jump to 26%, and that the latest 33% growth may reflect a cyclical surge I shouldn't extrapolate. At roughly 30 times earnings and about a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price rather than a bargain for a wonderful business, which is a trade I'm willing to make with moderate rather than high conviction.

This is a remarkable economic engine. It keeps 81 cents of every revenue dollar as gross profit and converts about 37% to net income, with no debt, a current ratio above 5, and book value per share compounding at roughly 22% a year. Management went through a heavy spending phase in the middle of this record, when operating margins fell from about 50% to 34%, but earnings power has since recovered to 43% operating margins. Revenue growth has re-accelerated to 39%, which suggests the money went into the moat rather than down the drain. At about 26.6 times earnings and roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business, not a bargain. The slow slide in gross margin and the uncertainty inherent in a fast-moving services franchise keep my conviction short of the top tier.

This is plainly a fine business: gross margins have held near 60% through a full cycle, net margins run in the high twenties, the balance sheet carries modest debt with a current ratio above 4, and book value per share has roughly tripled over the period shown. But it is cyclical. When revenue fell 19%, ROE dropped from about 50% to 21%, and this looks like technology manufacturing I can't forecast with confidence a decade out. At 74 times earnings, a 1.3% earnings yield, the market is paying for perfection in a business that has shown it can stumble. A wonderful company at a price that leaves no margin of safety is one I'd admire from the sidelines rather than buy.

This looks like a large, well-run bank, a business I understand. It kept earning roughly 9-14% on equity through a visible downturn (t-4 to t-2) without ever posting a loss, and book value per share compounded about 6% a year on top of what I assume were dividends and buybacks. The latest 12.60 EPS is flattered by what looks like cyclical tailwinds such as reserve releases. On normalized earnings of roughly $10 a share you're paying about 15 times earnings and around 1.7 times book, which is a fair price rather than a bargain for a franchise with modest leverage and steady 25-33% net margins. A wonderful-enough business at a fair price earns a measured yes. My conviction is tempered, though, because bank returns ride the credit cycle and I can't see the deposit base or loan book from these figures.

At about 26.6 times earnings and roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business, not a bargain. The slow slide in gross margin and the uncertainty inherent in a fast-moving services franchise keep my conviction short of the top tier.

Reported earnings here swing wildly, from a P/E of 124 to 6, which in a finance business usually means mark-to-market investment gains and losses flowing through the income statement. So I ignore the headline P/E and look at book value. Book value per share has compounded from about 109 to 208 over the period, roughly 14-15% a year, and it dipped only once, in the t-5 period. Free cash flow per share has held steady and grown, and the price is roughly 1.4 times book, a fair price for a business that compounds its intrinsic value at double digits with apparent resilience. Leverage and current-ratio data are missing, so my conviction stops short of the highest level. Still, this looks like a durable compounder bought at a sensible price, one I'd be comfortable holding for a decade.

This is a highly profitable manufacturer: gross margins in the low 60s, net margins near 30%, returns on equity back above 30%, and book value per share compounding about 30% a year. Those are the marks of a real competitive advantage. But the record also shows a cyclical business. Revenue fell as much as 19% at t-7, and ROE dropped from about 50% to about 21% within a few periods, so I can't treat today's 68% revenue growth as the new normal. The numbers don't hang together cleanly: a 33% ROE on $8.46 of book implies roughly $2.80 a share, not the reported $7.97. That makes the headline 26 P/E suspect, since for most of the past four years the stock traded at 65-90 times earnings. Add missing free cash flow data and debt/equity climbing from about 0.2 to 0.56, and I see a wonderful-looking business at a price I can't confidently call fair, so I'll stay on the sidelines rather than bet against it.

This looks like a large, well-run financial franchise. It stayed solidly profitable through the rough patch around t-5 to t-3, when ROE bottomed near 9%. Book value per share has compounded about 7% a year without a single down period, and EPS has more than doubled from 5.80 to 14.99. The latest 17% ROE and 40% net margin look flattered by cyclical tailwinds, so I'd underwrite something closer to the 12-13% the business earns in normal times. At about 1.6x book and roughly 13x normalized earnings, that's a fair price for a durable, disciplined compounder, though not a steal. Leverage near 1.2x debt to equity has been steady and even trended down from 1.39, which I like. I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, but I'm tempering my enthusiasm because peak-looking margins rarely persist and book value growth slowed in the latest period.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Operating margins have held at about 65% for four years, net margins are near 50%, ROE runs around 28-36% on modest leverage, and free cash flow of $6.53 a share actually exceeds reported earnings, which is the kind of toll-bridge economics I love. But revenue has shrunk for three straight periods and EPS has slipped from $6.42 to $5.59, yet the market has pushed the multiple from 27x to 44x. That means paying roughly a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield for a business that is currently shrinking, however temporary the dip may prove. I'd happily own this for ten years at the right price, but today the price already assumes a full recovery and then some, so I'll wait for a fatter pitch.

This business earns returns on equity in the mid-20s on gross margins that have held around 66-70% across twenty periods. That kind of consistency points to real pricing power and a durable franchise. Free cash flow per share has climbed from about $4.81 to $8.45 while leverage stayed modest (D/E ~0.48). The flat book value per share looks to reflect cash returned to owners plus one large charge, which crushed earnings for four periods, rather than a deteriorating business. At roughly 26 times earnings and about a 5% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful company rather than a bargain. Top-line growth has been mostly low single digits, and the charge history reminds me there can be lumpy liabilities, so I'd own it with moderate rather than high conviction.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins have held at 38-41% for twenty periods, and operating margins at 24-29%. Free cash flow per share has more than doubled, from 2.41 to 5.65, and consistently runs ahead of reported earnings. The falling book value and the 1.89 debt-to-equity look like deliberate, heavy share repurchases rather than distress, though the current ratio sliding from 1.6 to 1.06 tells me management is running the balance sheet tighter than I'd like. The trouble is the price. I'd have backed up the truck at 14-18 times earnings, but at 28 times, and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying for a 27% revenue spike that history says may not persist. So I'd happily keep owning it but wouldn't be eager to add at this quote.

This is a business I'd love to own. Returns on equity have climbed to 43%, gross margins have widened from 61% to 69%, operating margins have nearly doubled to 42%, and book value per share has roughly doubled while debt/equity fell from above 1.2 to 0.41, with free cash flow tracking earnings closely. That is a wide and widening moat run by people who allocate capital sensibly. But at roughly 36 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 2.6%, the market has already priced in years of 15%-plus compounding, which leaves little margin of safety if growth merely normalizes. So I'd admire it from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a remarkable business. But at about 58 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share collapsing to $13.75 from over $42 as capital spending surges, I'd be paying a price that already assumes years of flawless execution, a free-cash yield well under 1%. A wonderful company at a fair price is my game; this is a wonderful company at a full price, so I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than bet against it.
