Book value per share has compounded about 7% a year without a single down period, and EPS has more than doubled from 5.80 to 14.99. The latest 17% ROE and 40% net margin look flattered by cyclical tailwinds, so I'd underwrite something closer to the 12-13% the business earns in normal times. At about 1.6x book and roughly 13x normalized earnings, that's a fair price for a durable, disciplined compounder, though not a steal. Leverage near 1.2x debt to equity has been steady and even trended down from 1.39, which I like. I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, but I'm tempering my enthusiasm because peak-looking margins rarely persist and book value growth slowed in the latest period.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Operating margins have held at about 65% for four years, net margins are near 50%, ROE runs around 28-36% on modest leverage, and free cash flow of $6.53 a share actually exceeds reported earnings, which is the kind of toll-bridge economics I love. But revenue has shrunk for three straight periods and EPS has slipped from $6.42 to $5.59, yet the market has pushed the multiple from 27x to 44x. That means paying roughly a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield for a business that is currently shrinking, however temporary the dip may prove. I'd happily own this for ten years at the right price, but today the price already assumes a full recovery and then some, so I'll wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a durable franchise. Gross margins have held around 66-70% for twenty periods and ROE runs in the mid-20s, apart from one year hit by what looks like a large one-time charge. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $5.57 to $8.40, and debt is moderate at roughly 0.48 times equity. Book value per share has barely grown, which tells me the owners are getting the earnings back as dividends and buybacks rather than reinvestment. At about 24 times earnings, or roughly a 5% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue growth recently picking up to 11-13%, I'd call it a wonderful business at a fair, not cheap, price, and I'd be content to own it for a decade.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Gross margins have crept up from 38% to 42%, operating margins sit at 30%, and free cash flow per share has more than doubled from $2.49 to $5.51 over the period, which tells me customers pay up willingly and the moat is real. The shrinking book value and rising debt/equity don't come from losses. They come from management returning far more cash than the business needs, which inflates ROE to 150% and shrinks the share count. That leverage is worth watching, but it is supported by consistent cash generation. At roughly 27 times earnings and a FCF yield near 3.7%, I'm not getting a bargain, and the recent 33% revenue surge may not repeat. Still, a wonderful business at a fair price is one I'd be comfortable holding for a decade.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I use: ROE has climbed to 45%, gross margins have widened from 61% to 69%, operating margins from 23% to 42%, and revenue growth has actually accelerated to 20% at enormous scale, which tells me there is real pricing power and a widening moat. Management has done its job. Book value per share has compounded near 19% a year, debt-to-equity has fallen from 1.23 to 0.35, and free cash flow per share has more than doubled with hardly a hiccup. The rub is price: at about 35 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 2.6%, I'm paying up front for years of continued excellence, so my margin of safety is thin. Still, a wonderful company at a full-but-not-absurd price that keeps compounding owner earnings at mid-teens or better is one I'd be content to hold for a decade, so I lean bullish with tempered conviction.

This is plainly a formidable franchise. Revenue has compounded at 20-40% a year, gross margins have widened from 35% to 41%, ROE has climbed from single digits to the mid-20s, and book value per share has risen roughly sixfold with debt/equity drifting down. Those are the fingerprints of a moat and a management that reinvests well. But at 66 times earnings on a razor-thin 6% net margin, and with free cash flow per share falling from about $50 to negative $4.41 as spending ramps, the price already assumes years of flawless execution. I'd happily own this wonderful business at a fair price, but this isn't one, so I'll watch rather than buy.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Net margins have widened to 30%, return on equity has climbed from the mid-teens to 29%, book value per share has compounded at about 14% a year, and it carries almost no debt (D/E 0.06) and plenty of liquidity. Free cash flow per share has roughly tripled over the period and tracks reported earnings closely, which tells me the profits are real cash. My hesitation is the price: at 28 times earnings and a free cash flow yield of about 3.5%, I'm paying for 39% revenue growth and peak margins that may well cool, so this is a fair price for an exceptional franchise rather than a bargain, and I'd buy it for the long haul with measured rather than table-pounding conviction.

This is a toll-road kind of business: 81% gross margins, operating margins back above 40%, net margins in the mid-30s, and no debt to speak of. It has compounded book value per share at about 20% a year and earnings per share roughly fourfold across the periods shown, while funding it all internally with a current ratio above 4. At about 22.6 times earnings and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue still growing around 40%, the price is fair for a franchise of this quality. The slow erosion in gross margin from 87% to 81%, and not fully understanding what drives the product's durability, keep me short of full conviction.

Reported earnings here swing wildly, from a P/E of 124 to one of 6. That tells me the income statement is carrying mark-to-market gains and losses on an investment portfolio, so I look past it to book value per share. Book value has compounded from about $115 to $212 in under five years, roughly 14% a year, and dipped only once. Free cash flow per share has held steady and edged up to about $13. With the market cap barely moving over the last three periods while book kept growing, the price appears to be a modest premium to a steadily compounding net worth rather than a demand for perfection. The data doesn't show leverage or underwriting detail, so I'm not swinging with full conviction, but this looks like a durable compounder at a fair price that I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a fine business. Gross margins have held in the low 60s through a full cycle, net margins run near 30%, returns on equity are in the 30s, and the balance sheet is strong, with a current ratio above 7 and modest debt. But the record also shows cyclicality I'd be foolish to ignore. Not long ago revenue fell 19% and ROE sank to 21%, and today's 64% revenue growth looks like a boom rather than a steady state. At nearly $800 billion and 38 times earnings, near the top of a surge, the price assumes the good times persist, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines until it's offered at a price that allows for a normal downturn.

The business absorbed a sharp revenue decline of about 11% without margins cracking, and it has since resumed growth at 19%, with free cash flow per share at a new high of $7.96. Flat book value per share alongside rising EPS tells me earnings are being returned to owners rather than hoarded. At 33 times earnings and roughly a 3.5% free cash flow yield, I'm paying a full price rather than a bargain one. But for a wonderful business compounding per-share earnings at double digits, a fair price is good enough to own for ten years.

This is a durable franchise. Gross margins have held around 66-70% for twenty periods and ROE runs in the mid-20s, apart from one year hit by what looks like a large one-time charge. Free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about $5.57 to $8.40, and debt is moderate at roughly 0.48 times equity. Book value per share has barely grown, which tells me the owners are getting the earnings back as dividends and buybacks rather than reinvestment. At about 24 times earnings, or roughly a 5% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue growth recently picking up to 11-13%, I'd call it a wonderful business at a fair, not cheap, price, and I'd be content to own it for a decade.

This is a wonderful business by the numbers. Gross margins widened from 38% to 43% and operating margins from 27% to 31%, and free cash flow per share compounded from $2.53 to $6.17, roughly 2.4 times, across the periods shown. That combination tells me customers keep paying up and the moat is widening. The shrinking book value and the 1.71 debt-to-equity ratio don't trouble me much here, since free cash flow runs above reported earnings and management appears to be returning capital aggressively, which also flatters that towering ROE. What tempers my enthusiasm is price. At 28 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3.6%, after a 29% revenue surge that may not repeat, I'm paying for a lot of good news, so I'd be a contented owner for a decade but not an eager buyer at this quote.

This is a wonderful business by every measure I care about. Returns on equity have climbed from the mid-20s to 44%, gross margins widened from 61% to 69% and operating margins nearly doubled to 43%, which is the signature of real pricing power. All of this happened while debt-to-equity fell from 1.2 to 0.33 and book value compounded at about 20% a year, so management has been allocating capital with discipline, and revenue growth has accelerated to 21% at enormous scale. The price is the rub. At roughly 31 times earnings and under a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full price that leaves little margin of safety, but a durable compounder growing near 20% is worth owning at a fair price, so I lean bullish with tempered conviction.

This is plainly a formidable retailer. Gross margins have widened from 36% to 42%, ROE has held in the 20s, and book value per share has compounded roughly fivefold, so the moat and the owner-minded reinvestment are there to see. What gives me pause is recent: free cash flow per share has swung from about $50 to negative $28.59, and operating margin has slipped from 7% to 5% while revenue growth has cooled from roughly 40% to 22%. Net margin now running above operating margin tells me some of that $64.81 in EPS may be non-operating and not repeatable. At about 49 times earnings and $1.6 trillion, I'd be paying a full price for a wonderful business just as its cash generation has stalled, so I'll admire it from the sidelines until the price or the cash flow gives me a margin of safety.

This is a toll-bridge sort of business: 57% gross margins, operating margins that have widened from 20% to 31%, practically no debt (D/E 0.06), a current ratio near 3, and book value per share compounding at about 13% a year, apparently without leaning on leverage. Free cash flow of about $101 a share tracks reported earnings of $112 closely, so the profits are real cash rather than accounting. At roughly 26 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of about 3.4%, I'm not getting a bargain. I'd also be wary that the recent 41% revenue growth and 30% ROE flatter the long-run picture, since returns averaged nearer 17% through most of the history and gross margin has slipped about 4 points. Still, a wonderful business at a fair price beats a fair business at a wonderful price, and I'd be comfortable owning this one for a decade.

This business earns 80%-plus gross margins, a 40% operating margin and a 32% return on equity with no debt. It also throws off about $13.68 per share in free cash flow, nearly matching reported earnings, which tells me the profits are real. Mr. Market has marked it down from about $1 trillion to $647 billion, so I'd be paying roughly 17 times earnings and getting close to a 6% free-cash yield for a company still growing revenue above 30%. That is a wonderful business at a fair price. The slight dip in book value per share looks like cash going back to owners through buybacks rather than a deterioration. My reservations are the slow slide in gross and operating margins and the fact that a technology moat is harder for me to judge ten years out than a candy company's, so I'm leaning in rather than backing up the truck.

This looks like an insurance-and-investment business whose reported earnings swing widely, with ROE anywhere from 1% to 23%. That is almost certainly mark-to-market noise on a securities portfolio rather than real volatility in the operations, so I look past it to book value per share. Book value has compounded at about 15% a year, from 118.71 to 228.61, with only one real dip (t-8 to t-7), and free cash flow per share has held positive and stable at roughly $9-14. The implied price of about $322 against $229 of book is roughly 1.4 times book, and the free cash flow yield is near 3.7%, a fair price for a business compounding owners' equity this steadily. The missing leverage and liquidity data keep me from betting the farm, but I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

This is a fine business. Gross margins have held in the low 60s through a full cycle, net margins run near 30%, returns on equity are in the 30s, and the balance sheet is strong, with a current ratio above 7 and modest debt. But the record also shows cyclicality I'd be foolish to ignore. Not long ago revenue fell 19% and ROE sank to 21%, and today's 64% revenue growth looks like a boom rather than a steady state. At nearly $800 billion and 38 times earnings, near the top of a surge, the price assumes the good times persist, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines until it's offered at a price that allows for a normal downturn.

This looks like a large, well-run money-center bank. Book value per share has compounded steadily from about $72 to nearly $100 over twenty periods, falling in none of them, even through a period when earnings dipped. Profits were paid out and shares likely repurchased along the way, which is the mark of disciplined capital allocation. ROE has climbed from about 10% to 16-17%, and at roughly 10x earnings and about 1.5x book the price is fair for a franchise earning well above its cost of capital. I temper my enthusiasm because bank balance sheets are never fully transparent from the outside, and today's 40% net margins are probably flattered by a favorable credit and rate cycle that won't last forever. Still, this is a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade at this price.

This is plainly a formidable retailer. This business keeps 80 cents of gross profit on every revenue dollar, earns roughly 30% on equity without debt, and has grown free cash flow per share from under $5 to over $14 across these periods. Those are the marks of a real economic franchise. The market has cut its valuation nearly in half, so the price is now about 15.6 times earnings with a free cash flow yield near 7%, a sensible price for a company still growing revenue at 27%. My caution is real, though. Operating margins have slid from 50% to 37%, EPS has dipped for three straight periods, and falling book value per share suggests heavy buybacks alongside heavy spending, so I'd want confidence that management's reinvestment will earn its keep. Even so, a wonderful business at a fair price is what I look for, and this one looks close to it.

This looks like an insurance-and-investment business whose reported earnings swing widely, with ROE anywhere from 1% to 23%. That is almost certainly mark-to-market noise on a securities portfolio rather than real volatility in the operations, so I look past it to book value per share. Book value has compounded at about 15% a year, from 118.71 to 228.61, with only one real dip (t-8 to t-7), and free cash flow per share has held positive and stable at roughly $9-14. The implied price of about $322 against $229 of book is roughly 1.4 times book, and the free cash flow yield is near 3.7%, a fair price for a business compounding owners' equity this steadily. The missing leverage and liquidity data keep me from betting the farm, but I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

This is plainly a fine business. Returns on equity run in the mid-30s, gross margins have widened to 65%, book value per share has compounded at roughly 35% a year, leverage is modest and liquidity is ample. But the record also shows real cyclicality: revenue shrank for several periods in the middle of this history and ROE nearly halved, so today's 60%-plus growth should not be projected forward as if it were a law of nature. At $664 billion and a P/E somewhere between 38 and 69 (the EPS series looks distorted, perhaps by a share split), the price already assumes the boom keeps going. That leaves little margin of safety for a manufacturer whose economics I can't fully see through the cycle, so I'd admire it from the sidelines rather than buy at this price.

This looks like a large, well-run money-center bank. Book value per share has compounded steadily from about $72 to nearly $100 over twenty periods, falling in none of them, even through a period when earnings dipped. Profits were paid out and shares likely repurchased along the way, which is the mark of disciplined capital allocation. ROE has climbed from about 10% to 16-17%, and at roughly 10x earnings and about 1.5x book the price is fair for a franchise earning well above its cost of capital. I temper my enthusiasm because bank balance sheets are never fully transparent from the outside, and today's 40% net margins are probably flattered by a favorable credit and rate cycle that won't last forever. Still, this is a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade at this price.

This is a toll-bridge business. Operating margins have held around 63-67% and net margins near 50% for twenty straight periods, and it earns 38% on equity with no gross-margin line to protect, which tells me it barely needs capital to grow. It rode out a sharp revenue decline of about 11% without the margins cracking, then came back with 26% revenue growth and record EPS of $7.24 and free cash flow of $8.04 a share, well above earnings. Book value per share is flat because the cash goes back to owners, and debt at 0.58 times equity is comfortable against those earnings. At roughly 30 times earnings, or about a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield, I'm not getting a bargain, but paying a fair price for a wonderful business I'd happily own for ten years is a trade I'll make.

This business has a real moat. Gross margins have held at 66-69% for twenty periods, ROE runs in the mid-20s, and free cash flow of about $7.40 a share comes in steadily whatever the reported earnings do. The collapse to 2% net margins at t-14 through t-17 looks like a one-off charge rather than a broken franchise, since cash flow never budged. Debt at 0.44x equity is conservative, and book value compounds slowly only because the owners are being paid out. At about 24 times earnings and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, with revenue growth recently back to 11-14%, this is a wonderful company at a fair but not bargain price, so I'd buy it and hold it with moderate rather than table-pounding conviction.

This is a remarkable economic engine. Gross margins have widened from 38% to 43% and operating margins from 27% to 31%, and free cash flow per share has climbed from $2.46 to $6.45, which is the mark of real pricing power. The shrinking book value and the 1.78 debt/equity ratio don't come from losses. They reflect management handing back more cash than the business retains, mostly through share repurchases, and that is why ROE sits at an eye-popping 151%. I'd watch the sub-1.0 current ratio and the slowdown from 33% to 19% revenue growth, since recent years may have pulled demand forward. Still, at roughly 25x earnings and about a 4% free-cash-flow yield, you're paying a fair price for a wonderful business, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This is a business with a real moat. Gross margins have crept up from 62% to 69%, operating margins have climbed from 25% to 43%, and it earns 44% on equity while cutting debt/equity from 1.19 to 0.31, all while revenue grows about 20% a year. Management has compounded book value per share at roughly 19% and more than tripled EPS from $2.71 to $9.58, with free cash flow per share rising steadily. The multiple has also come down from about 35 to 28 times earnings, which works out to roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield. That isn't a bargain, but it is a fair price for a wonderful business I'd be happy to own for ten years, and a $2 trillion size means the growth runway, not the quality, is my main question.

This business has a real moat. Revenue has compounded at 20-40% a year, gross margins have widened from 36% to 42%, and book value per share has grown roughly fivefold, which tells me customers keep coming back and management keeps reinvesting at decent returns. What gives me pause is the recent turn: free cash flow per share has swung from about +$50 to -$48, trailing EPS has fallen from $64.81 to $41.46, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The market still asks 60 times depressed earnings for a business that earns about four cents on the sales dollar. It's a wonderful franchise, but at this price and with cash burning during a heavy spending cycle, I'd rather watch from the sidelines than pay up for hope.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I use. ROE has climbed from the high 30s to 44%, operating margins have widened from 25% to 42%, and gross margins have held near 68% while revenue grows 18–20% a year. That is pricing power and a moat that is getting wider, not narrower. At 28–29 times earnings, roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm not getting a bargain. But the multiple has come down from the mid-30s as earnings kept compounding, and I'd rather pay a fair price for a business like this and hold it for a decade.

This is a remarkably profitable business that has grown stronger. Returns on equity climbed from roughly 10% to 28%, operating margins widened from about 20% to 30%, and gross margins held near the mid-50s through the whole record. Book value per share has compounded at around 12% with almost no debt (D/E 0.06) and a current ratio near 3, while free cash flow per share has more than tripled over the period. The latest P/E of 1.01 is plainly a data artifact, since the EPS jump to 111.96 doesn't square with a 28% ROE on $19.53 of book, so I lean on the prior reading of about 21 times earnings. Growth is decelerating and net margins have slipped from 30% to 26%, which keeps me from pounding the table, but a wonderful, cash-gushing franchise at roughly 20 times earnings is a fair price I'd happily hold for a decade.

This is a big retailer with a moat I can respect. Gross margins have widened steadily from 36% to 43%, book value per share has compounded roughly fivefold, and returns on equity sat in the 20s for years. But the recent numbers are going the wrong way: ROE has fallen from 26% to 9%, operating margin has shrunk from 7% to 3%, free cash flow per share has been negative for three straight periods, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The latest 2.15 P/E does not square with a 2% net margin and a $12.90 book value per share; it looks like a share-count or split quirk in the data rather than a bargain. On the more reliable figures, at roughly 60 times earnings with no free cash flow, a $1.37 trillion price leaves no margin of safety, so I'd watch this one rather than buy it.

This business has transformed itself. It went from years of losses, negative free cash flow and debt near twice equity to a 26% return on equity, 14% net margins, gross margins that widened from about 17% to 27%, and almost no debt. That is an impressive turnaround, but two or three good years in a capital-hungry manufacturing industry don't yet prove a durable moat, and much of the early growth in book value came during a period of heavy losses. At roughly 97 times earnings and an owner's yield under 1% on free cash flow, an $841 billion price already assumes many more years of this growth. I admire the operating progress, but a price that demands perfection keeps me on the sidelines rather than buying or betting against it.

Book value per share has compounded about 12% a year and free cash flow has run at or above reported earnings, which tells me management allocates capital sensibly and the moat of scale is real. The trouble is the price: earnings per share are barely higher than they were seven periods ago (17.79 then versus 18.27 now), yet the market cap has climbed from about 289B to 476B as the P/E expanded from 17 to nearly 28. Free cash flow is $13.21 a share against a P/E of about 13, which is roughly a 7-8% owner's yield on a company that still grew revenue 14% in the latest year. The worry is real, though. That tells me either the moat is being tested or management is spending heavily on something I can't evaluate from these numbers. When a business with this much cash generation and this little leverage sells at a market-average multiple, I'd rather lean in modestly than run. I'd size the position mindful that I can't fully see where those shrinking margins bottom out.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins widened from 38% to 43% and operating margins from 27% to 31% while revenue compounded, which is pricing power you can see in the numbers. The shrinking book value per share and the ROE above 170% are not signs of distress. Management has been returning more than it earns through buybacks, so free cash flow per share nearly tripled from $2.43 to $6.62 and EPS rose from $2.30 to $6.05. The leverage (D/E 2.06, current ratio 0.86) would worry me in a lesser company, and at about 27 times earnings with EPS flat over the last two periods I'm paying a full price. Still, a fair price for a franchise of this quality is one I'd hold for a decade, so I'm bullish but not with table-pounding conviction.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I use. ROE has climbed from the high 30s to 44%, operating margins have widened from 25% to 42%, and gross margins have held near 68% while revenue grows 18–20% a year. That is pricing power and a moat that is getting wider, not narrower. Management has cut debt/equity from about 1.1 to 0.30 while compounding book value about 15% a year, and free cash flow per share has roughly doubled without a hiccup; the earlier EPS dip looks like a one-time charge, since cash flow never faltered. At 28–29 times earnings, roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm not getting a bargain. But the multiple has come down from the mid-30s as earnings kept compounding, and I'd rather pay a fair price for a business like this and hold it for a decade.

This is a remarkably profitable business that has grown stronger. Returns on equity climbed from roughly 10% to 28%, operating margins widened from about 20% to 30%, and gross margins held near the mid-50s through the whole record. Book value per share has compounded at around 12% with almost no debt (D/E 0.06) and a current ratio near 3, while free cash flow per share has more than tripled over the period. The latest P/E of 1.01 is plainly a data artifact, since the EPS jump to 111.96 doesn't square with a 28% ROE on $19.53 of book, so I lean on the prior reading of about 21 times earnings. Growth is decelerating and net margins have slipped from 30% to 26%, which keeps me from pounding the table, but a wonderful, cash-gushing franchise at roughly 20 times earnings is a fair price I'd happily hold for a decade.

This is a big retailer with a moat I can respect. Gross margins have widened steadily from 36% to 43%, book value per share has compounded roughly fivefold, and returns on equity sat in the 20s for years. But the recent numbers are going the wrong way: ROE has fallen from 26% to 9%, operating margin has shrunk from 7% to 3%, free cash flow per share has been negative for three straight periods, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The latest 2.15 P/E does not square with a 2% net margin and a $12.90 book value per share; it looks like a share-count or split quirk in the data rather than a bargain. On the more reliable figures, at roughly 60 times earnings with no free cash flow, a $1.37 trillion price leaves no margin of safety, so I'd watch this one rather than buy it.

This business has transformed itself. It went from years of losses, negative free cash flow and debt near twice equity to a 26% return on equity, 14% net margins, gross margins that widened from about 17% to 27%, and almost no debt. That is an impressive turnaround, but two or three good years in a capital-hungry manufacturing industry don't yet prove a durable moat, and much of the early growth in book value came during a period of heavy losses. At roughly 97 times earnings and an owner's yield under 1% on free cash flow, an $841 billion price already assumes many more years of this growth. I admire the operating progress, but a price that demands perfection keeps me on the sidelines rather than buying or betting against it.

This is a diversified insurance and finance enterprise whose reported earnings swing wildly, with P/E ranging from 6 to 124. That tells me mark-to-market investment results are distorting the income statement, so I'd look at book value and cash generation instead. On that score the record is fine: book value per share compounded at roughly 14% a year, from about $122 to $230, including through a down year, and free cash flow stayed positive in every period while revenue growth picked up to 12-13%. At roughly 8.4 times earnings and about 1.4 times book (implied from the P/E and EPS shown), you are paying a fair price for a compounder of that quality. I would temper conviction for three reasons: free cash flow per share has slipped from $13 to about $10.50, there is no debt or current-ratio data to judge financial strength, and the underlying earnings power is hard to pin down from these figures.

This is a wonderful, understandable franchise. It is a high-volume, thin-margin insurer earning a steady 20-25% return on equity with modest leverage, around 0.6x debt to equity. Book value per share has compounded about 12% a year and free cash flow has run at or above reported earnings, which tells me management allocates capital sensibly and the moat of scale is real. The trouble is the price: earnings per share are barely higher than they were seven periods ago (17.79 then versus 18.27 now), yet the market cap has climbed from about 289B to 476B as the P/E expanded from 17 to nearly 28. I'd happily own this business at a fair price, but today's multiple assumes a growth resumption the recent numbers haven't yet delivered, so I'll wait.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. Gross margins have held at 66-68% for five years, ROE runs in the mid-20s outside one charge-laden stretch, leverage is modest at 0.43 debt/equity, and free cash flow of roughly $7-8 per share arrives like clockwork. But per-share free cash flow has only crept from about $6.75 to $7.48 over the full span, and earnings slipped from $7.81 to $6.87 as net margin eased from 22% to 19%. That one-year collapse in earnings (P/E above 230) tells me there are large, lumpy liabilities I can't fully size from these numbers. At about 25 times earnings and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full price for a slow grower, so I'd be glad to own it but would rather wait for a fatter pitch.

This business keeps 80 cents of every revenue dollar as gross profit, carries no debt, has a current ratio above 2.5, and has compounded book value per share at about 15% a year while buying back stock. Free cash flow is $13.21 a share against a P/E of about 13, which is roughly a 7-8% owner's yield on a company that still grew revenue 14% in the latest year. The worry is real, though. Operating margin has slid from 50% to 33%, EPS has fallen from its $13.98 peak, and the market has cut the price by more than half. That tells me either the moat is being tested or management is spending heavily on something I can't evaluate from these numbers. When a business with this much cash generation and this little leverage sells at a market-average multiple, I'd rather lean in modestly than run. I'd size the position mindful that I can't fully see where those shrinking margins bottom out.

This looks like a diversified insurance and finance enterprise whose reported earnings jump from $1.63 to $46.79 a share depending on the year. That tells me GAAP net income is dominated by mark-to-market swings on investments, so the P/E of 55 means little. The better yardstick is book value per share, which has compounded about 12% a year from $124.95 to $209.55 across this history, with free cash flow of roughly $9-13 a share every period. At an implied price near $292, the stock sells for about 1.4 times book, a fair price for a business that has grown its net worth this steadily. I'd want to know whether the latest drop in book value from $230 to $210 is a market mark or a genuine loss, and debt data is missing, but I'd be comfortable owning this for ten years.

This is a fine business. Returns on equity have held between 21% and 26% for nearly twenty periods, book value per share has compounded at about 11%, and free cash flow per share (21.53) runs ahead of reported earnings (19.14), which tells me the profits are real cash. Margins are thin at about 6% net, but they have not budged across the whole record, and leverage around 0.67 debt-to-equity is sensible for a scale operator whose float-like cash flows support a current ratio below one. My hesitation is the price. The multiple has climbed from about 17 times earnings to over 28, while per-share earnings rose only from 17.79 to 19.14 over the last eight periods. That leaves me buying at roughly a 3.5–4% owner's yield for a business compounding at around 10%, a full price for a wonderful company rather than a fair one, so I would watch and wait for a better pitch.

Management has cut debt/equity from about 1.1 to 0.30 while compounding book value about 15% a year, and free cash flow per share has roughly doubled without a hiccup; the earlier EPS dip looks like a one-time charge, since cash flow never faltered. At 28–29 times earnings, roughly a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm not getting a bargain. But the multiple has come down from the mid-30s as earnings kept compounding, and I'd rather pay a fair price for a business like this and hold it for a decade.

This is a remarkably profitable business that has grown stronger. Returns on equity climbed from roughly 10% to 28%, operating margins widened from about 20% to 30%, and gross margins held near the mid-50s through the whole record. Book value per share has compounded at around 12% with almost no debt (D/E 0.06) and a current ratio near 3, while free cash flow per share has more than tripled over the period. The latest P/E of 1.01 is plainly a data artifact, since the EPS jump to 111.96 doesn't square with a 28% ROE on $19.53 of book, so I lean on the prior reading of about 21 times earnings. Growth is decelerating and net margins have slipped from 30% to 26%, which keeps me from pounding the table, but a wonderful, cash-gushing franchise at roughly 20 times earnings is a fair price I'd happily hold for a decade.

This is a big retailer with a moat I can respect. Gross margins have widened steadily from 36% to 43%, book value per share has compounded roughly fivefold, and returns on equity sat in the 20s for years. But the recent numbers are going the wrong way: ROE has fallen from 26% to 9%, operating margin has shrunk from 7% to 3%, free cash flow per share has been negative for three straight periods, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The latest 2.15 P/E does not square with a 2% net margin and a $12.90 book value per share; it looks like a share-count or split quirk in the data rather than a bargain. On the more reliable figures, at roughly 60 times earnings with no free cash flow, a $1.37 trillion price leaves no margin of safety, so I'd watch this one rather than buy it.

This business has made a remarkable turnaround. Operating margins went from a loss of 17% to a profit of 16%, return on equity reached 26%, debt/equity fell from above 2 to 0.06, and book value compounded handsomely. But good returns for two or three years in a capital-hungry manufacturing industry are not yet proof of a durable moat, and the long history of losses tells me the economics can swing hard. At roughly 97 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 1% on an $841 billion market cap, the price assumes years of near-flawless high growth, and I would rather admire this one from the sidelines than pay for perfection.

This looks like a diversified insurance and finance enterprise whose reported earnings jump from $1.63 to $46.79 a share depending on the year. That tells me GAAP net income is dominated by mark-to-market swings on investments, so the P/E of 55 means little. The better yardstick is book value per share, which has compounded about 12% a year from $124.95 to $209.55 across this history, with free cash flow of roughly $9-13 a share every period. At an implied price near $292, the stock sells for about 1.4 times book, a fair price for a business that has grown its net worth this steadily. I'd want to know whether the latest drop in book value from $230 to $210 is a market mark or a genuine loss, and debt data is missing, but I'd be comfortable owning this for ten years.

This is a fine business. Returns on equity have held between 21% and 26% for nearly twenty periods, book value per share has compounded at about 11%, and free cash flow per share (21.53) runs ahead of reported earnings (19.14), which tells me the profits are real cash. Margins are thin at about 6% net, but they have not budged across the whole record, and leverage around 0.67 debt-to-equity is sensible for a scale operator whose float-like cash flows support a current ratio below one. My hesitation is the price. The multiple has climbed from about 17 times earnings to over 28, while per-share earnings rose only from 17.79 to 19.14 over the last eight periods. That leaves me buying at roughly a 3.5–4% owner's yield for a business compounding at around 10%, a full price for a wonderful company rather than a fair one, so I would watch and wait for a better pitch.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. Gross margins have held at 66-68% for five years, ROE runs in the mid-20s outside one charge-laden stretch, leverage is modest at 0.43 debt/equity, and free cash flow of roughly $7-8 per share arrives like clockwork. But per-share free cash flow has only crept from about $6.75 to $7.48 over the full span, and earnings slipped from $7.81 to $6.87 as net margin eased from 22% to 19%. That one-year collapse in earnings (P/E above 230) tells me there are large, lumpy liabilities I can't fully size from these numbers. At about 25 times earnings and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full price for a slow grower, so I'd be glad to own it but would rather wait for a fatter pitch.

This business keeps 80 cents of every revenue dollar as gross profit, carries no debt, has a current ratio above 2.5, and has compounded book value per share at about 15% a year while buying back stock. Free cash flow is $13.21 a share against a P/E of about 13, which is roughly a 7-8% owner's yield on a company that still grew revenue 14% in the latest year. The worry is real, though. Operating margin has slid from 50% to 33%, EPS has fallen from its $13.98 peak, and the market has cut the price by more than half. That tells me either the moat is being tested or management is spending heavily on something I can't evaluate from these numbers. When a business with this much cash generation and this little leverage sells at a market-average multiple, I'd rather lean in modestly than run. I'd size the position mindful that I can't fully see where those shrinking margins bottom out.

A trillion-dollar price on a 2% net margin and negative free cash flow asks for a margin recovery I can't count on, so I'll admire this one from the sidelines.

But the recent picture is plainly deteriorating: operating margins have halved from 7% to 3%, ROE has fallen from 26% to 8%, free cash flow per share has swung from +$2.50 to about -$2.50, growth has slowed to 10%, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The reported P/E of 1.65 is clearly a per-share data artifact, since EPS jumps from about 2 to 62 while margins fall. Backing into earnings from an 8% ROE on $13.48 of book gives roughly $1 a share, so I estimate, rather than know, that the true multiple is still very rich. A trillion-dollar price on a 2% net margin and negative free cash flow asks for a margin recovery I can't count on, so I'll admire this one from the sidelines.

This is a remarkable turnaround. A manufacturer that lost money for years has cut debt/equity from about 2 to 0.04, lifted gross margins from 14% to 27% and now earns a 28% return on equity while growing revenue about 60% a year. But the record of real profitability is only a few years long, in a capital-hungry industry where moats have historically been hard to hold. That makes me cautious about calling this a durable franchise rather than a cyclical high point. At roughly 32 times earnings, about 17 times book and a free-cash-flow yield near 1%, the price already assumes years of flawless growth, so I would admire the progress from the sidelines rather than pay up for it.

This looks like a diversified insurance and finance enterprise whose reported earnings jump from $1.63 to $46.79 a share depending on the year. That tells me GAAP net income is dominated by mark-to-market swings on investments, so the P/E of 55 means little. The better yardstick is book value per share, which has compounded about 12% a year from $124.95 to $209.55 across this history, with free cash flow of roughly $9-13 a share every period. At an implied price near $292, the stock sells for about 1.4 times book, a fair price for a business that has grown its net worth this steadily. I'd want to know whether the latest drop in book value from $230 to $210 is a market mark or a genuine loss, and debt data is missing, but I'd be comfortable owning this for ten years.

This is a fine business. Returns on equity have held between 21% and 26% for nearly twenty periods, book value per share has compounded at about 11%, and free cash flow per share (21.53) runs ahead of reported earnings (19.14), which tells me the profits are real cash. Margins are thin at about 6% net, but they have not budged across the whole record, and leverage around 0.67 debt-to-equity is sensible for a scale operator whose float-like cash flows support a current ratio below one. My hesitation is the price. The multiple has climbed from about 17 times earnings to over 28, while per-share earnings rose only from 17.79 to 19.14 over the last eight periods. That leaves me buying at roughly a 3.5–4% owner's yield for a business compounding at around 10%, a full price for a wonderful company rather than a fair one, so I would watch and wait for a better pitch.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have held at 66-68% for twenty periods, ROE runs in the mid-20s, net margins sit near 20%, and the balance sheet is conservative, with debt/equity down to 0.43 and a current ratio of 1.43. That kind of consistency, with only one tax-type earnings dip years back, tells me the moat is real. But at 24 times earnings I'm paying roughly a 4% earnings yield and a similar free-cash-flow yield, while revenue growth has slowed to 5%, FCF per share has slipped from about 8.45 to 6.67, and book value per share has compounded only about 5%. A great company at a full price earns a hold-and-watch from me, and I'd be a far keener buyer a good deal lower.

This is an extraordinary economic engine. Gross margins sit around 80%, return on equity has held at roughly 20-30% for years, debt is negligible at 0.08 debt/equity, and the current ratio of 2.57 is comfortable. The trend is troubling, though. Operating margin has slid from 50% to 30%, revenue growth has fallen from the 40s to 5%, and both EPS and free cash flow per share are down from their peaks, so management is spending heavily and I would want to see that capital earn its keep. Still, at about 9 times earnings, with free cash flow near 10% of the price and a pristine balance sheet, Mr. Market is pricing this wonderful business as if it were a fair one, and that is a margin of safety I am willing to accept.

This is a toll bridge. Operating margins have held around 63-67% and net margins near 50% for twenty straight periods, a shock that cut revenue by as much as 11% barely dented them, and growth has since come back at 19-26%. Book value per share is flat only because management returns the cash through buybacks; ROE has climbed to 41%, and free cash flow per share has roughly doubled from 4.10 to 8.50 while debt stays modest against that cash generation. At about 27 times earnings, the cheapest multiple here in several years and roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield on a business still compounding at double digits, I'd call it a wonderful company at a fair price and be glad to own it for a decade.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Gross margins have widened from 38% to 43%, operating margins sit near 30%, and free cash flow per share has climbed from $2.56 to $6.83 over the period, so the owners are clearly being served. The shrinking book value and 2.37 debt-to-equity reflect heavy buybacks rather than distress, though a current ratio below 1 tells me management is running the balance sheet lean. My hesitation is price: at roughly 25 times earnings, EPS has been flat around $6 for four periods and revenue growth has slowed from 33% to 8%, so I'd be paying a full price for a business that has paused. A great company at a fair-to-full price is one I'd happily keep owning but not rush to add to.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I use. Returns on equity have held near 40%, gross margins have crept up to 68%, and operating margins have widened from 25% to 42%. There are some soft spots: revenue growth has slowed from about 20% to 15%, net margin has slipped from 39% to 34%, and EPS dipped slightly in the latest period, so I wouldn't pay anything that assumes perfection. At about 27 times earnings, down from the mid-30s, and roughly a 3.4% free cash flow yield, this looks like a fair price for an exceptional franchise, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

Here is a financial enterprise whose reported earnings swing wildly, from an ROE of 23% to below zero, while revenue grows steadily at 10% or better. That tells me the headline numbers are dominated by marking investments to market rather than by the underlying business, which has compounded book value per share at a respectable 8% a year with no evident leverage problem. This is a durable, understandable franchise. The market has re-rated the stock from about 17-18x earnings to nearly 27x, an earnings yield under 4% for a business growing in the low teens. That is a wonderful company at a full price, so I'd be happy to own it but would rather wait for a fatter pitch before buying more.

The reported P/E of 1.65 is clearly a per-share data artifact, since EPS jumps from about 2 to 62 while margins fall. My hesitation is price: at roughly 25 times earnings, EPS has been flat around $6 for four periods and revenue growth has slowed from 33% to 8%, so I'd be paying a full price for a business that has paused. A great company at a fair-to-full price is one I'd happily keep owning but not rush to add to.

This business has the marks of a real moat. Gross margins have held at 65-69% for twenty periods, operating margins widened from 26% to 41%, and returns on equity have stayed near 40%, all while debt-to-equity fell from 0.97 to 0.26 and book value per share compounded at about 20%. The recent softening is real: revenue growth has slowed from 21% to 10%, and EPS and free cash flow per share have slipped a few percent from their peak. But margins barely budged, which looks like a cyclical pause rather than a crack in the franchise. At about 27 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 3.3%, down from mid-30s multiples, I'm not getting a bargain, but I am paying a fair price for a wonderful business I'd be glad to own for a decade.

This is a fortress. Returns on equity run in the high 20s with debt at just 6% of equity, a current ratio above 2.5, and book value per share compounding about 13% a year for two decades of quarters. The reported P/E of 0.85 is plainly a data mismatch, since EPS jumps twentyfold while book value and free cash flow per share don't budge. Underlying earnings look like roughly $5.5 a share, so at a 1.23 trillion market cap, down about 37% from the peak, I'm paying something like 17 times earnings for a business still growing revenue 18% with 24% net margins. Margins are slipping a bit and growth is cooling from the 40% pace, so I'm not pounding the table. But a wonderful business at a fair price is exactly what I want to own for ten years.

This retailer has built something formidable. Revenue has compounded at 20-40% a year for much of this history, gross margins have crept up from 37% to 43%, and book value per share has roughly quadrupled. But the recent picture is plainly deteriorating: operating margins have halved from 7% to 3%, ROE has fallen from 26% to 8%, free cash flow per share has swung from +$2.50 to about -$2.50, growth has slowed to 10%, and the current ratio has slipped below 1. The reported P/E of 1.65 is clearly a per-share data artifact, since EPS jumps from about 2 to 62 while margins fall. Backing into earnings from an 8% ROE on $13.48 of book gives roughly $1 a share, so I estimate, rather than know, that the true multiple is still very rich. A trillion-dollar price on a 2% net margin and negative free cash flow asks for a margin recovery I can't count on, so I'll admire this one from the sidelines.

This business has transformed itself. It went from years of heavy losses, a debt-to-equity ratio near 2 and a current ratio below 1 to a 28% return on equity, a 17% operating margin, almost no debt and book value per share compounding rapidly. That is impressive work, and the balance sheet is now a fortress. But carmaking has historically been a brutal, capital-hungry trade, and three or so years of strong profits is too short a record for me to call the moat durable. Even after the market cap fell by nearly half from its peak, I'd be paying about 48 times earnings and roughly 80 times free cash flow per share, which is a price that assumes the 50%-plus growth keeps coming. It's a fine business at a price that leaves no margin of safety, so I'll watch from the sidelines rather than bet against it.

Here is a financial enterprise whose reported earnings swing wildly, from an ROE of 23% to below zero, while revenue grows steadily at 10% or better. That tells me the headline numbers are dominated by marking investments to market rather than by the underlying business, which has compounded book value per share at a respectable 8% a year with no evident leverage problem. But the recent picture gives me pause: book value per share has slipped from about 230 to 207 over the last two periods, and free cash flow per share has fallen from roughly 13 to 9 even as revenue grew. At a roughly flat market cap near 638B, the price looks fair rather than a bargain, so I'd want either clearer evidence that cash generation is recovering or a better price before calling it a buy.

This is a durable, understandable franchise. Return on equity has held at 21-26% for roughly twenty periods, margins have been steady on thin but reliable spreads, and EPS has nearly doubled from 10.72 to 20.41 while book value per share compounded at about 11% with sensible leverage around 0.6x. Free cash flow per share has consistently matched or beaten reported earnings, which is the mark of real, owner-friendly economics. The trouble is price. The market has re-rated the stock from about 17-18x earnings to nearly 27x, an earnings yield under 4% for a business growing in the low teens. That is a wonderful company at a full price, so I'd be happy to own it but would rather wait for a fatter pitch before buying more.

This is a wonderful franchise by the numbers. It earns 55% gross margins and a mid-20s operating margin through the cycle, has averaged about 20% returns on equity with almost no debt (D/E 0.06), and carries a current ratio above 2. Free cash flow of $4.67 a share slightly exceeds reported EPS of $4.56, so the earnings are real cash. At about 23 times earnings, roughly a 4.5% free-cash-flow yield, the price is fair for a business of this quality and well below the 30-plus multiples it carried earlier. There is plainly a moat here. Gross margins have widened steadily from 38% to 44% over five years, revenue has compounded at 20-40% for most of that stretch, and book value per share has grown more than fourfold with sensible leverage around 0.5 debt/equity. But the recent picture is troubling. Revenue growth has slowed to 9%, operating margins have been squeezed to 2%, trailing earnings have turned negative, and free cash flow has been negative for five straight periods, with the current ratio below 1. A business like this at over a trillion dollars, with no current earnings or owner cash to anchor the price, asks me to pay for a recovery I can't yet see in the numbers. So I'll admire it from the sidelines rather than call it cheap.

Reported earnings here swing wildly, from 0.42 net margins to losses, while free cash flow per share holds steady at roughly $9–13. That tells me the red ink looks like mark-to-market noise on an investment portfolio rather than a broken operating business, though the data doesn't let me confirm it. What I care about is book value per share, which has compounded about 9% a year from $140.79 to $215.95 over the period, with revenue now growing 9–13% and only a modest drawdown in book from its $230 peak. I can't pin down price-to-book or a free-cash-flow yield without a share count, so my conviction is tempered. Still, a steadily compounding financial enterprise whose market cap has barely moved in recent periods while book value kept rising looks like a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a scale insurance-and-services franchise earning a steady 23-25% return on equity on thin but remarkably stable 5-6% net margins. That consistency across twenty periods tells me the moat is scale and float, not luck. Earnings per share have nearly doubled from $11.36 to $21.18, book value has compounded at roughly 11% a year, and free cash flow per share of $24.64 exceeds reported earnings. Debt at 0.71x equity is sensible, and a current ratio under 1 is normal when you hold policyholders' money. At about 23 times earnings, down from 28, and roughly a 5% free-cash-flow yield, this is a wonderful business at a fair price, though not a bargain. The thin margins leave it exposed to medical-cost or regulatory surprises, which keeps my conviction moderate.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. Gross margins have held around 66-68% for twenty periods, returns on equity sit in the mid-20s, and net margins near 19% show real pricing power. Debt is modest, and aside from a one-time earnings hit several years back, results have been steady as a metronome. But the recent trend gives me pause. Revenue growth has slowed to 1%, free cash flow per share has slid from about $8.45 to $6.45, and the current ratio has dropped below 1 as debt rose, which suggests a sizable commitment I can't yet judge. At roughly 23.5 times earnings and about a 4% free cash flow yield, I'm paying a full price for a slowing grower. I'd happily own this business, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch.

At a P/E of about 22 on shrinking earnings, and a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3.7%, the bargain available one period ago at 9 times earnings is gone, so I would watch rather than buy.

This business has transformed itself. It went from years of heavy losses, a debt-to-equity ratio near 2 and a current ratio below 1 to a 28% return on equity, a 17% operating margin, almost no debt and book value per share compounding rapidly. That is impressive work, and the balance sheet is now a fortress. But carmaking has historically been a brutal, capital-hungry trade, and three or so years of strong profits is too short a record for me to call the moat durable. Even after the market cap fell by nearly half from its peak, I'd be paying about 48 times earnings and roughly 80 times free cash flow per share, which is a price that assumes the 50%-plus growth keeps coming. It's a fine business at a price that leaves no margin of safety, so I'll watch from the sidelines rather than bet against it.

Reported earnings here swing wildly, from 0.42 net margins to losses, while free cash flow per share holds steady at roughly $9–13. That tells me the red ink looks like mark-to-market noise on an investment portfolio rather than a broken operating business, though the data doesn't let me confirm it. What I care about is book value per share, which has compounded about 9% a year from $140.79 to $215.95 over the period, with revenue now growing 9–13% and only a modest drawdown in book from its $230 peak. I can't pin down price-to-book or a free-cash-flow yield without a share count, so my conviction is tempered. Still, a steadily compounding financial enterprise whose market cap has barely moved in recent periods while book value kept rising looks like a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

The turnaround here is remarkable. This looks like a large insurance-and-investment enterprise whose reported earnings swing wildly, from a 42% net margin to a loss, which tells me mark-to-market investment gains and losses dominate the income statement. It's a sturdy, well-financed business I'd be comfortable owning, but at this price I'd expect returns closer to 7% than 12%, so I'm content to wait for a better entry.

Paying 68 times shrinking earnings, with a free cash flow yield near half a percent, is a price that demands perfection from a business showing compression, so I'll stand aside and lean bearish.

Reported earnings here swing from losses to 40-plus dollars a share, which tells me they are dominated by mark-to-market moves on investments rather than by the business itself. So I look past them to book value per share, which has compounded at about 11% a year across these periods with only brief dips, and to free cash flow per share, which has crept steadily upward. That is a sensible price for a financial enterprise that keeps compounding its equity at double digits without apparent strain. The one thing that tempers my conviction is that price is about 30 times free cash flow per share, and the data don't let me separate underlying operating earnings from investment gains. So I'm comfortable owning it for a decade, but at a fair price rather than a bargain.

This is a formidable retail franchise. This is a business with about 79% gross margins, returns on equity running 17-32% across the cycle, and a balance sheet with almost no debt (D/E 0.13, current ratio 2.57). Those are the marks of a real franchise rather than a commodity. What gives me pause is that operating margins have slid from the low-40s to about 29%, and management has spent heavily enough that book value per share grew slowly for several years even as earnings piled up. That tells me some capital went into bets I can't evaluate from these figures. Still, revenue growth has resumed, EPS has rebounded to $11.33, and free cash flow of $14.23 a share gives roughly a 5% owner's yield at 25 times earnings, which is a fair price for a wonderful business rather than one demanding perfection. I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, provided management shows more discipline on spending than the margin trend suggests it has so far.

This is a toll bridge, not a factory. Operating margins have held at 63-67% for twenty straight periods, net margins sit above 50%, and returns on equity have climbed to 45%. Leverage is modest, and the business came through a sharp revenue decline without margins so much as flinching. Earnings per share rose from 5.36 to 9.41, and free cash flow per share grew from about 6.21 to 10.73. At roughly 26 times earnings and about a 4.3% free-cash-flow yield, down from the 44 times the market paid a few years ago, you're paying a fair price for a wonderful business with double-digit growth, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This looks like a large, understandable health-insurance and services franchise. It has earned 20-26% on equity every period shown, net margins have held steady around 6%, and it has compounded EPS from about $12 to $23 and book value per share at roughly 12% a year, with free cash flow per share generally at or above earnings. That consistency, together with 13-14% revenue growth at this scale, points to a durable moat and sensible capital allocation. Leverage of 0.74 debt-to-equity is reasonable, and a current ratio below one is normal for an insurer holding float. At 23 times earnings you are paying a fair price rather than a bargain, but a wonderful business at a fair price is a deal I'd take and hold for ten years, while watching for regulatory risk to those thin margins.

The steadier measures tell the true story: book value per share compounded from about 142 to 243, roughly 12% a year, with only brief dips. Free cash flow per share rose from 9.29 to 12.34, and revenue is growing about 18%. At about 9.8 times trailing earnings and roughly 1.4 times book (my estimate from the figures shown), you are paying a fair price for a business that keeps compounding owner's equity, and I'd be comfortable holding it for a decade. Confidence is tempered because no leverage or liquidity data is shown and the earnings volatility makes normalized returns harder to pin down.

This is a business with about 79% gross margins, returns on equity running 17-32% across the cycle, and a balance sheet with almost no debt (D/E 0.13, current ratio 2.57). Those are the marks of a real franchise rather than a commodity. What gives me pause is that operating margins have slid from the low-40s to about 29%, and management has spent heavily enough that book value per share grew slowly for several years even as earnings piled up. That tells me some capital went into bets I can't evaluate from these figures. Still, revenue growth has resumed, EPS has rebounded to $11.33, and free cash flow of $14.23 a share gives roughly a 5% owner's yield at 25 times earnings, which is a fair price for a wonderful business rather than one demanding perfection. I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade, provided management shows more discipline on spending than the margin trend suggests it has so far.

This is a toll bridge, not a factory. Operating margins have held at 63-67% for twenty straight periods, net margins sit above 50%, and returns on equity have climbed to 45%. Leverage is modest, and the business came through a sharp revenue decline without margins so much as flinching. Earnings per share rose from 5.36 to 9.41, and free cash flow per share grew from about 6.21 to 10.73. Book value compounded slowly because the cash is being handed back to owners rather than piled up, which is exactly what I want from a business that needs little capital. At roughly 26 times earnings and about a 4.3% free-cash-flow yield, down from the 44 times the market paid a few years ago, you're paying a fair price for a wonderful business with double-digit growth, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

This looks like a large, understandable health-insurance and services franchise. It has earned 20-26% on equity every period shown, net margins have held steady around 6%, and it has compounded EPS from about $12 to $23 and book value per share at roughly 12% a year, with free cash flow per share generally at or above earnings. That consistency, together with 13-14% revenue growth at this scale, points to a durable moat and sensible capital allocation. Leverage of 0.74 debt-to-equity is reasonable, and a current ratio below one is normal for an insurer holding float. At 23 times earnings you are paying a fair price rather than a bargain, but a wonderful business at a fair price is a deal I'd take and hold for ten years, while watching for regulatory risk to those thin margins.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Gross margins have widened from 38% to 44%, operating margins hold near 30%, and free cash flow per share of $6.30 exceeds reported earnings. The shrinking book value and 150%+ ROE reflect heavy buybacks rather than trouble, and I'm comfortable with that. But revenue has gone flat to slightly down over the last three periods, and EPS has sat around $6 for two years. Paying nearly 29 times earnings, roughly a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield, for a business that isn't currently growing leaves little margin of safety. I'd happily keep owning it, but at this price I wouldn't be pounding the table to buy more.

I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but the market is already charging for much of that future, so I'll admire it and wait for a fatter pitch rather than swing here.

ROE has climbed from the high-20s to 45% on modest leverage (D/E 0.51), EPS has risen from 6.00 to 10.06, and free cash flow per share consistently exceeds earnings, so owners are receiving real cash. Book value creeps up only about 5% a year, which tells me management is sensibly returning that cash rather than hoarding it. At roughly 27 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 4%, this is no bargain, but it is a fair price for a wonderful business compounding at double digits, and I'd be comfortable owning it for ten years.

For nearly five years this was a fine franchise. Return on equity held steady around 23-25% on razor-thin but dependable 6% net margins, book value per share compounded about 12% a year, and revenue growth accelerated into the low teens. That kind of consistency usually means scale advantages in a business customers can't easily leave. But the latest period shows real cracks: earnings per share fell from $23.86 to $16.38, free cash flow per share collapsed from $27 to $11, net margin slipped to 4%, book value per share dipped, and debt-to-equity climbed to 0.88. At nearly 31 times depressed earnings, or roughly 21 times the prior peak, I'd be paying a full price for a recovery that isn't yet in hand, so I'll wait for either evidence that the margin damage is temporary or a price that pays me for the risk.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins have climbed steadily from 38% to 46%, operating margins hold near 31%, and free cash flow of about $6.59 a share exceeds reported earnings. The sky-high ROE and shrinking book value reflect aggressive repurchases rather than weakness, and the leverage looks manageable against that cash generation. What gives me pause is price: at roughly 28.5 times earnings, about a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a growth multiple while revenue has been flat to slightly down for six straight periods and EPS has barely moved in two years. It's a great company at a full price, so I'd be happy to own it but wouldn't chase it here.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I know. ROE has run between 34% and 45%, operating margins have widened from 34% to 45%, and debt/equity has fallen from 0.71 to 0.26 while book value per share compounded at about 22%. The price asks a great deal, though: about 35 times earnings, and free cash flow of $9.45 a share gives an owner's yield of only about 2.4%. Free cash flow per share has also grown much more slowly than reported earnings over the last couple of years, and the current ratio has dropped from nearly 3 to 1.24, which tells me heavy reinvestment is soaking up cash. I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but at today's price the margin of safety is thin, so I'd admire it and wait for a better pitch rather than swing now.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Returns on equity have climbed back to 28%, gross margins have held at 54-57% for twenty periods, and operating margins are widening again to 29%. All of that comes with essentially no debt (D/E 0.05) and a current ratio above 2, and revenue growth has re-accelerated to 12%. At about 26 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3%, I'm paying a fair price rather than a bargain. What tempers my enthusiasm is that free cash flow per share has stalled at 5.58 while earnings rose, which suggests heavier reinvestment whose returns I can't yet verify. Still, a durable, cash-rich franchise at a fair price is one I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a formidable retailer with real momentum. Gross margin has widened steadily from 40% to 48%, operating margin has recovered from 2% to 8%, ROE is back to 17%, and free cash flow has swung from roughly -$2.9 to +$4.28 per share, all while debt/equity fell to 0.31. But the record is not the steady, predictable one I prize: earnings collapsed into a loss only a few periods ago, net margins still run just 4-6%, and the current ratio hovers near 1. At 50 times earnings and roughly a 2.4% free-cash-flow yield, the price already assumes years of continued margin expansion and double-digit growth, so I'd admire this business from the sidelines rather than pay up for it today.

The economics right now are extraordinary: 75% gross margins, a 53% net margin, an 87% return on equity with little debt, and free cash flow of $15.80 a share that nearly matches earnings. But the record also shows a cyclical business. Just four periods ago, margins were cut roughly in half, ROE fell to 20%, and revenue shrank, so today's earnings, up sharply on 208% revenue growth, may be a peak rather than a plateau I can count on for ten years. Paying 67 times those peak earnings for a $2.8 trillion company leaves no margin of safety. This is a wonderful business at a price that demands perfection, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This business has done remarkable things. It went from losses and 1.7x debt/equity to a near debt-free balance sheet, and book value compounded handsomely. But the moat is being tested in plain sight: gross margin has slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin has halved from 17% to 8%, and revenue growth has cooled from 60%+ to 10%. That is what price competition looks like, not pricing power. Free cash flow per share has dropped to $0.40 against reported EPS of $3.91, which makes the earnings quality questionable. Paying $517B, 41 times earnings and well over 100 times free cash flow, for a manufacturer with shrinking margins asks for perfection I can't count on, so I'll pass.

This is a finance and insurance business whose reported earnings swing wildly. EPS ran from -10 to +46, which looks like mark-to-market noise on an investment portfolio rather than trouble in the underlying operations. Look past the noise and book value per share has compounded at about 12% a year, rising from roughly 156 to 265 over the period, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about 9 to 14 without a single down year of consequence. At about 12 times trailing earnings and roughly 1.5 times book (a price of about 405 per share against book of 265), I'm paying a fair price for a well-capitalized compounder. My caveats: ROE averaging only 11% shows the sheer size of the equity base is a drag, and the data give no view of leverage, so I'm confident rather than exuberant.

This business keeps about 81 cents of gross profit on every revenue dollar, and that figure has barely moved across twenty periods. It now earns a 31% return on equity and a 32% net margin with debt at only 0.12 of equity and a current ratio near 2.7. Those are the fingerprints of a real moat, though the stretch from t-6 to t-3 is a warning. Revenue went flat, operating margin fell from the low 40s to 24%, and EPS dropped by roughly 40% from its peak, which tells me heavy spending or a soft market can hurt this franchise badly for a while. Still, earnings have recovered to $17.38, above the old high, and free cash flow of $18.86 a share at about 25 times earnings gives an owner's yield of roughly 4%, a fair price for a business growing revenue 22%. That is a wonderful company at a sensible price, and I'd hold it for ten years, but with eyes open to management's appetite for big reinvestment bets.

Still, a durable, cash-rich franchise at a fair price is one I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is a formidable retailer with real momentum. Gross margin has widened steadily from 40% to 48%, operating margin has recovered from 2% to 8%, ROE is back to 17%, and free cash flow has swung from roughly -$2.9 to +$4.28 per share, all while debt/equity fell to 0.31. But the record is not the steady, predictable one I prize: earnings collapsed into a loss only a few periods ago, net margins still run just 4-6%, and the current ratio hovers near 1. At 50 times earnings and roughly a 2.4% free-cash-flow yield, the price already assumes years of continued margin expansion and double-digit growth, so I'd admire this business from the sidelines rather than pay up for it today.

The current numbers are extraordinary: an 87% return on equity, 75% gross margins, little debt, a 3.5 current ratio, and book value per share compounding while free cash flow tracks earnings. That tells me there is real pricing power here, at least for now. But this history also shows a cyclical business: a few periods ago revenue shrank, margins fell by half, and ROE dropped to 20%, and a technology manufacturer growing revenue 208% in a year sits near the edge of my circle of competence. At $2.8 trillion and 67 times what may prove to be peak earnings, the price assumes this boom lasts. I admire the business, but I won't pay a price that demands perfection, so I'll watch from the sidelines.

This business has done remarkable things. It went from losses and 1.7x debt/equity to a near debt-free balance sheet, and book value compounded handsomely. But the moat is being tested in plain sight: gross margin has slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin has halved from 17% to 8%, and revenue growth has cooled from 60%+ to 10%. That is what price competition looks like, not pricing power. Free cash flow per share has dropped to $0.40 against reported EPS of $3.91, which makes the earnings quality questionable. Paying $517B, 41 times earnings and well over 100 times free cash flow, for a manufacturer with shrinking margins asks for perfection I can't count on, so I'll pass.

This is a finance and insurance business whose reported earnings swing wildly. EPS ran from -10 to +46, which looks like mark-to-market noise on an investment portfolio rather than trouble in the underlying operations. Look past the noise and book value per share has compounded at about 12% a year, rising from roughly 156 to 265 over the period, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about 9 to 14 without a single down year of consequence. At about 12 times trailing earnings and roughly 1.5 times book (a price of about 405 per share against book of 265), I'm paying a fair price for a well-capitalized compounder. My caveats: ROE averaging only 11% shows the sheer size of the equity base is a drag, and the data give no view of leverage, so I'm confident rather than exuberant.

This business keeps about 81 cents of gross profit on every revenue dollar, and that figure has barely moved across twenty periods. It now earns a 31% return on equity and a 32% net margin with debt at only 0.12 of equity and a current ratio near 2.7. Those are the fingerprints of a real moat, though the stretch from t-6 to t-3 is a warning. Revenue went flat, operating margin fell from the low 40s to 24%, and EPS dropped by roughly 40% from its peak, which tells me heavy spending or a soft market can hurt this franchise badly for a while. Still, earnings have recovered to $17.38, above the old high, and free cash flow of $18.86 a share at about 25 times earnings gives an owner's yield of roughly 4%, a fair price for a business growing revenue 22%. That is a wonderful company at a sensible price, and I'd hold it for ten years, but with eyes open to management's appetite for big reinvestment bets.

This is a toll-road business. Operating margins have held around 63-67% and net margins above 50% for twenty straight periods, and it kept those margins even when revenue fell 11% in the downturn. That kind of stability shows real pricing power and a network moat. ROE has climbed from the high-20s to 45% on modest leverage (D/E 0.51), EPS has risen from 6.00 to 10.06, and free cash flow per share consistently exceeds earnings, so owners are receiving real cash. Book value creeps up only about 5% a year, which tells me management is sensibly returning that cash rather than hoarding it. At roughly 27 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 4%, this is no bargain, but it is a fair price for a wonderful business compounding at double digits, and I'd be comfortable owning it for ten years.

For nearly five years this was a fine franchise. Return on equity held steady around 23-25% on razor-thin but dependable 6% net margins, book value per share compounded about 12% a year, and revenue growth accelerated into the low teens. That kind of consistency usually means scale advantages in a business customers can't easily leave. But the latest period shows real cracks: earnings per share fell from $23.86 to $16.38, free cash flow per share collapsed from $27 to $11, net margin slipped to 4%, book value per share dipped, and debt-to-equity climbed to 0.88. At nearly 31 times depressed earnings, or roughly 21 times the prior peak, I'd be paying a full price for a recovery that isn't yet in hand, so I'll wait for either evidence that the margin damage is temporary or a price that pays me for the risk.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I know: 70% gross margins that have widened over five years, operating margins climbing from 35% to 45%, returns on equity in the mid-30s with little debt, and book value per share compounding above 20% a year. The trouble is the price. At roughly 36 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 2.3%, with free cash flow per share ($9.92) now trailing reported EPS ($11.80), the market is already paying for many years of flawless execution. I'd be delighted to own this business for a decade, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than pay a price that leaves no margin of safety.

This looks like a large, well-run financial franchise. It has earned 13-17% on equity through most of the cycle and dipped only to about 9-10% in its worst stretch without ever losing money, while book value per share compounded from about $82 to $117, roughly 8% a year. At about 11.6 times earnings and roughly 1.6 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business that earns about 15% on its capital, and the leverage is modest for a bank. I temper my enthusiasm because bank balance sheets are hard to see into from summary data, and the recent 19-25% revenue growth likely reflects a favorable rate environment that may not last. A credit cycle could also pull that 31% net margin down the way it did before.
