I'd happily own this franchise at a sensible price, but at this one the math leaves no margin of safety, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This business did something remarkable, climbing from losses and heavy debt to a fortress balance sheet (D/E 0.08, current ratio 1.91) with book value compounding nicely. But the moat is eroding before my eyes: gross margin has slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin from 17% to 7%, and revenue growth has stalled to 1%. That is what price competition looks like, not pricing power. Net margin of 13% sitting above a 7% operating margin, and free cash flow of just $0.49 a share against $3.56 of reported EPS, tell me the headline earnings flatter the true owner earnings. Paying 60 times those earnings for a manufacturer whose economics are deteriorating demands perfection, and I'd rather watch from the sidelines.

This looks like a large, well-run banking franchise. Over roughly twenty periods it has earned mid-teens returns on equity, and book value per share has compounded about 8% a year through a rate shock and a credit scare. Earnings dipped to about 9-10% ROE in the tough stretch and then recovered to 16%, which is the resilience I want from a lender. At 11 times earnings and about 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a durable business, though not a bargain one. My caution is that the recent 16-25% revenue growth likely reflects a favorable interest-rate backdrop that won't last forever, and a bank's leverage means I must trust management's credit discipline. The steady book-value record gives me reason to do so.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I know: 70% gross margins that have widened over five years, operating margins climbing from 35% to 45%, returns on equity in the mid-30s with little debt, and book value per share compounding above 20% a year. The trouble is the price. At roughly 36 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 2.3%, with free cash flow per share ($9.92) now trailing reported EPS ($11.80), the market is already paying for many years of flawless execution. I'd be delighted to own this business for a decade, but I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than pay a price that leaves no margin of safety.

This is a wonderful business. Returns on equity run well above 100%, gross margins have widened from 38% to 46%, and free cash flow per share has more than doubled over the period. The shrinking book value and the debt/equity ratio of 1.5 reflect aggressive buybacks funded by abundant cash, not distress. But revenue has been flat for roughly six periods, and EPS has crept up only from about $5.90 to $6.57, while the market has bid the price up to 33 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of about 3%. I'd be delighted to own this business for ten years, but at a price that assumes growth the recent numbers aren't showing, I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than swing here.

This is a remarkable business right now: 76% gross margins, 55% net margins, ROE above 90%, very little debt, a current ratio over 4, and book value per share compounding at over 40% a year. But the record also shows a cyclical, technology-driven business. Just a few periods ago, revenue shrank, operating margins fell to 16% and ROE to 20%, so I can't treat today's peak economics as a durable moat I fully understand. The headline P/E of 9.76 doesn't square with the other figures. The EPS jump from 1.71 to 12.87 isn't matched by book value or free cash flow per share, so I suspect a share-count artifact. On free cash flow of about $1.88 a share, a $3 trillion price looks closer to the prior 60-70 times earnings, which prices in perfection. It's a wonderful business at a price that leaves no margin of safety, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Returns on equity have climbed back to 29% on almost no debt (D/E 0.05). Gross margins hold steady around 57% while operating margins widened from 25% to 30%. Book value per share has compounded about 12% a year, and revenue growth has re-accelerated to 13%. At roughly 25 times earnings, or a 4% earnings yield, with earnings per share up nearly 50% in four periods, the price looks fair rather than cheap. My main caution is that free cash flow per share has slipped from 6.19 to 4.86 even as reported earnings rose, which tells me heavy reinvestment is under way. I'd want to see that spending earn its keep, and the technology keeps this near the edge of my circle of competence. Still, a fortress balance sheet, pricing power and a fair price make it a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

The business is clearly getting better. Gross margin has widened from about 40% to 48%, operating margin has tripled from 3% to 9%, and free cash flow per share has gone from minus $2.93 to plus $4.51 while debt-to-equity fell from 0.48 to 0.27. That tells me management tightened the ship after a heavy spending cycle, and a moat is showing through. But this is still a retailer with a 7% net margin, a current ratio barely above 1, and a history of burning cash when it chases growth. At roughly 40 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 3%, I'm paying today for a decade of flawless execution. I'd call it a wonderful business at a full price, and I'm happy to wait for a fatter pitch (the odd $62 EPS figures a couple of years back look like a share-count artifact, not real earnings).

This business shows the marks of a real moat: gross margins pinned near 80% for twenty periods, returns on equity now around 33%, and free cash flow that closely tracks reported earnings. The earlier stumble, when operating margins fell from 43% to 24% and the stock sold at 9 times earnings, showed that management will spend heavily and that results can swing. But the franchise came back stronger, with EPS more than doubling to 19.55 while debt stayed modest at 0.12 debt-to-equity and the current ratio stayed near 2.8. At about 25 times earnings, or roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, for a business growing revenue 24% at these margins, I'd call it a wonderful company at a fair price. My conviction is tempered by that history of lumpy reinvestment and by how hard it is to judge a moat in this kind of business ten years out.

This looks like a diversified financial and insurance enterprise whose reported earnings swing on mark-to-market investment gains and losses. That explains the lumpy EPS, ranging from -10 to +46 per share, and I'd tell you to ignore it. What matters is that book value per share has compounded at roughly 12% a year, from about 163 to 279, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about 8.9 to 15.0 without a single real stumble. Implied price to book is modest, near 1.5x, and the stock trades around 13x earnings with ROE averaging about 11%. That is a fair price for a durable, conservatively run compounder rather than a bargain, and without debt or liquidity figures I'm leaning on the steady book and cash-flow record. Still, I'd be comfortable owning it for ten years.

Just a few periods ago, revenue shrank, operating margins fell to 16% and ROE to 20%, so I can't treat today's peak economics as a durable moat I fully understand. The headline P/E of 9.76 doesn't square with the other figures. The EPS jump from 1.71 to 12.87 isn't matched by book value or free cash flow per share, so I suspect a share-count artifact. On free cash flow of about $1.88 a share, a $3 trillion price looks closer to the prior 60-70 times earnings, which prices in perfection. It's a wonderful business at a price that leaves no margin of safety, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This is a wonderful business on the numbers. Returns on equity have climbed back to 29% on almost no debt (D/E 0.05). Gross margins hold steady around 57% while operating margins widened from 25% to 30%. Book value per share has compounded about 12% a year, and revenue growth has re-accelerated to 13%. At roughly 25 times earnings, or a 4% earnings yield, with earnings per share up nearly 50% in four periods, the price looks fair rather than cheap. My main caution is that free cash flow per share has slipped from 6.19 to 4.86 even as reported earnings rose, which tells me heavy reinvestment is under way. I'd want to see that spending earn its keep, and the technology keeps this near the edge of my circle of competence. Still, a fortress balance sheet, pricing power and a fair price make it a business I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

The business is clearly getting better. Gross margin has widened from about 40% to 48%, operating margin has tripled from 3% to 9%, and free cash flow per share has gone from minus $2.93 to plus $4.51 while debt-to-equity fell from 0.48 to 0.27. That tells me management tightened the ship after a heavy spending cycle, and a moat is showing through. But this is still a retailer with a 7% net margin, a current ratio barely above 1, and a history of burning cash when it chases growth. At roughly 40 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 3%, I'm paying today for a decade of flawless execution. I'd call it a wonderful business at a full price, and I'm happy to wait for a fatter pitch (the odd $62 EPS figures a couple of years back look like a share-count artifact, not real earnings).

This business shows the marks of a real moat: gross margins pinned near 80% for twenty periods, returns on equity now around 33%, and free cash flow that closely tracks reported earnings. The earlier stumble, when operating margins fell from 43% to 24% and the stock sold at 9 times earnings, showed that management will spend heavily and that results can swing. But the franchise came back stronger, with EPS more than doubling to 19.55 while debt stayed modest at 0.12 debt-to-equity and the current ratio stayed near 2.8. At about 25 times earnings, or roughly a 4% free-cash-flow yield, for a business growing revenue 24% at these margins, I'd call it a wonderful company at a fair price. My conviction is tempered by that history of lumpy reinvestment and by how hard it is to judge a moat in this kind of business ten years out.

This looks like a diversified financial and insurance enterprise whose reported earnings swing on mark-to-market investment gains and losses. That explains the lumpy EPS, ranging from -10 to +46 per share, and I'd tell you to ignore it. What matters is that book value per share has compounded at roughly 12% a year, from about 163 to 279, and free cash flow per share has climbed steadily from about 8.9 to 15.0 without a single real stumble. Implied price to book is modest, near 1.5x, and the stock trades around 13x earnings with ROE averaging about 11%. That is a fair price for a durable, conservatively run compounder rather than a bargain, and without debt or liquidity figures I'm leaning on the steady book and cash-flow record. Still, I'd be comfortable owning it for ten years.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have widened from about 75% to 81%, returns on equity have stayed high, and revenue growth has picked up to 32% with net margins recovering toward 19%. But at 104 times earnings and an $803 billion market cap, I'd be paying for perfection, and free cash flow per share has fallen from around $6-7 to just $0.29 as the company spends heavily and leans on debt (D/E 2.13). I'd happily own this franchise at a sensible price, but at this one the math leaves no margin of safety, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This business did something remarkable, climbing from losses and heavy debt to a fortress balance sheet (D/E 0.08, current ratio 1.91) with book value compounding nicely. But the moat is eroding before my eyes: gross margin has slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin from 17% to 7%, and revenue growth has stalled to 1%. That is what price competition looks like, not pricing power. Net margin of 13% sitting above a 7% operating margin, and free cash flow of just $0.49 a share against $3.56 of reported EPS, tell me the headline earnings flatter the true owner earnings. Paying 60 times those earnings for a manufacturer whose economics are deteriorating demands perfection, and I'd rather watch from the sidelines.

This looks like a large, well-run banking franchise. Over roughly twenty periods it has earned mid-teens returns on equity, and book value per share has compounded about 8% a year through a rate shock and a credit scare. Earnings dipped to about 9-10% ROE in the tough stretch and then recovered to 16%, which is the resilience I want from a lender. At 11 times earnings and about 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a durable business, though not a bargain one. My caution is that the recent 16-25% revenue growth likely reflects a favorable interest-rate backdrop that won't last forever, and a bank's leverage means I must trust management's credit discipline. The steady book-value record gives me reason to do so.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick: 69-70% gross margins, operating margins that have widened from 37% to 44%, returns on equity above 30%, debt-to-equity cut from 0.63 to 0.16, and book value per share compounding at about 23% a year. This is plainly a wonderful franchise. That is the signature of real pricing power. But the owner's cash tells a less comfortable story: free cash flow per share has fallen from around $6-7 to $1.55 as the company pours money into growth, debt-to-equity sits at 2.19, and EPS has only just climbed past the level it reached years ago. At roughly 92 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 0.2%, the price assumes everything goes right for a decade, so I'd admire this business from the sidelines until the price offers a margin of safety.

This looks like a large, well-run bank, and banking is understandable if you respect the leverage. Returns on equity have held around 15-16% for the last several years. They fell to 9-10% in a stressed stretch and then recovered, which is what a franchise with a real deposit and scale advantage should do. Revenue growth is slowing from 25% to 13% and margins may give back some rate-driven gains, so I'd own it with moderate rather than full conviction.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick: 69-70% gross margins, operating margins that have widened from 37% to 44%, returns on equity above 30%, debt-to-equity cut from 0.63 to 0.16, and book value per share compounding at about 23% a year. But at roughly 36 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share stuck near $9.50-9.90 for the last four periods while reported EPS kept rising, I'm paying up front for growth that increasingly depends on heavy reinvestment. ROE has also slid from 45% to 31% as equity piles up. A free cash flow yield of about 2.3% leaves little margin of safety, so I'd be glad to own it at a better price but won't stretch for it here.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I know. Gross margins have widened from 38% to 46%, operating margins sit above 30%, and free cash flow per share has nearly doubled over the period. The sky-high ROE and shrinking book value come mainly from management handing enormous sums back to owners through buybacks, not from any weakness in the business. But revenue has been essentially flat for about two years, and EPS actually slipped from 6.57 to 6.08. Yet the market asks nearly 37 times earnings, a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 3%, for a company that isn't currently growing, and at that price you are paying for perfection. I'd be delighted to own it for ten years, but I'd rather wait for a fairer price than chase it here.

The current numbers are remarkable: 76% gross margins, 63% operating margins, ROE near 96%, little debt and a current ratio above 4. But the record also shows how fast this can turn. Only a few periods back, revenue shrank, margins roughly halved and ROE fell to 20%, which tells me this is a cyclical technology business whose future I can't confidently predict ten years out. The reported P/E of about 11 doesn't square with the rest of the data. Book value of $2.69 a share and a 96% ROE imply earnings nearer $2.50 a share, which puts the real multiple around 55-60 times earnings at the peak of a boom with revenue up 152%. That is a wonderful business at a price that assumes the good times last, so I'll stand aside rather than bet against it or pay up for it.

This business has 81% gross margins that have held steady for twenty periods, a 36% net margin, a 34% return on equity, debt at only 0.18 of equity and a current ratio of 2.73. Those are the marks of a real moat with pricing power, and earnings per share have compounded from about $6.43 to $21.19. What gives me pause is the stretch around t-8 to t-6, when operating margin fell from 43% to 24% and earnings per share dropped roughly 40%. It tells me management is willing to spend enormous sums on bets I can't evaluate from these numbers, and the recent rise in leverage suggests the spending hasn't stopped. At about 27 times earnings and a free cash flow yield near 3.5%, with revenue still growing 23%, I'd call the price fair for a wonderful business rather than a bargain, so I lean bullish but with measured conviction.

This is a financial and insurance enterprise whose reported earnings swing widely, from losses at t-7 to a 0.42 net margin at t-14. That volatility looks like marks on an investment portfolio rather than trouble in the business, so book value is the yardstick to watch. Book value per share has compounded steadily from about 174 to 292 over the period, roughly 11% a year, with only a couple of shallow dips. Revenue has grown in most periods, which tells me the underlying operations are healthy. At a P/E near 9 on the latest earnings, the price works out to roughly 1.5 times book, a fair price for a business compounding owner capital at low double digits. My reservations are real: free cash flow per share is modest against the price, leverage and balance-sheet detail are missing, and a company approaching a trillion dollars in value will find it hard to keep compounding at 11%. Even so, I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade at today's price.

Wonderful as the business looks today, I'd rather watch than pay a price that demands perfection.

This business has lifted return on equity from the mid-teens to 31% with almost no debt (D/E 0.04), while gross margins crept up to 58% and operating margins widened from 20% to 32%. That is the fingerprint of a real moat with pricing power and operating leverage, not borrowed returns. Book value per share has compounded at about 13%, and revenue is still growing 14% at enormous scale, so at roughly 24 times earnings, about a 4.2% earnings yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business. My main reservation is that free cash flow per share ($5.85) trails reported earnings ($8.04), meaning heavy reinvestment has to earn its keep, but the balance sheet and returns give me comfort owning this for a decade.

This is a remarkable business on the mend. Gross margins have widened steadily from 40% to 49%, operating margins have climbed from 2% to 11%, ROE is back above 20%, and debt-to-equity has fallen from 0.48 to 0.20. Those are the fingerprints of real scale advantages and pricing power, and management has plainly tightened the ship since the loss period. But at 41 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share falling from $4.51 to $3.07 as spending ramps, the owner earns only about a 1.3% cash yield on a $2.4 trillion price. That price assumes years of flawless execution, so I'd admire this wonderful company from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a remarkable economic engine: 82% gross margins that have held steady for twenty periods, operating margins back above 40%, ROE of 34% on a balance sheet with only 0.16 debt-to-equity and a near 3x current ratio. The history also shows a sharp stumble, when revenue growth went negative, net margins fell to 18% and the market cap was cut by more than half, and a second, rarer thing, a recovery to record EPS of $23.86 with revenue again growing 22%. That tells me the franchise is durable, though management showed it will spend very heavily, and free cash flow per share now trails reported earnings, a trend I'd watch. At roughly 29 times earnings and about a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full but fair price for a wonderful business rather than getting a bargain, so my conviction is real but measured.

Reported earnings here swing about, including losses at t-8 and t-9 that look like mark-to-market noise rather than operating failure. What an owner should watch is book value per share, which roughly doubled from about $153 to $301 over this stretch, around 15% a year, and it held up even through the loss periods. At about 12 times trailing earnings and roughly 1.65 times book (implied from EPS, P/E and BVPS), you're paying a fair price for a business that has proven it can compound shareholder capital, though not a bargain one. I'd note the recent slide in free cash flow per share from about $15 to $5 and revenue growth slowing to 2%, and without debt or balance-sheet detail I'm holding my conviction to moderate. Still, this looks like something I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. Gross margins have widened from 74% to 81%, net margins sit near 24%, revenue is growing over 30% a year, and returns on equity are outstanding. That combination points to real pricing power and a durable moat. But at 74 times earnings, with free cash flow of just $4.16 a share against $11.71 of reported earnings (well under a 1% cash yield on the price), and with debt-to-equity climbing back to 2.4, the market is already paying for years of flawless execution. A great business at a price that demands perfection earns my admiration, not my capital, so I'll sit on my hands and wait for a fatter pitch.

This business once earned 27% gross margins and a 28% return on equity while growing revenue 60-70% a year. Today gross margin is 18%, operating margin is 7%, ROE is 10%, revenue growth has stalled at about 1%, and EPS has fallen from 3.65 to 2.04 in a single period, so whatever moat looked evident has not held against competition and price cuts. The balance sheet is admirably clean (debt/equity 0.08, current ratio 2.0) and book value has compounded nicely, but at $1.29 trillion and nearly 200 times earnings, the price assumes a renaissance that the recent numbers do not support. When a shrinking-margin business is priced for perfection, I'd rather stand aside and wait.

This looks like a top-tier bank. Return on equity has held at 13-17% through the whole cycle, net margins run above 30%, and book value per share has compounded steadily from about $86 to $123 without a single meaningful setback. That is the mark of a durable franchise run by people who allocate capital sensibly. Earnings per share have more than doubled, but some of that surely reflects a favorable interest-rate climate. At 14 times earnings and roughly 2.2 times book, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain one, noticeably richer than the 8-11x multiples of recent years. A wonderful business at a fair price is still worth owning for a decade, so I lean bullish, tempered by the leverage inherent in banking and the risk that peak-cycle earnings normalize.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have held at 68-70% for five years, operating margins have widened from 37% to 45%, net margins run around 35%, and book value per share has compounded at about 23% while debt/equity fell from 0.58 to 0.15. That is a real moat run by people who know how to allocate capital. But the price already assumes all of that: at about 36 times earnings the earnings yield is under 3%, and free cash flow of $9.38 a share gives a yield near 2%. Free cash flow has actually slipped for two periods, lagging EPS of $12.41, and ROE has drifted down from 44% to 31%, which suggests heavy reinvestment whose returns are not yet proven. I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but at this price I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than swing.

This is a wonderful business by any measure. Gross margins have climbed from 38% to 47%, operating margins sit above 30%, and free cash flow per share runs consistently above earnings. The sky-high ROE and flat book value reflect a management that sends nearly all its cash back to owners through buybacks, which I admire, though it leaves the balance sheet running with a current ratio below 1 and debt above equity. The trouble is the price. Earnings per share have gone essentially nowhere for three years ($6.03 to $6.30) on revenue growth of 0–3%, yet the multiple has risen from about 26 to 37 times. That leaves a free-cash-flow yield under 2%, which assumes growth the recent record doesn't show. I'd be happy to own this business for a decade, but not at a price that asks for perfection, so I'll wait for a fatter pitch.

The balance sheet is admirably clean (debt/equity 0.08, current ratio 2.0) and book value has compounded nicely, but at $1.29 trillion and nearly 200 times earnings, the price assumes a renaissance that the recent numbers do not support. When a shrinking-margin business is priced for perfection, I'd rather stand aside and wait.

This looks like a top-tier bank. Return on equity has held at 13-17% through the whole cycle, net margins run above 30%, and book value per share has compounded steadily from about $86 to $123 without a single meaningful setback. That is the mark of a durable franchise run by people who allocate capital sensibly. Earnings per share have more than doubled, but some of that surely reflects a favorable interest-rate climate. At 14 times earnings and roughly 2.2 times book, I'm paying a fair price, not a bargain one, noticeably richer than the 8-11x multiples of recent years. A wonderful business at a fair price is still worth owning for a decade, so I lean bullish, tempered by the leverage inherent in banking and the risk that peak-cycle earnings normalize.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have held at 68-70% for five years, operating margins have widened from 37% to 45%, net margins run around 35%, and book value per share has compounded at about 23% while debt/equity fell from 0.58 to 0.15. That is a real moat run by people who know how to allocate capital. But the price already assumes all of that: at about 36 times earnings the earnings yield is under 3%, and free cash flow of $9.38 a share gives a yield near 2%. Free cash flow has actually slipped for two periods, lagging EPS of $12.41, and ROE has drifted down from 44% to 31%, which suggests heavy reinvestment whose returns are not yet proven. I'd be delighted to own this for ten years, but at this price I'd rather wait for a fatter pitch than swing.

This is a wonderful business by any measure. Gross margins have climbed from 38% to 47%, operating margins sit above 30%, and free cash flow per share runs consistently above earnings. The sky-high ROE and flat book value reflect a management that sends nearly all its cash back to owners through buybacks, which I admire, though it leaves the balance sheet running with a current ratio below 1 and debt above equity. The trouble is the price. Earnings per share have gone essentially nowhere for three years ($6.03 to $6.30) on revenue growth of 0–3%, yet the multiple has risen from about 26 to 37 times. That leaves a free-cash-flow yield under 2%, which assumes growth the recent record doesn't show. I'd be happy to own this business for a decade, but not at a price that asks for perfection, so I'll wait for a fatter pitch.

The current numbers are extraordinary: a 92% return on equity, 56% net margins, 75% gross margins, debt at about a tenth of equity, and free cash flow backing the earnings. But the record shows how cyclical this business is. Only a few years back, margins fell to the mid-teens and ROE to 20%, so I'm looking at what may be peak-cycle profits in a technology business whose ten-year economics I can't confidently predict. At $3.2 trillion and roughly 45 times earnings after revenue already more than doubled, the price assumes the boom continues. Wonderful as the business looks today, I'd rather watch than pay a price that demands perfection.

This business has lifted return on equity from the mid-teens to 31% with almost no debt (D/E 0.04), while gross margins crept up to 58% and operating margins widened from 20% to 32%. That is the fingerprint of a real moat with pricing power and operating leverage, not borrowed returns. Book value per share has compounded at about 13%, and revenue is still growing 14% at enormous scale, so at roughly 24 times earnings, about a 4.2% earnings yield, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful business. My main reservation is that free cash flow per share ($5.85) trails reported earnings ($8.04), meaning heavy reinvestment has to earn its keep, but the balance sheet and returns give me comfort owning this for a decade.

This is a remarkable business on the mend. Gross margins have widened steadily from 40% to 49%, operating margins have climbed from 2% to 11%, ROE is back above 20%, and debt-to-equity has fallen from 0.48 to 0.20. Those are the fingerprints of real scale advantages and pricing power, and management has plainly tightened the ship since the loss period. But at 41 times earnings, and with free cash flow per share falling from $4.51 to $3.07 as spending ramps, the owner earns only about a 1.3% cash yield on a $2.4 trillion price. That price assumes years of flawless execution, so I'd admire this wonderful company from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a remarkable economic engine: 82% gross margins that have held steady for twenty periods, operating margins back above 40%, ROE of 34% on a balance sheet with only 0.16 debt-to-equity and a near 3x current ratio. The history also shows a sharp stumble, when revenue growth went negative, net margins fell to 18% and the market cap was cut by more than half, and a second, rarer thing, a recovery to record EPS of $23.86 with revenue again growing 22%. That tells me the franchise is durable, though management showed it will spend very heavily, and free cash flow per share now trails reported earnings, a trend I'd watch. At roughly 29 times earnings and about a 3% free-cash-flow yield, I'm paying a full but fair price for a wonderful business rather than getting a bargain, so my conviction is real but measured.

Reported earnings here swing about, including losses at t-8 and t-9 that look like mark-to-market noise rather than operating failure. What an owner should watch is book value per share, which roughly doubled from about $153 to $301 over this stretch, around 15% a year, and it held up even through the loss periods. At about 12 times trailing earnings and roughly 1.65 times book (implied from EPS, P/E and BVPS), you're paying a fair price for a business that has proven it can compound shareholder capital, though not a bargain one. I'd note the recent slide in free cash flow per share from about $15 to $5 and revenue growth slowing to 2%, and without debt or balance-sheet detail I'm holding my conviction to moderate. Still, this looks like something I'd be comfortable owning for a decade.

This is plainly a wonderful business. Gross margins have widened from 74% to 82%, revenue is compounding above 30% a year, and returns on equity near 70% speak to real pricing power. But I have to weigh what I'm paying. At 65 times earnings, and with free cash flow of only about $4 a share against $12 of reported earnings (a cash yield near 1%), the price already assumes years of flawless execution. Debt at 2.4 times a thin equity base leaves little room for disappointment, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch.

This business had a magnificent run: gross margins reached 27%, ROE hit 28%, and it paid down nearly all its debt, so the balance sheet today is a fortress with debt/equity at 0.07 and a current ratio of 2.0. The last several years tell a different story, though. Revenue growth has stalled at about 1%, gross margin has slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin has fallen from 17% to 7%, and ROE is down to 8%, which looks like a company cutting prices to hold volume rather than one with durable pricing power. Paying roughly 143 times shrinking earnings, about $808 billion for a manufacturer earning single-digit returns on equity, prices in a perfection the recent numbers don't support. I'd happily admire it from the sidelines, but I wouldn't own it at this price.

This looks like a first-rate bank. Return on equity has climbed from about 9-10% in the lean years to a steady 16-17%, net margins hold near a third of revenue, and book value per share has compounded roughly 8% a year on top of whatever was paid out, with no year of losses anywhere in the record. At about 12 times earnings and roughly 2 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a wonderful franchise, an earnings yield near 8%, rather than getting a bargain. Banking is leverage and trust, and today's returns may be near a cyclical high as revenue growth cools from 25% to 12%, so I'd buy with conviction tempered by the knowledge that credit cycles always come back.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I use. It earns 69% gross margins, operating margins that have widened from 37% to 45%, and ROE of about 30% with almost no debt, since debt/equity fell from 0.54 to 0.13. Book value per share has compounded steadily, which tells me management allocates capital sensibly and the moat is real. What gives me pause is that free cash flow per share has sat flat around $9.30–9.90 for four periods while EPS rose to $12.94, and ROE has slid from 45% to 30%, so more of each dollar of earnings is going back into the business with returns yet to be proven. At 30.5 times earnings, and roughly a 2.4% free-cash-flow yield on the implied price of about $395, I'm paying a full price for a great company whose cash generation has stalled, so I'd happily own it but would rather wait for a fatter pitch.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick. Gross margins widened from 38% to 47% over the period and operating margins held near 31-32%. That kind of steady margin expansion tells me customers pay up and competitors can't dent it, and free cash flow per share consistently runs at or above reported earnings. The eye-popping ROE is mostly the product of management shrinking the equity base through heavy buybacks, and I don't mind that given the cash generation, though the sub-1 current ratio and 1.47 debt/equity are a bit leaner than I'd prefer. My hesitation is price: EPS has sat around $6 to $6.50 for roughly three years with revenue growth near zero to 5%, yet the market asks 32 times earnings, about a 3% owner's yield, which prices in growth the recent record doesn't show, so I'd happily hold it but wouldn't reach to buy more here.

The numbers describe an extraordinary business right now. At roughly $3.3 trillion and 43 times earnings, with growth slowing from 208% to 86% and gross margin slipping from 76% to 70%, the price assumes the good times endure. So I'd admire it from the sidelines rather than buy.

This business earns about a 32% return on equity with almost no debt (debt/equity 0.04). Still, at about 18 times earnings, the lowest multiple in this history, you are paying a fair price for a wonderful, fortress-like business, and I'd be comfortable owning it for a decade.

Debt is only 0.08 of equity, and book value per share has compounded at about 15% a year, all signs of a real moat and pricing power. My one reservation is that free cash flow per share ($5.47) has fallen well behind reported earnings ($9.38) as heavy reinvestment ramps up, so I'll be watching closely whether that spending earns the same outsized returns the business has historically delivered.

This is plainly a wonderful business. It earns 82% gross margins and 44% operating margins, returns on equity have climbed back to 37%, debt is modest at 0.15 times equity, and revenue is still growing 19% a year at enormous scale. What gives me pause is the gap between reported and owner earnings. EPS rose from 19.55 to 27.56 over the last four periods, yet free cash flow per share actually slipped from 20.69 to 19.51, and the current ratio has fallen from about 3 to under 2. That tells me heavy reinvestment is consuming the cash, and I can't yet judge the return on that spending. At 28 times earnings, which works out to roughly a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield on about $1.9 trillion, I'd be paying a full price. This business has already shown once, in its earnings slump roughly a decade ago, how quickly margins and the multiple can compress when spending runs ahead of results. So I'd call it a great company at a fair-to-full price and would wait for a better pitch or for evidence the capex is earning its keep.

This is a wonderful franchise by the numbers. This is a sturdy, conservatively run financial enterprise. Book value per share compounded about 12% a year, from roughly $177 to $310, and the business came through a loss period at t-10 and t-11 without damage to the balance sheet. The reported earnings swing widely, which looks like mark-to-market noise, so I judge it on book value and cash generation. On those measures the momentum is fading: book value grew only about 6% over the last three periods, revenue growth is flat, and free cash flow per share has fallen from about $15 to under $4. At roughly 15.7 times earnings and about 1.5 times book, the price is fair for a quality business but not cheap enough to make up for that slowdown, so I'd hold rather than add.

The balance sheet is sound, with debt at 0.06 of equity and a current ratio of 2, and book value per share has compounded nicely. But the business itself is going the wrong way. Paying roughly 182 times shrinking earnings, with a free-cash-flow yield under 1%, is paying for a miracle rather than a business, and I'd rather wait on the sidelines than bet on perfection.

Gross margin has slid to 17%, operating margin to 5%, ROE to 6%, and revenue is shrinking, which tells me whatever pricing power existed has been competed away. The balance sheet is sound, with debt/equity of 0.07 and a current ratio above 2, but a fortress balance sheet doesn't justify paying roughly 310 times deteriorating earnings for a $1.5 trillion company. At that price you are betting on a future that looks nothing like the present numbers. That is speculation, not investment, and I'd pass.

This is a first-class banking franchise. It has earned 15-17% on equity through a full cycle, book value per share has compounded about 8% a year on top of what it paid out, and it kept a 30%-plus net margin even when revenue briefly shrank. That is the mark of a durable moat and disciplined management. But the price has moved from 8-11 times earnings to nearly 15 times, and to roughly 2.25 times book. Meanwhile revenue growth has slowed to 3% and trailing EPS just slipped from 20.38 to 19.50, so I'd be paying a full price for what may be near-peak earnings in a leveraged, cyclical business. It's a wonderful company I'd happily own, but at this price I'd rather wait for a better entry than chase it.

The business economics are remarkable: 83% return on equity, 53% net margins, 70% gross margins, almost no debt, a current ratio near 4.5, and book value per share up roughly fivefold in about two years. But this record comes from a technology manufacturer with a visibly cyclical past. Only about ten periods ago, margins fell to 16%, returns on equity dropped to 20%, and revenue stopped growing, so I can't be sure today's peak economics are the durable norm rather than the top of a boom. Revenue growth has already slowed from over 200% to 65%. At $4.5 trillion and 46 times earnings, the price assumes those peak margins last a long time, which is too much faith for me to pay in a business whose ten-year competitive position I can't confidently predict. It's a wonderful business at a price that leaves little margin of safety, so I'll admire it from the sidelines.

This is a wonderful business by any measure: gross margins steady near 69%, operating margins widening from 39% to 46%, net margins around 36%, revenue still growing 16% a year at enormous scale, and debt down to a trivial 0.12 of equity while book value per share has compounded briskly. What gives me pause is the gap between earnings and cash. EPS has climbed from 8.94 to 14.06 over four years, but free cash flow per share has only moved from 7.98 to 10.45. That tells me the business is pouring far more capital back into itself, which also shows up in ROE sliding from 45% to 29%. At roughly 38 times earnings and something like 50 times free cash flow, a $4 trillion price already assumes that heavy reinvestment will earn handsome returns, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines and wait for a fatter pitch rather than pay up for perfection.

This is a wonderful business. Gross margins have widened from 39% to 47%, operating margins hold steady around 32%, and free cash flow of roughly $6.50 a share comes in like clockwork. This is a formidable business. Gross margin has widened from 40% to 50%, operating margin has nearly quadrupled from its trough to 11%, ROE sits above 20%, and debt/equity has fallen from 0.48 to 0.15, all signs of a real and strengthening moat. What gives me pause is that owner earnings are not keeping up with reported earnings: free cash flow per share has fallen from $4.51 to $0.97 while EPS rose to $7.08, which means a very heavy reinvestment cycle whose returns I cannot yet verify. At roughly 34 times earnings and well under a 1% free-cash-flow yield on a $2.6 trillion valuation, I am being asked to pay handsomely today for capital spending that must pay off later, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines until the price or the cash conversion improves.

This is a wonderful franchise by the numbers. Gross margins hold in the high-60s, operating margins have recovered to 38% after a large acquisition, and free cash flow per share has risen steadily every period, from 2.75 to 5.13. Management clearly knows how to buy businesses and wring cash from them. At a P/E near 94 and a free-cash-flow yield of roughly 1.4%, the price demands years of flawless growth, so this is a great business at a clearly excessive price, and I'd rather wait on the sidelines for a fatter pitch.

This is a large financial enterprise whose reported earnings swing widely, from losses at t-11 to a 42% net margin at t-18. At about 15 times earnings and roughly 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business that has reliably grown owner's equity. The flies in the ointment are revenue growth that has stalled near zero, ROE drifting down to about 10%, and free cash flow per share well below the earlier $13-15 range. Those keep me from pounding the table, but I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

At roughly 69 times earnings, and about a 1.7% free-cash-flow yield on a $1.5 trillion market value, the price already assumes years of flawless execution. A wonderful business at a price that demands perfection earns my admiration, not my money, so I'll stay on the sidelines.

This is a large financial enterprise whose reported earnings swing widely, from losses at t-11 to a 42% net margin at t-18. That pattern suggests mark-to-market investment results, so I judge it by book value, which has compounded at roughly 11-12% a year from $193 to $324 per share with only minor dips. At about 15 times earnings and roughly 1.5 times book, I'm paying a fair price for a business that has reliably grown owner's equity. The flies in the ointment are revenue growth that has stalled near zero, ROE drifting down to about 10%, and free cash flow per share well below the earlier $13-15 range. Those keep me from pounding the table, but I'd be comfortable owning this for a decade.

This manufacturer's economics have gone the wrong way for three straight years. Gross margin slid from 27% to 18%, operating margin from 17% to 5%, and ROE from the high twenties to 5%. Revenue is now shrinking and EPS has fallen from over $4 to about $1. The balance sheet is admirably clean, with 0.08 debt/equity and a 2.16 current ratio, and free cash flow is positive, but that is not a moat. A business earning 5% on equity with falling prices and margins behaves like a commodity producer, and paying 386 times earnings, $1.56 trillion, for a deteriorating franchise is betting on a future the numbers don't show. I'd pass.

This is a bank I can understand. It has earned a steady 15-17% return on equity through a full cycle, kept net margins around 31-33%, and grown book value per share about 8% a year while also paying out capital. That is a sign of a durable franchise run by disciplined managers. Leverage of 1.38x debt to equity is conservative for a financial institution, and earnings per share have climbed from about $9 to $20 over the period. The margin of safety has shrunk, though: the market cap has doubled, the P/E has moved from 8 to 15 (about 2.3x book), and revenue growth has slowed to 3%. So I'd call this a wonderful business at a fair price rather than a bargain, one worth owning for a decade but without the cushion I'd like.

The economics right now are extraordinary: 76% return on equity, 71% gross margins, 56% net margins, almost no debt, a current ratio near 4, and book value per share up roughly sevenfold in a few years. But the record also shows net margins falling to 16% and revenue shrinking not long ago, which tells me this is a cyclical, fast-changing technology business where I can't confidently predict the moat ten years out. At nearly $4.8 trillion and 40 times earnings, with revenue growth slowing from over 200% to 65%, the price assumes the boom lasts. A wonderful business today at a price that leaves little room for a downturn leaves me on the sidelines.

This is a wonderful business by any measure I use. Gross margins have held at about 69% for twenty periods, operating margins have widened from 40% to 47%, and book value per share has compounded from 17.86 to 52.64 while debt/equity fell from 0.43 to 0.10. What gives me pause is that free cash flow per share has stalled around 9.4–10.5 for three years even as EPS climbed to 15.98, and ROE has slid from 45% to 31%. That tells me earnings are being reinvested heavily into the business and are not yet showing up as owner cash. At 30 times earnings, and roughly 46 times free cash flow (a yield of about 2%), the price already assumes that heavy spending pays off handsomely, so I'd be happy to own this at a fatter margin of safety but won't stretch for it today.

This is a wonderful business by any yardstick I know. Returns on equity run well above 100%, and gross margins have crept up steadily from 40% to 47%, which tells me customers aren't shopping on price. Free cash flow per share of $8.33 exceeds reported earnings, and the thin book value and sub-1.0 current ratio look like the product of aggressive buybacks rather than financial strain. My hesitation is the price. At nearly 33 times earnings, and with per-share earnings compounding only about 10% a year over the last three years, I'm getting roughly a 3% earnings yield. That leaves little margin of safety, so I'd be glad to own it but would rather wait for a fairer price than chase it here.

This is plainly a wonderful franchise. Gross margin has widened from 40% to 50%, operating margin has climbed from 2% to 11%, return on equity has recovered to around 19-22%, and debt has fallen to just 0.17 of equity while book value per share compounded handsomely. What gives me pause is cash: free cash flow per share has slid from $4.51 to $0.71 while reported EPS rose to $7.17, which means the business is pouring nearly everything it earns back into capital spending. At 29 times earnings that works out to roughly a 0.3% free-cash-flow yield, so I'd be paying up for owner earnings that haven't shown up yet. It's a great business at a full price with a heavy reinvestment bet I can't yet judge, so I'll watch rather than swing.

This is a wonderful business by the numbers. Returns on equity have held above 30%, margins have widened (net margin rose from about 21% to 33%), the balance sheet carries little debt, and revenue is still growing about 15% a year. But the owner's earnings tell a different story: free cash flow per share has barely moved from roughly $5.58 to $5.99 over eight periods while reported EPS nearly doubled, which suggests heavy reinvestment whose returns I can't yet verify. At 30 times earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 2%, up sharply from 18 times just a few periods ago, the market is already paying for that reinvestment to work, so I'd admire this one from the sidelines until the price or the cash conversion improves.
